title: The End of Consensus Research?
abstract: Consensus is a fundamental problem in distributed computing and at the core of state machine replication (SMR). Despite decades of active human research, discovering practical low-latency solutions to the problem is still open, as it requires combining protocol knowledge, correctness reasoning, implementation, and experimental evaluation. We report on how AI helped us discover A-greement, a new consensus protocol for geo-replicated state machines that significantly outperforms state-of-the-art solutions. Averaged across six deployments with 5 or 9 replicas, A-greement reduces the mean latency of a geo-distributed key-value store over the fastest baseline by 12.2% and 33.3% on write-heavy and read-heavy workloads, respectively, and matches the fastest baseline on read-only workloads. A-greement combines lease-authorized local reads, direct client learning for leader-ordered writes, and a fast fixed-quorum per-key write path, selected according to network topology and workload. At the heart of our discovery lies AI-greement, an agent harness for the "autonomous" discovery, implementation, experimentation, and verification of candidate protocols. AI-greement integrates (1) a concept-oriented protocol knowledge base, (2) a modular implementation skeleton, and (3) a Lean-based verification framework with reusable safety definitions, reference specifications, and proofs. AI-greement is of independent interest: its Lean formalization uncovers several previously unreported vulnerabilities in existing consensus protocols, and it provides guidelines on how domain-specific harnesses can turn general-purpose coding agents into effective tools for (distributed) computing research. Yet we argue that human consensus experts remain essential before, during, and after the search: agents reshape the researcher's role rather than end consensus research.

body_start:
Abstract

Consensus is a fundamental problem in distributed computing and at the core of state machine replication (SMR). Despite decades of active human research, discovering practical low-latency solutions to the problem is still open.
This endeavor is very challenging since it requires combining protocol knowledge, correctness reasoning, implementation, and experimental evaluation.
We report on how AI helped us discover A-greement, a new consensus protocol for geo-replicated state machines that significantly outperforms state-of-the-art solutions.
Averaged across six deployments with 5 or 9 replicas, A-greement reduces the mean latency of a geo-distributed key-value store over the fastest baseline by 12.2% and 33.3% on write-heavy and read-heavy workloads, respectively, and matches the fastest baseline on read-only workloads.
A-greement combines lease-authorized local reads, direct client learning for leader-ordered writes, and
a fast fixed-quorum per-key write path.
It selects replica roles and write paths according to network topology and workload, accounting for both write completion and read waiting.
At the heart of our consensus discovery lies AI-greement, an agent harness for the “autonomous” discovery, implementation, experimentation, and verification of candidate protocols.
AI-greement integrates (1) a concept-oriented protocol knowledge base that explores consensus mechanisms through published protocols, (2) a modular implementation skeleton that structures protocol development, and (3) a Lean-based verification framework with reusable safety definitions, reference specifications, and proofs.
Our harness supports iterative design exploration, using performance measurements and fault-injection feedback to refine protocols.
AI-greement is of independent interest, beyond A-greement. Its Lean formalization uncovers several previously unreported vulnerabilities
in existing consensus protocols.
AI-greement provides guidelines on how domain-specific harnesses can turn general-purpose coding agents into effective tools for (distributed) computing research.
Yet we argue that human consensus experts remain essential before, during, and after the search: agents reshape the researcher’s role rather than end consensus research.

## 1 Introduction

In SMR (SMR) [37, 65], a universal paradigm to build highly-available computing systems, consensus enables replicas to agree on a common sequence of client commands, maintaining consistent state despite concurrent requests and failures.
Consensus is a fundamental building block of modern distributed systems, underpinning replicated databases [17, 71, 30], storage systems [6], cloud coordination services [10] and blockchain infrastructures [8, 81].
Consensus has been an active research area for over four decades.
However, designing and implementing consensus protocols that are both correct and practically efficient remains an exceptionally challenging task [12, 55].
Protocol decisions involving ordering, quorums, recovery, and execution are tightly coupled: an optimization that shortens the common-case path may complicate recovery or introduce subtle correctness violations [12, 70, 64], as we also find for the optimizations of EPaxos Revisited [75] (§ 8). Translating a protocol design into a working system further requires preserving its safety properties throughout implementation optimizations [25, 79, 68], as well as demonstrating performance improvements across diverse network topologies and workloads.
Advancing the state of the art in consensus therefore requires tightly integrating protocol knowledge, correctness reasoning, implementation and experimental evaluation.

The overall question we address in this paper is whether, just like in other fields of computing, AI could help “crack” the consensus problem. More specifically, we aim to come up with a new practically effective solution that would, on the one hand, tolerate, besides failures of the processes, failures of the network (i.e., asynchronous periods) and, on the other hand, expedite decisions in common failure-free executions.
In particular, we ask whether we can develop a consensus protocol that would yield an SMR scheme in which, in the common case, (a) read-only commands complete at a nearby replica and (b) commands with updates take one round trip to a majority of replicas. This would essentially be optimal. Importantly, and unlike many recent AI-assisted results in mathematics and theoretical computer science, we seek a protocol that is practically useful and hence, besides algorithmic design and proofs, consider the implementation, deployment and evaluation as part of the AI-assisted task.

In short, we show in this paper that the answer is positive.
Yet, we highlight the crucial role of the human researcher in the development of an adequate AI agent, the prompting of the agent as well as the certification of the agent’s output. We furthermore argue that this human researcher needs to be a consensus expert to effectively steer and leverage the capabilities of agents.

Recent advances in the capabilities of LLM have indeed enabled coding agents to autonomously perform increasingly complex software engineering tasks [35, 80].
For example, Codex by OpenAI [57], Claude Code by Anthropic [4], and Cursor Agent by Anysphere [5] can navigate repositories, modify code, execute tests, and iteratively refine implementations based on execution feedback.
However, these general-purpose capabilities do not necessarily translate into the autonomous discovery of consensus protocols.
Existing AI-driven systems research frameworks optimize self-contained policies such as schedulers and load balancers in simulators [54, 14], but do not seem an adequate fit for consensus, whose logic is spread across many communicating, failure-prone nodes [14].
Our preliminary experiment in § 2.3 also suggests that a coding agent combined with a frontier LLM, starting from a single existing consensus codebase, finds only marginal improvements.
This gap motivates the need for specific support for consensus research beyond general-purpose coding capabilities.

We present AI-greement, an agent harness that equips general-purpose coding agents with domain-specific support for autonomous consensus research.
AI-greement addresses three key challenges in consensus discovery.
First, synthesizing new protocols requires understanding and combining mechanisms scattered across the consensus literature.
To support this, a concept-oriented protocol knowledge base organizes consensus mechanisms and grounds them in concrete examples from published protocols.
Second, translating novel designs into executable implementations is challenging because consensus mechanisms often have complex protocol states and message flows.
A modular implementation skeleton structures this scheme through well-defined components and interfaces, allowing the agent to focus on protocol-specific logic.
Third, subtle correctness violations can escape conventional testing, which covers only a limited set of message orderings and failure scenarios.
Formal verification closes this gap by proving safety for every execution of a protocol model, but writing such models and proofs from scratch for each candidate is too costly.
A Lean-based verification framework therefore provides reusable safety definitions, reference specifications, and proof libraries, so the agent can obtain machine-checked evidence that its design, as modeled, is safe.
These components work together in an iterative discovery process, where performance measurements and fault-injection results guide the agent toward more efficient and robust designs.

We demonstrate the capabilities of AI-greement through A-greement, a new consensus protocol that significantly outperforms state-of-the-art solutions.
To the best of our knowledge, A-greement is the first consensus protocol that is designed and implemented by an LLM agent.
When replicating a key-value store,
A-greement jointly optimizes read and write latency.
A-greement builds on the quorum-lease local reads of PQL (PQL) [50], generalizes Bodega’s leader-side gating of writes [29] to any replica, and adds a leaderless write path in the style of SwiftPaxos [63].
Its design couples write completion with read availability: for frequently accessed keys, a designated completion owner can continue serving reads while a write is pending; for ordinary keys, clients learn leader-ordered writes directly from acceptor votes; and for infrequently accessed keys, writes can bypass leader ordering through a fixed-majority per-key path.
These paths share rules ensuring that local reads do not miss completed writes.
A planner uses network delays and workload statistics to select replica roles and write paths, accounting for both write latency and the time reads spend waiting behind pending writes.

Averaged across six deployments with 5 or 9 replicas, on write-intensive workloads (50% writes) A-greement reduces mean latency by 12.2% relative to SwiftPaxos, the best alternative, at the cost of a 13.8% higher p99 latency.
On read-dominated workloads (5% writes), A-greement reduces mean and p99 latency by 33.3% and 30.1%, respectively, relative to Bodega, the alternative with the lowest mean latency, with a p99 latency within 3.4% of the best alternative on that metric, SwiftPaxos.
In the common case, A-greement’s reads complete at a single nearby replica, and writes to rarely accessed keys complete in one round trip.
AI-greement completed the discovery process (including the verification) of A-greement in around 24 hours, consuming 778.45 million tokens at an estimated API-equivalent cost of $198.69.

To summarize, we make the following contributions:

• 

We design AI-greement, an agent harness designed for the automated discovery of consensus protocols (§ 3).
AI-greement integrates a consensus knowledge base, a modular consensus skeleton, and Lean-based formalization and verification.

• 

Using AI-greement, we synthesize A-greement, a new consensus protocol “autonomously” designed and implemented by AI-greement.
A-greement combines localized reads, complementary write paths, as well as topology- and workload-aware planning (§ 4,5,6).

• 

We perform an extensive experimental evaluation of A-greement across replica counts, workloads, and network topologies. Averaged across six deployments with 5 or 9 replicas, A-greement reduces mean latency relative to the best alternative by 12.2% and 33.3% on write-heavy and read-heavy workloads, respectively, while matching the best-performing baseline on the read-only workload (§ 7).

• 

Using AI-greement, we describe four previously unreported safety vulnerabilities in existing consensus protocols, found through agent-driven Lean formalization and verification, demonstrating AI-greement’s ability to uncover subtle protocol flaws (§ 8).

• 

We reflect on our results and ask whether this marks the end of human-driven consensus research, based on where our agent succeeded, where it needed human steering, and what remains for researchers to do (§ 10). Our findings imply that a human consensus expert is (still) badly needed. Many of these findings should apply to other (distributed) computing problems, especially when the goal is to discover, formally prove and practically evaluate a solution.

## 2 Background & Motivation

We first provide the background needed to motivate AI-greement by explaining consensus and state machine replication (§ 2.1).
We then describe how LLM agents and their harnesses can solve complex problems (§ 2.2).
Finally, we show that a frontier general-purpose coding agent, given an existing consensus codebase and repeated experimental feedback, rarely improves on existing designs, and we identify the shortcomings that directly motivate the design of our AI-greement (§ 2.3) agent.

## 2.1 Consensus & State Machine Replication

SMR (SMR) implements a fault-tolerant service by maintaining copies of its state at multiple replicas [65].
The service is modeled as a deterministic state machine: a command and the current state uniquely determine the next state and the response.
Clients submit commands and receive their results through the SMR protocol, which coordinates execution across replicas to present the behavior of a single state machine.

This behavior is formalized by linearizability: the responses observed by all clients must be consistent with a single sequential execution of their commands by the state machine, preserving real-time order across clients [26].
Our verification framework uses linearizability, with the corrected definition of Sela et al. [66], as a uniform proof target for all candidate SMR protocols.
Command ordering can exploit commutativity: replicas may choose different execution orders for commuting commands while agreeing on the order of conflicting commands [39, 60].
Two commands commute if exchanging their order from any state leaves both the resulting state and each command’s response unchanged; otherwise, they conflict.

To coordinate command execution, SMR protocols use consensus, in which processes propose values and agree on one of them [38].
For example, consensus can be used to commit commands in an order proposed by a leader, as in Multi-Paxos [38].
It can also establish agreement on command dependencies from which replicas determine an execution order, as in EPaxos [49, 75, 64].

An SMR protocol must also provide liveness: requests from non-faulty clients eventually complete under the protocol’s stated assumptions.
Our verification currently targets safety only; we discuss the extension to liveness in § 10.

The performance of SMR protocols is commonly measured using four metrics.

(i) Mean latency measures the average time between a client submitting a request and receiving its response, while

(ii) tail latency (P99) measures the 99th percentile of request completion times.

(iii) Throughput measures the number of requests completed per unit of time.

(iv) Recovery time measures how long it takes for request latency or throughput to stabilize after the failure of a leader or replica.

Figure 1: The workflow of an LLM agent.

## 2.2 LLM Agents

\Acfp

LLM are neural networks trained on large text corpora to predict the next token given the preceding context.
The underlying transformer architecture was originally developed for natural language tasks such as machine translation [77], and early LLM were primarily used for tasks such as translation, summarization, and question answering [7].
Instruction tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback turned these models into general-purpose conversational assistants, which have been popularized by ChatGPT [56].
As their capabilities improved, LLM also became capable at reasoning and more complex tasks such as writing code, extending their use beyond language tasks [78].

On its own, an LLM can only produce text in response to its input prompt.
Agentic AI removes this limitation by placing the model in a loop with tools and an environment, as shown in Figure 1 [1].
At each step, the model decides on an action, such as reading a file, running a command, or querying a search engine; the action is executed in the environment, and its result is returned to the model as an observation that informs the next decision.
This loop lets an LLM agent pursue multi-step goals, gather information it was not given up front, and correct its own mistakes based on feedback.
Coding agents, such as Codex [57], Claude Code [4], and Cursor Agent [5], apply this paradigm to software development and enable agents to solve complex coding tasks.
Given a task, a coding agent iteratively inspects relevant files, edits code, executes programs, and runs tests, and it revises its approach based on the results until the task is complete.
LLM agents are also increasingly used for scientific discovery [23].
Our objective is to use agentic AI and LLM agents to synthesize and discover new consensus protocols.

An agent harness is the software infrastructure that organizes this interaction between the LLM, its tools, and the environment [53].
At each step, it supplies the model with instructions and relevant context, dispatches the model’s tool calls, and feeds the resulting observations back into subsequent model inputs.
It also manages execution state and stopping conditions across steps.
The model proposes actions and interprets feedback, while the harness makes those actions executable and maintains the interaction loop.
Beyond these general functions, a harness can provide domain-specific knowledge, implementation interfaces, and evaluation tools for a particular class of tasks.
The harness has a large effect on agent performance: changing the harness around a fixed LLM can produce a $6\times$ performance gap on the same benchmark [74].
In this work, we build on this observation by providing a harness specialized for consensus research.

Figure 2: Mean and tail (P99) latency of discovered consensus protocols across 20 search iterations, using the original Codex harness and the GPT-6.1 Sol model (with high reasoning effort).

Unlike AI-greement, this agent receives no curated protocol knowledge: it may search for the state of the art itself, but the codebase includes neither Bodega nor PQL, on which A-greement builds.
This experiment is therefore not a controlled comparison with AI-greement, but an illustration of the difficulties a general-purpose agent faces.

Figure 2shows the mean (left) and tail (P99) latency (right) across the 20 search iterations, with the latency of SwiftPaxos indicated by a blue dotted line.
For reference, the red line reports the latency of A-greement, discovered with the domain-specific support of our AI-greement (§ 4).

We observe an initial latency reduction in the first two rounds, followed by a plateau.
The agent begins with a basic leader-based replication protocol in round 0, in which both reads and writes undergo Paxos-style consensus and execution before clients receive replies.
Our manual inspection of the agent trajectories reveal that the early gains mainly come from applying established optimizations: quorum-validated reads, early write completion, and improved leader placement shorten read and write completion paths.
Later rounds mainly explore secondary engineering optimizations, including batching, message encoding, and caching, which only result in marginal reductions in latency.
Mean latency spikes in round 12 which stems from processing and reply-traffic overhead introduced by periodic snapshot refreshes.
Moreover, we noticed that candidate implementations between rounds 3–14 violate availability despite a surviving majority, due to defects in client registration, recovery transfers, or peer connection handling.
At an offered load of $20\,000$ commands per second, the best candidate achieves $179.87\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}$ mean latency and $289.77\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}$ average P99, averaged across deployments with 5, 9, and 13 replicas.
These results are only marginally better than the corresponding mean and P99 latencies of $196.16\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}$ and $297.62\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}$ , respectively, for SwiftPaxos.

After careful inspection of the traces, we identify three potential problems that limit the ability by the general-purpose agent to discover consensus algorithm with more substantial gains.
conclusion:
Our answer is no; this is just a new beginning.
We believe this work marks a turning point in how consensus research is conducted. The low latency achieved might still be decreased in specific situations we did not focus on. More generally, our consensus solution could be extended to other failure models and settings.
Our results show that AI agents can take on substantial parts of the research process, including retrieving protocol knowledge, designing and implementing candidates, as well as constructing formal arguments and counterexamples.
Human expertise, however, remains essential for defining performance objectives and safety requirements, designing evaluation environments, and reviewing agent behavior and research outcomes.
A crucial question therefore is: how do our results reshape the role of consensus researchers?

title: Quant-Arena: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Quantitative Trading Research
abstract: Quantitative research is an iterative loop: a researcher proposes a market hypothesis, implements it as an executable signal, tests it on historical data, and decides what to keep. Existing benchmarks score formulas, code, or individual trading decisions, leaving open whether large language models (LLMs) can complete this loop and produce strategies that work beyond the research period. We introduce Quant-Arena, a benchmark and public leaderboard for end-to-end quantitative research on real A-share market data. A model constructs features and stock-scoring code, receives feedback only on 2022--2023, and freezes one strategy for assessment on the sealed year 2024. A cash-account evaluator applies trading constraints and costs, including market impact estimated from a simulated order book. Scores are dominated by realized excess return and complemented by signal quality and the diversity of features used by the strategy. We evaluate nine frontier models, among which GPT-6 Astra scores highest; yet no model beats the equal-weight market in 2024. Quant-Arena is open to submissions from any model or agent harness.

body_start:
Abstract

Quantitative research is an iterative loop: a researcher proposes a market hypothesis, implements it as an executable signal, tests it on historical data, and decides what to keep. Existing benchmarks score formulas, code, or individual trading decisions, leaving open whether large language models (LLMs) can complete this loop and produce strategies that work beyond the research period. We introduce Quant-Arena, a benchmark and public leaderboard for end-to-end quantitative research on real A-share market data. A model constructs features and stock-scoring code, receives feedback only on 2022–2023, and freezes one strategy for assessment on the sealed year 2024. A cash-account evaluator applies trading constraints and costs, including market impact estimated from a simulated order book. Scores are dominated by realized excess return and complemented by signal quality and the diversity of features used by the strategy. We evaluate nine frontier models, among which GPT-6 Astra scores highest; yet no model beats the equal-weight market in 2024. Quant-Arena is open to submissions from any model or agent harness.

Figure 1: Quant-Arena evaluates LLMs on complete quantitative research runs. Banners show total scores on the iterative research track.

## 1 Introduction

Quantitative research turns hypotheses about market behavior into executable trading strategies. Researchers construct features from market observations, combine them into predictive factors or signals, and use those signals to build and test portfolios. Large language models (LLMs) are a natural fit for this research loop: they can propose hypotheses, implement them in code, interpret feedback, and revise their approach. Recent systems already explore this potential through interactive alpha discovery and iterative factor search (Wang et al., 2023; Tang et al., 2025; Han et al., 2026).

Existing benchmarks measure different parts of this workflow. AlphaQT-Bench evaluates the correctness of quantitative trading code, while AlphaBench studies the generation, evaluation, and search of formulaic factors (AlphaQT-Bench, ; Luo et al., 2026). StockBench evaluates agents that make sequential trading decisions from market information (StockBench, ). AlphaForgeBench extends evaluation to generating factor and strategy code from natural-language objectives and backtesting it on historical daily market data (Zhang et al., 2026).
To our knowledge, this is the first benchmark on real market data in which models construct features from raw order and trade records, revise their signals using bounded feedback, and submit a frozen strategy for out-of-sample assessment under common trading rules. This setting evaluates feature construction, signal combination, and strategy selection through their joint effect on the final portfolio.

We introduce Quant-Arena, a benchmark for end-to-end quantitative research on real A-share market data (Figure 2). At the input end, model-generated Python programs access raw Level-2 records, including individual orders and trades and order-book snapshots, through a controlled data interface. Models determine which features to construct and how to combine them into daily stock scores. During research, they can evaluate candidate strategies on 2022–2023, inspect the permitted feedback, and revise their code within a fixed budget. Each run then commits one frozen strategy. At the output end, the platform executes that strategy on the sealed year 2024 and measures the portfolio’s returns after trading costs.

Quant-Arena applies common portfolio and execution rules to make these outcomes comparable. Daily scores determine an equal-weight portfolio of the highest-ranked stocks, and a cash-account evaluator applies lot-size constraints and order-dependent costs, including market impact estimated from a simulated order book. Out-of-sample return and excess return over the market provide direct measures of profitability. Risk and signal statistics and the diversity of features used by the strategy provide complementary views of the result. Together, these measurements distinguish finding a predictive signal from turning it into a profitable portfolio.

A common research budget controls how much search each run can undertake. Repeated backtests favor candidates that fit historical noise (Bailey et al., 2017), so the selected strategy must be assessed on data that its research never observed. The platform also records candidate evaluations and final submissions. These records allow us to examine how models use feedback and select strategies alongside their eventual financial outcomes.

Our contributions are:

• 

An end-to-end quantitative research benchmark. Quant-Arena connects feature and signal construction from real market events to the out-of-sample performance of an executable strategy, making the complete research run the unit of evaluation.

• 

A common research and financial evaluation protocol. A bounded research process, frozen strategy submission, and sealed assessment under shared portfolio and trading rules support comparisons of profitability, risk, signal quality, and feature diversity.

• 

An empirical analysis of LLM quantitative research. We evaluate nine frontier models. No model beats the equal-weight market in 2024: the stocks a model ranks highest typically underperform the market average. The strongest model gains mainly by learning when to stay out of the market rather than by selecting better stocks.

• 

A public evaluation platform. Quant-Arena is released as a public arena that accepts submissions from any model or agent harness under the same protocol and sealed assessment.

The public leaderboard also lists Kepler-1, a proprietary strategy developed by Einsia AI.

## 2 The Quant-Arena Benchmark

Quant-Arena evaluates the out-of-sample profitability of stock-selection strategies developed by models from historical market data.

Figure 2: A model constructs features and stock-scoring code from raw market observations, revises candidates using research-period feedback, and freezes one strategy for assessment on the sealed period under common portfolio and execution rules.

## 2.1 Task Formulation

A model receives a research objective, market-data access, and documentation for the data and evaluation interfaces. Within a fixed research budget, it writes a strategy $f$ that constructs features, combines them into predictive signals, and scores stocks. For each trading day $t$ , the strategy computes

 $\mathbf{s}_{t}=f(\mathcal{H}_{t}),$ 

where $\mathcal{H}_{t}$ contains the authorized historical observations available at that time and $\mathbf{s}_{t}$ contains stock scores. The model determines the features and scoring function. A common financial evaluator converts these scores into portfolio positions and returns. The final submission is the frozen strategy program $f$ .

## 2.2 Market Data and Benchmark Construction

We use real market observations from a fixed data release, stock universe, and trading calendar. Models construct features from the raw inputs without a predefined factor library. Missing observations and delisted stocks are retained without redefining daily universe membership.

Table 1: Market data and temporal split used by the benchmark.

Property

Specification

Stock universe

Selected universe of 3,042 stocks

Inputs

Daily market data and raw Level-2 quotes, orders, and trades

Research period

2022–2023

Out-of-sample period

Sealed year 2024

The data interface restricts access by date, instrument, and field. At each decision date, the strategy can access authorized historical observations, including permitted warmup history. The same input definitions and access rules apply during research and assessment.

## 2.3 Research and Assessment Protocol

Models may evaluate candidate strategies on the research period and revise their code using aggregate return, signal-quality and coverage statistics, and execution errors. Each run may evaluate at most five candidates on the research period. Participants may define training and validation splits within the research period; the benchmark prescribes no separate training window.

At the end of research, one strategy’s source code, execution environment, and declared features are frozen. The evaluator applies this strategy once to the sealed out-of-sample period. The strategy accesses the observations needed for execution through the authorized data interface. Neither these observations nor assessment feedback is returned to the model for further development.

## 2.4 Financial Evaluation and Metrics

The evaluator converts stock rankings into an equal-weight long portfolio targeting 75 stocks. The backtest maintains a cash account with 100-share lots, order-dependent trading costs, and market impact estimated from a simulated order book. Idle cash earns zero return, and daily net asset value includes cash and outstanding positions. Account returns are compounded over each evaluation period.

We report out-of-sample annualized return and excess return over a full-market equal-weight reference aligned to the same trading days. The reference is gross of costs. Long-only Sharpe ( $\mathrm{SR}_{\mathrm{L}}$ ) measures risk-adjusted performance, and maximum drawdown measures downside risk. Signal metrics include mean daily RankIC, its annualized information ratio ( $A$ ), long–short Sharpe ( $\mathrm{SR}_{\mathrm{LS}}$ ) between the highest- and lowest-scored deciles, and turnover, the average daily replacement fraction of the portfolio. Daily RankIC is the rank correlation between stock scores and next-period returns; $A$ is its mean divided by its standard deviation, multiplied by $\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{ann}}}$ , where $N_{\mathrm{ann}}$ denotes the number of trading days per year used for annualization.

The published in-sample score combines strategy quality and feature diversity. Let $r$ be the strategy’s annualized return minus the reference’s annualized return, expressed as a decimal. Each metric is mapped to $(0,1)$ by a smooth, monotone transform,

 $g_{c}(x)=\tfrac{1}{2}\left(1+\frac{x}{c+|x|}\right),$ 

which equals $0.5$ at $x=0$ , rewards gains with diminishing returns, and penalizes losses without truncating them to zero. The component scores are

 $\displaystyle s_{\mathrm{R}}$ 
 $\displaystyle=g_{0.3}(r),$ 
 $\displaystyle s_{\mathrm{L}}$ 
 $\displaystyle=g_{1}(\mathrm{SR}_{\mathrm{L}}),$ 
 $\displaystyle s_{\mathrm{LS}}$ 
 $\displaystyle=g_{3}(\mathrm{SR}_{\mathrm{LS}}),$ 

(1)

 $\displaystyle s_{\mathrm{IC}}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\left(1+\tanh\frac{\mathrm{RankIC}}{0.03}\right),$ 
 $\displaystyle s_{\mathrm{ST}}$ 
 $\displaystyle=g_{2}(A),$ 
 $\displaystyle s_{\mathrm{TO}}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\frac{1}{1+\mathrm{Turnover}}.$ 

Quality is a weighted sum that places most of its weight on realized excess return:

 $Q=0.6\,s_{\mathrm{R}}+0.2\,s_{\mathrm{L}}+0.05\left(s_{\mathrm{LS}}+s_{\mathrm{IC}}+s_{\mathrm{ST}}+s_{\mathrm{TO}}\right).$ 

(2)

Excess return and long-only Sharpe measure what the portfolio earned; the four signal terms carry small weights because they vary less across runs and do not by themselves determine portfolio value. A strategy that tracks the market with no excess return and zero Sharpe has $s_{\mathrm{R}}=s_{\mathrm{L}}=0.5$ .

A strategy may declare up to 300 named features. Correlated features are grouped, and $K$ counts the qualifying clusters whose contribution to the strategy’s scores is detected. Diversity is

 $D=Q\,\frac{\min(K,32)}{32}.$ 

(3)

The fixed scale of 32 makes diversity grow linearly with $K$ up to saturation, independently of the 300-feature declaration limit. Diversity scales with quality, so additional features add little to a weak strategy. The in-sample score is

 $S_{\mathrm{in}}=90\,Q+10\,D.$ 

(4)

The out-of-sample score $S_{\mathrm{out}}$ uses the same metric dimensions with an unpublished combination rule fixed for each benchmark version. The overall score is

 $S=0.3\,S_{\mathrm{in}}+0.7\,S_{\mathrm{out}}.$ 

(5)

We report individual metrics alongside the 0–100 scores.

## 3 Experiments

## 3.1 Experimental Setup

Our experiments address five questions. To evaluate how far current models are from a strong research agent, and how reasoning effort changes this, we compare 38 iterative configurations of nine models (Section 3.2). To evaluate why predictive skill does not become profit, we analyze next-day returns by signal decile (Section 3.3). To evaluate whether any strategy adapts to the market regime, we trace Astra’s account and exposure (Section 3.4). To evaluate what iteration contributes, we pair iterative and one-shot runs and follow candidates through the research period (Section 3.5). To evaluate whether models share a trading style, we measure their holding exposures (Section 3.6).

We run Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Terra, Gemini 3.8 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3 in the iterative and one-shot settings at every reasoning effort they support: six levels for Terra, five for Opus, Sonnet, Astra, and Sol, four for DeepSeek, three for Gemini and Kimi, and two for GLM. This gives 38 iterative and 38 one-shot configurations. The one-shot results are in Appendix B. We report the total score $S$ with its research-period and sealed-period components, and for the sealed 2024 window the annualized return (ARR), excess ARR over the gross equal-weight market, mean RankIC, long-only Sharpe ratio, and maximum drawdown. The diagnostics in Sections 3.3–3.6 use, for each model, the iterative configuration with the highest total score (the shaded rows of Table 2).

conclusion:
Quant-Arena evaluates a complete quantitative research run, from constructing features on raw market observations to revising candidates and committing one strategy for sealed financial assessment. A shared stock-scoring interface, portfolio rule, and cash-account evaluator connect model-authored research to comparable simulated outcomes.

Across 38 iterative configurations, the best model scores 51.3 against 77.6 for Kepler-1, a proprietary strategy developed by Einsia AI, and only one configuration, Sol at medium effort, beats the equal-weight market. Pairing each model’s best iterative and one-shot configurations, iteration raises the overall score for all nine models but sealed-period ARR for only four. Decile returns show why: most models rank stocks with some skill, yet the top-ranked names that the portfolio buys earn less than middle-ranked ones, so an average predictive correlation is insufficient to judge an investable strategy. The best-performing Astra configuration profits mainly by staying in cash during the early-2024 decline, which lowers drawdown without beating the market. Candidate trajectories show that research progress comes early and plateaus, and the effort sweep shows that a higher reasoning setting does not consistently improve the result. Together, these findings support evaluating quantitative research through both its development process and the financial outcome of its committed strategy.

title: Multimodal Embodied Agents: A Unified Capability-centric Perspective from Computer-Use to Robot-Use
abstract: Multimodal agents (MMAs) sustain interaction through reasoning, memory, tools, and feedback, most visibly as computer-use agents, while robotic systems (RSs) couple sensing and actuation under physical dynamics. We define multimodal embodied agents (MMEAs) as goal-directed systems that couple multimodal task reasoning with physical action and revise decisions from the resulting feedback. This raises a central question: what changes when a multimodal agent moves from computer-use to robot-use? We introduce PAPAV, a unified capability-centric framework of five recurring functions: Perceive the current state, Anticipate action effects, Plan a feasible course, Act through an interface or body, and Verify the outcome. Defined by function rather than architecture, these capabilities let PAPAV identify what all three share and then compare MMEAs with MMAs and with RSs. Five physical constraints, from partial observability to unverifiable outcomes, leave fewer choices fixed in advance and less room to reverse errors. Across 64 benchmarks, explicit evaluation centers on Act; only 5 assess Anticipate and 3 assess Verify, leaving both largely hidden behind task success. These constraints also frame the open challenges we identify. PAPAV therefore provides a common basis for designing reliable physical agents and measuring progress across all five capabilities rather than task success alone.

Abstract

Multimodal agents (MMAs) sustain interaction through reasoning, memory, tools, and feedback, most visibly as computer-use agents, while robotic systems (RSs) couple sensing and actuation under physical dynamics. We define multimodal embodied agents (MMEAs) as goal-directed systems that couple multimodal task reasoning with physical action and revise decisions from the resulting feedback. This raises a central question: what changes when a multimodal agent moves from computer-use to robot-use?
We introduce PAPAV, a unified capability-centric framework of five recurring functions:
Perceive the current state,
Anticipate action effects, Plan a feasible course, Act through an interface or body, and Verify the outcome.
Defined by function rather than architecture, these capabilities let PAPAV identify what all three share and then compare MMEAs with MMAs and with RSs.
Five physical constraints, from partial observability to unverifiable outcomes, leave fewer choices fixed in advance and less room to reverse errors.
Across 64 benchmarks, explicit evaluation centers on Act; only 5 assess Anticipate and 3 assess Verify, leaving both largely hidden behind task success.
These constraints also frame the open challenges we identify. PAPAV therefore provides a common basis for designing reliable physical agents and measuring progress across all five capabilities rather than task success alone.

Figure 1: A Unified Capability-centric Perspective (PAPAV) from computer-use to robot-use.
Perceive,
Anticipate,

are five functional roles that recur in goal-directed interaction, whether an agent operates a computer (top) or a robot (bottom).
Defined by function rather than architecture, they place both settings on a common coordinate and isolate what changes once actions acquire physical consequences.

## 1  Introduction

Multimodal agents (MMAs) have grown from one-shot generation into systems that interact over time, use external tools, and revise decisions from feedback, and they now operate browsers, desktops, and phones as computer-use agents [217, 213, 168, 171, 186, 239, 198]. Robotic systems (RSs) have followed a complementary path: foundation models and generalist policies increasingly connect language and perception to physical action across a widening range of tasks [4, 79, 108, 37, 14, 13, 88, 150, 149, 12]. Robotics offers a mature account of how to close the loop under physical dynamics [69, 91, 46, 41, 92, 17, 50], while agent research offers ways to sustain the loop through longer interactions [217, 171, 186, 98, 29, 67, 28, 31].

We use multimodal embodied agent (MMEA) for a goal-directed system that uses multimodal evidence to guide physical action and feedback from that action to revise later decisions. Bringing the two traditions together changes more than the action interface. Computer-use agents can draw on structured state and direct feedback supplied by software, while conventional robotic systems can rely on constraints chosen for a known operating setting [239, 198, 216, 17, 50]. Open-ended physical interaction offers neither in full: the same loop becomes less predictable and less forgiving, and more decisions move into the interaction itself. This motivates our central question:
What changes when a multimodal agent moves from computer-use to robot-use?

X

Figure 2: Chronological overview of representative work.
Robotic systems progress from visual foresight and task planning to generalist policies, world models, and multi-site evaluation; multimodal agents from tool-augmented reasoning to GUI grounding and computer-use benchmarks.
The middle trunk appears in 2022 as language-model planners meet robot skills and keeps widening.

A unified basis for cross-domain comparison

Survey taxonomies still tend to follow the field in which they were developed. Surveys of computer-use agents foreground computational architectures and digital interaction [40, 197, 181, 215, 16], whereas surveys of embodied AI, VLA models, and robot autonomy emphasize physical tasks and execution [120, 133, 164, 185]. Several recent accounts cover both computer-use and robot-use [40, 120, 164, 215, 16, 143], but covering both is different from drawing the analogy between them (Table 1): existing categories describe systems within each setting and do not show how the same function changes when its actions acquire physical consequences. The need for such an analogy is growing. Foundation models, world models, and broader robot datasets now connect capabilities that were once developed separately [37, 13, 15, 64, 209, 150, 97], yet strong components do not by themselves form a coherent physical agent. Coherence depends on coordination across the full loop as the environment changes, which calls for a unit of comparison that remains stable across both settings. Figure 2 traces the two research paths and their recent convergence.

A capability view of the task loop

We introduce PAPAV, a unified capability-centric perspective built around five functions in a recurring task loop, the cycle through which an agent advances a task one step at a time. Perceive establishes the current state; Anticipate estimates the effects of candidate actions; Plan selects a feasible course; Act realizes that course through an interface or body; and Verify judges the outcome and whether further interaction is needed. Each function is defined by what it contributes to the loop rather than by the component that implements it: one model may support several functions, and one function may be distributed across several models or tools. A click, a skill call, and a robot trajectory differ in form, but PAPAV asks what each contributes to the same task loop rather than whether the systems share an architecture or action space. PAPAV also sharpens two boundaries often folded into a standard observation–decision–action loop: Anticipate asks what a candidate action may cause before Plan chooses a course, and Verify asks whether post-action evidence supports the intended outcome rather than merely recording another observation. These distinctions make prediction and outcome judgment visible as separate functions while remaining compatible with existing agent and control-loop taxonomies [215, 120, 164, 143, 185].

{forest}

Figure 3: Research landscape and taxonomy of PAPAV.
The capability branch groups representative work by non-exclusive evidence lineages; the benchmark branch groups the curated corpus by primary evaluation target.

The shared coordinate then isolates what embodiment changes. We study five constraints that recur in physical interaction: partial observability, limited simulatability, irreversibility, real-time coupling, and unverifiable outcomes. Together they make the loop less predictable and less forgiving, increasing the weight of what the agent decides during interaction rather than what the interface or system design fixes in advance. Memory and orchestration keep the five functions connected across time; we call this coordinating substrate the agentic harness rather than a sixth capability.

Position and scope of this survey

Our scope spans MMAs, conventional RSs, and their intersection. We borrow computer-use and robot-use as shorthand for the two ends of this transition [198, 83], and use digital and physical throughout the body for the interaction settings along it. Robot-use here covers any configuration in which multimodal task reasoning acts through a robot body, by remote tool-style control or by an end-to-end policy, and is thus broader than cloud-controlled robots alone. The MMA and RS categories are system classes rather than settings, and they overlap. MMAs commonly operate through software interfaces, including games and simulated worlds [151, 186], whereas RSs center body-specific sensing and control, even when evaluated in simulation. We include virtual embodied work when it informs a capability, while whole-system MMEA membership follows the physical task-loop criteria in Section 2.3. The task loop is therefore the unit of comparison: evidence for one capability does not by itself classify an entire system as an MMEA. Table 1 compares related surveys in terms of computer-use and robot-use coverage, benchmark analysis, and digital–physical analogy, highlighting PAPAV’s emphasis on a shared capability perspective across settings.

Contributions

This survey makes three contributions:

• 

A unified capability-centric perspective. PAPAV enables unified comparison of MMAs, RSs, and MMEAs through five functional roles in a task loop, spanning computer-use and robot-use.

• 

A three-way capability comparison. For each capability, we identify what MMAs, RSs, and MMEAs share, then separately analyze MMEA–MMA and MMEA–RS differences.

• 

A capability-level benchmark analysis. We analyze PAPAV coverage in 64 benchmarks, distinguishing explicit capability evaluation from evidence available only through task outcomes. Explicit evaluation concentrates on Act, with few benchmarks isolating Anticipate or Verify.

Figure 3 summarizes the research landscape: its capability branch organizes representative evidence by PAPAV relation and literature lineage, and its benchmark branch organizes the curated corpus by primary evaluation target. Neither placement is a shortcut for whole-system MMEA membership.

Organization

Section 2 defines the shared task-loop setting and PAPAV. Section 3 compares the five capabilities across digital and physical systems, with particular attention to the five physical constraints. Section 4 analyzes benchmark coverage at the capability level, Section 5 discusses open challenges for reliable physical interaction, and Section 6 concludes.

## 2  Background and Problem Formulation

We adopt a task-level loop to compare multimodal agents (MMAs) and robotic systems (RSs). Each step contains one operation that advances the task, the evidence used to select it, and the feedback returned after it. In computer-use, this operation may be a GUI action or tool call. In robot-use, it may be a robot skill, waypoint, or trajectory command that a lower-level controller realizes over time. Working at the task level places both settings on a common time scale: a click and a control tick are not comparable, but a task step is. PAPAV describes five functional roles within this loop. It focuses on what each role contributes rather than how the system is implemented. This abstraction allows us to compare systems with different architectures and embodiments.

## 2.1  Multimodal Agents

A multimodal agent is a goal-directed system that interacts with the environment through multimodal observations and external actions. Its observations may comprise language, images, structured states, and tool outputs. Its actions may involve language generation, GUI operations, API calls, or tool execution. At task step $k$ , the agent selects an action according to $a_{k}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid g,h_{k},m_{k})$ , where $g$ denotes the task goal, $h_{k}$ the interaction history, and $m_{k}$ the persistent memory. The action $a_{k}$ queries or modifies the external environment and yields a new observation $o_{k+1}$ . The resulting observation is incorporated into the interaction history or persistent memory, providing context for subsequent decisions. This process forms a closed interaction loop in which the agent can adjust its behavior based on environmental feedback [217, 213, 198, 236, 171, 186].

## 2.2  Robotic Systems

A robotic system interacts with the environment through sensing and actuation. Its observations may comprise vision, proprioception, force, and tactile signals. Its task-level actions may be represented as skills, waypoints, trajectories, or motion commands. These actions must be grounded with respect to the robot’s embodiment and estimated state. Their execution is further subject to geometric, dynamic, safety, and control constraints [17, 50, 30, 69].

At task step $k$ , this grounding can be expressed as $a_{k}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Exec}_{e}}u(t)$ for $t\in[t_{k},t_{k+1})$ . Here, $\mathrm{Exec}_{e}$ denotes the execution operator conditioned on embodiment $e$ . The control input $u(t)$ may represent joint-position, velocity, or torque commands. This formulation also covers learned and end-to-end policies that implement the grounding process implicitly [14, 13, 12, 21].

## 2.3  Multimodal Embodied Agents

A multimodal embodied agent (MMEA) can be characterized by five PAPAV capabilities: multimodal perception, consequence anticipation, task-level planning, embodied action, and outcome verification. The system maintains task state throughout sensing and execution. Execution feedback informs subsequent decisions. These functions operate as a persistent closed loop between multimodal task processing and physical execution. Observed effects may differ from anticipated outcomes during execution. These discrepancies can prompt the agent to revise its task belief, reassess action feasibility, and adjust the remaining plan. Failure of an individual action does not necessarily imply failure of the overall task. The agent can use available evidence to assess recovery options and select an alternative action consistent with the task goal. At step $k$ , $h_{k}$ denotes the interaction history, $g$ the task goal, and $b_{k}$ the task-conditioned belief. The PAPAV loop can be formulated as:

 $(h_{k},g)\xrightarrow{\mathsf{Perceive}}b_{k}\xrightarrow{\mathsf{Anticipate}}\widehat{\Delta}_{k}\xrightarrow{\mathsf{Plan}}p_{k}\xrightarrow{\mathsf{Act}}(a_{k},\rho_{k})\xrightarrow{T_{d},O_{d}}o_{k+1}\xrightarrow{\mathsf{Verify}}v_{k}\circlearrowleft.$ 

(1)

Here, $\widehat{\Delta}_{k}$ is the predicted task-relevant effect, $p_{k}$ the intended action course, $a_{k}$ the environment-facing action, and $\rho_{k}$ its execution progress. The operators $T_{d}$ and $O_{d}$ denote the transition and observation models of domain $d$ . Verification produces a verdict $v_{k}$ , such as continue, success, retry, replan, or fail. The observation and verdict provide input to the next interaction step.

We classify a system as an MMEA when multimodal task reasoning forms a persistent feedback loop around physical execution. The evaluated system configuration must satisfy three conditions:

1. 

Persistent embodied task loop: task-relevant state persists across successive rounds of physical execution, and selected actions can produce observable changes in the physical environment.

2. 

Task-level capability returns: each claimed PAPAV capability provides a documented output that can influence a subsequent task-level decision within the interaction loop.

3. 

Embodiment-grounded commitments: task decisions explicitly account for physical feasibility, execution timing, and control constraints imposed by the deployed body and operating environment.

A system is indeterminate when evidence for any condition is missing. An explicitly absent condition places the evaluated configuration outside the MMEA class. The criteria apply to complete system configurations and cover both modular and end-to-end implementations.

Embodiment limits the actions available at each task step. Given belief $b_{k}$ and embodiment $e$ , the feasible action set can be expressed as:

 $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{feas}}(b_{k},e)=\left\{a\in\mathcal{A}\,\middle|\,\begin{aligned} &\Gamma_{j}(a,b_{k},e)\leq 0,\quad j\in\{\mathrm{geo},\mathrm{dyn},\mathrm{safe}\},\\
&\tau_{\mathrm{exec}}(a,e)\leq\tau_{\max}\end{aligned}\right\}.$ 

(2)

Here, $\mathcal{A}$ is the space of task-level interventions. The terms $\Gamma_{\mathrm{geo}}$ , $\Gamma_{\mathrm{dyn}}$ , and $\Gamma_{\mathrm{safe}}$ represent geometric feasibility, dynamic feasibility, and safety constraints, respectively. Geometric feasibility covers reachability and collision-free motion. Dynamic feasibility covers motion and actuator limits. Safety constraints capture task- and environment-specific risk bounds. An intervention satisfies a constraint when the corresponding value is non-positive. The term $\tau_{\mathrm{exec}}$ denotes the execution time required by the intervention, and $\tau_{\max}$ the time budget available at the current task step.

conclusion:
A recurring limitation in this corpus is limited evaluation granularity. Multimodal, long-horizon, and interactive tasks increasingly couple several PAPAV capabilities across digital and embodied environments [239, 220, 152, 20], yet aggregate outcomes rarely identify the source of failure. Future benchmarks should retain end-to-end performance while adding attributable signals such as grounding correctness, failure recognition, recovery effectiveness, controlled perturbations, and intermediate checkpoints. RoboCerebra [65] and AgenticLab [59] illustrate how checking and replanning signals can improve failure attribution within the PAPAV loop.

Future benchmarks should test how information passes between PAPAV capabilities and changes later decisions. They should record whether predictions affect action selection and whether execution feedback leads to revised plans. Verification requires particular care because an apparently completed action may not satisfy the task goal. A grasp, for example, may look correct while remaining unstable. REFLECT [122] uses observations of robot execution to explain failures and guide correction. Benchmarks should assess both the accuracy of these judgments and their effect on subsequent behavior.

The evidence available to the verifier is central to this evaluation. A dedicated verifier can specialize in detecting success and failure. A shared model can reuse the actor’s representations and context, which may reduce computation. However, separate models may still miss the same failures if they use the same observations or similar training data. Benchmarks should therefore test whether additional evidence helps the verifier detect errors that the actor overlooks. Such evidence may come from another sensing modality, a physical check, a specialized success detector, or human review.

The actor and verifier should then be evaluated together. Benchmarks should report the fraction of failed executions judged successful and the fraction of successful executions judged failed. They should also identify failure types that both components miss. Detection delay, recovery success, and the extra actions or time needed for recovery show whether verification helps the task. Comparisons should control task conditions and report the resources available to each system. Reference judgments should be established independently of the agent’s verdict. These measures assess both the reliability of verification and its contribution to recovery.

title: Asymmetric On-Policy Distillation Learns In-Context Exploration
abstract: Sequential decision-making under partial observability is difficult because agents must explore to infer hidden, task-relevant information before acting effectively. Learning such information-gathering behaviors tabula rasa via online reinforcement learning is sample-inefficient, whereas offline imitation averages expert actions across hidden states and fails to learn exploration. In this work, we propose ASTEROID, a simple and effective student--teacher supervised learning framework that can learn test-time exploration. Although a privileged expert never needs to explore, we demonstrate that a history-conditioned student can learn to do so when trained with on-policy contexts: the student first collects on-policy context under partial observability, and the privileged expert provides action labels conditioned on that context. By distilling expert actions directly conditioned on the student's on-policy history, the student learns to systematically resolve partial observability, i.e., search while uncertain and exploit once the hidden state is revealed. This enables efficient test-time exploration (similar to Bayesian posterior sampling) without incurring the impractical training-data costs of reinforcement learning. Across a diverse range of eleven different environments, including discrete exploration benchmarks, robotic manipulation, navigation, and Procgen environments, ASTEROID achieves ~2x higher returns under fixed exploration budgets, uses ~100x fewer interactions than RL baselines, and outperforms frontier models at exploration. Finally, our method transfers policies trained in simulation to vision-denied real-world robot manipulation, exhibiting efficient exploration and increasing success by +40% over standard distillation. Overall, it provides a simple yet surprisingly effective framework to learn efficient test-time exploration.

Abstract

Sequential decision-making under partial observability is difficult because agents must explore to infer hidden, task-relevant information before acting effectively.
Learning such information-gathering behaviors tabula rasa via online reinforcement learning is sample-inefficient, whereas offline imitation averages expert actions across hidden states and fails to learn exploration. In this work, we propose ASTEROID, a simple and effective student–teacher supervised learning framework that can learn test-time exploration. Although a privileged expert never needs to explore, we demonstrate that a history-conditioned student can learn to do so when trained with on-policy contexts: the student first collects on-policy context under partial observability, and the privileged expert provides action labels conditioned on that context. By distilling expert actions directly conditioned on the student’s on-policy history, the student learns to systematically resolve partial observability, i.e., search while uncertain and exploit once the hidden state is revealed. This enables efficient test-time exploration (similar to Bayesian posterior sampling) without incurring the impractical training-data costs of reinforcement learning. Across a diverse range of eleven different environments, including discrete exploration benchmarks, robotic manipulation, navigation, and Procgen environments, ASTEROID achieves $\sim$ 2 $\times$ higher returns under fixed exploration budgets, uses up to $\sim$ 100 $\times$ fewer interactions than RL baselines, and outperforms frontier models at exploration. Finally, our method transfers policies trained in simulation to vision-denied real-world robot manipulation, exhibiting efficient exploration and increasing success by $+40\%$ over standard distillation. Overall, it provides a simple yet surprisingly effective framework to learn efficient test-time exploration.

2Work partially done while at Meta

Figure 1: ASTEROID provides a simple and reliable method for learning efficient exploration in partially observed domains via on-policy asymmetric student-teacher distillation.

## 1 Introduction

Sequential decision-making under partial observability is a central challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) [34, 53]. In the real world, from robotics to embodied AI, agents receive only partial, noisy observations of the environment. To act successfully, agents must first explore to uncover hidden, task-relevant information [31, 79, 42, 74, 46, 71]. For example, a household robot searching for an object must use onboard sensing to infer likely object locations, track locations it has already searched, and adapt future exploration based on prior attempts [12, 11, 30]. These problems are formalized as partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) [34].

Solving these tasks requires policies with memory [28, 50]. Learning them from scratch via recurrent RL is sample-inefficient, since the agent must learn to gather information and exploit it at the same time [5, 79, 21]. One way to improve sample efficiency is to assume training-time access to a privileged expert that observes the hidden state and acts accordingly. For example, in household navigation, an oracle planner could use the full map of the training environments, which is unavailable at deployment. In practice, these teachers can be trained in fully observed tasks using RL, imitation learning, or hybrid approaches [78, 75, 60, 27, 52]. This expert can teach the student how to act once the hidden state is known, but not how to find it [44]. As a result, naively copying the expert does not teach the student to explore [70]. Interactive imitation [65] offers a natural fix by relabeling student mistakes with expert actions. However, standard approaches [59] train the student to predict the average expert action across possible hidden states, so it dithers between hypotheses instead of resolving them [37, 70]. Other approaches propose to address the student-teacher mismatch using expensive online RL [74], differentiable experts [73], or offline coverage assumptions [42].

In this work, we propose ASTEROID (Asymmetric Student Teacher Roll-Out In-context Distillation), a framework that shows that privileged experts can teach exploration through interactive imitation. The idea is simple: the student generates the history online, and the expert provides the labels. ASTEROID rolls out the current student under partial observability, producing a history of observations, actions, and rewards, then asks the expert what it would do from the state the student has reached. The expert does not explore; it only labels the student’s histories. As a result, failed searches and probes become useful context: they specify evidence accumulated so far, while the expert provides next actions given the hidden state. With on-policy history, the policy can identify inconsistent hypotheses and adapt its exploration and action distribution accordingly.

Why does this teach exploration? A partial history represents uncertainty over the hidden state. Returning to household navigation: suppose the object could be in location $A$ , $B$ , or $C$ . If the student searches $A$ and finds nothing, its history rules out $A$ but is still consistent with $B$ and $C$ . A privileged expert would label this history with search(B) when the object is at $B$ , and search(C) when it is at $C$ . The student therefore learns to act and explore the remaining valid actions: if it fails at $A$ , it samples search(B) or search(C). If it then fails at $B$ , every label is search(C), since only $C$ remains. Unlike random sampling of locations, the policy conditions on its history and never retries hypotheses it has ruled out. Across many training tasks, ambiguous histories are labeled with a distribution of potential, consistent expert trajectories. The student samples from this distribution to explore, and each new observation and feedback eliminates additional hypotheses. The key insight: the set of histories that the student needs to learn to adapt from (e.g., failing at $A$ , failing at $B$ and then moving to $C$ ) is entirely covered by on-policy behavior. This is in-context exploration, i.e., searching while uncertain, and exploiting once the hidden state is revealed. Additionally, we show that a curriculum over the student rollout horizon improves sample efficiency and enables longer-context adaptation (Section 5). Overall, ASTEROID incorporates very simple changes into standard online student-teacher distillation to enable test-time exploration behavior.

We show both empirically (Section 6) and theoretically (Appendix H) that ASTEROID approximates Bayesian posterior sampling, a provably efficient exploration strategy [53]. However, posterior sampling has been hard to scale: prior approaches maintain an explicit posterior [3] or assume infinite offline data [42], which are intractable in realistic settings. ASTEROID avoids both: it does not maintain an explicit posterior, and on-policy supervised learning avoids impractical data costs. Because it is a simple extension of student–teacher distillation, ASTEROID works with modern architectures and existing sim-to-real frameworks [75]. In summary, we make the following contributions:

1. 

We present ASTEROID, a simple student–teacher distillation framework that enables in-context exploration and test-time improvement learned solely from privileged experts.

2. 

We evaluate our method across 11 environments, including navigation in realistic household simulators and real-world robot manipulation, where it outperforms RL and supervised baselines under fixed exploration budgets while using two orders of magnitude fewer training interactions.

3. 

We show that learned policies exhibit efficient real-world exploration and, under appropriate assumptions, recover posterior sampling with error linear rather than quadratic in context length.

## 2 Related Work

Student–Teacher Distillation.
Learning from privileged experts arises in settings from self-driving [13] to robotic exploration [17]. Interactive imitation addresses the covariate shift that drives the learner into unseen states [59], and prior work suggests that on-policy imitation is necessary under partial observability [65]. Our work targets this non-realizable regime, where the learner must take information-gathering actions that are not recoverable from a fully observed expert [63, 40]. Prior approaches handle this via additional assumptions, such as differentiable experts [73], predicting hidden information [38], or incorporating RL with bootstrapping to induce exploration [74, 70, 61, 37]. In contrast, we learn information-gathering behavior using iterative distillation of expert actions conditioned on on-policy histories, which is more sample-efficient than RL-based alternatives.

Meta Learning.
Meta-RL learns adaptive exploration across task distributions using recurrent policies [28, 21, 79, 44], but requires extensive online interaction [5], making it difficult to scale to high-dimensional, sparse-reward domains. Our approach replaces this expensive RL-based adaptation with supervised learning, making it efficient to learn long-horizon exploration. Further, unlike prior work limited to Bayes-Adaptive MDPs [40, 79, 42], our method scales to POMDPs, where the policy explores within a single episode to estimate the underlying state and achieve task success.

Posterior Sampling.
Posterior sampling methods [67, 53] drive exploration by maintaining a belief over hidden parameters, acting optimally under samples from this belief, and updating it based on feedback. Despite strong empirical and theoretical results [10, 53], such approaches require maintaining an explicit posterior and solving for policies under sampled parameters [53, 3], limiting scalability to high-dimensional settings. ASTEROID does not explicitly optimize a posterior-sampling objective. Instead, posterior-sampling-like behavior emerges through iterative on-policy distillation, even in high-dimensional continuous environments (Section 6), and we include theoretical insights to show convergence to posterior sampling on the covered history support (Appendix H). In Section 6, we show that current frontier models are inefficient at performing such exploration under partial observability, motivating the need to explicitly learn such behavior.

In-Context Decision-Making.
Transformers trained autoregressively on sequential data exhibit in-context learning [9, 25], which Decision Transformer [15] and Algorithm Distillation [39] leverage for decision-making. These works focus on using online rollouts as context to adapt behavior without external prompts. Closest to our work, Decision-Pretrained Transformer [42] learns an in-context policy that performs posterior sampling by pairing randomly generated contexts with privileged expert supervision. Such methods assume the offline dataset covers all possible interaction histories, which is intractable in high-dimensional domains. ASTEROID, instead, uses on-policy contexts, removing the coverage assumption and scaling to much harder, higher-dimensional problems (Section 6).

We include an extended discussion of related work in Appendix A.

## 3 Problem Statement

We study decision-making under partial observability, modeled as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) [34]. A POMDP is represented by the tuple $(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{O},E,T,R,\rho_{0},\gamma)$ , where $\mathcal{S}$ is the state space, $\mathcal{A}$ is the action space, $\mathcal{O}$ is the observation space and $E,T,R,\rho_{0},\gamma$ are the emission function, transition kernel, reward function, initial state distribution and discount factor, respectively. In a POMDP, the policy does not observe the state $s_{t}$ but receives partial observations $o_{t}\sim E(\cdot\mid s_{t})$ . For simplicity, we also define the Bayes-Adaptive Markov decision process (BAMDP), a special case of POMDPs in which the only hidden variable is a latent parameter, denoted by $z$ , i.e., $s_{t}=(o_{t},z)$ . For each interaction, $z\in\mathcal{Z}$ is sampled from a prior $p(z)$ and remains fixed for $K$ episodes (unlike a POMDP, where hidden states may vary at each step). Given $z$ , BAMDPs are fully observed and can be represented as a collection of MDPs $M_{z}$ (or tasks).

As a running example, consider a three-door environment: a BAMDP with latent parameter $z$ denoting the target door. At the start of each interaction, $z$ is sampled uniformly from the three doors and remains fixed across multiple episodes, where the objective is to navigate to the correct door. The target is hidden, and the agent must use its interaction history to infer the hidden goal and then exploit that information. We can construct a POMDP by adding noise to agent observations at each time step.

Since observations $o_{t}$ are partial, optimal policies depend on the current observation $o_{t}$ and the history $h_{t}=(o_{0},a_{0},r_{0},\ldots,o_{t-1},a_{t-1},r_{t-1})$ . Let $d_{\pi}(h)$ denote the distribution over histories for a policy $\pi$ . Learning information-gathering behavior directly from sparse rewards is highly sample-inefficient, often requiring impractical amounts of experience [5]. To mitigate this, we study an asymmetric training–testing setting in which a privileged teacher $\pi^{*}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})$ can access the true state $s_{t}$ during training, while the deployed student $\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid o_{t},h_{t})$ acts under partial observability using $o_{t}$ and $h_{t}$ . During training, the learner interacts with the POMDP to collect transition tuples $(o_{t},a_{t},r_{t},o_{t+1})$ and queries the teacher for actions $a^{*}_{t}\sim\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid s_{t})$ . Our objective is to use these interactions and teacher supervision to learn a student $\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid o_{t},h_{t})$ that maximizes the expected return $J(\pi_{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r_{t}\right]$ . This asymmetric distillation setting arises naturally in navigation [33], sim-to-real robot manipulation [75], human-in-the-loop learning [36], and knowledge distillation [26].

## 4 Background: Student–Teacher Distillation

In the following sections, we focus on the key paradigms for teacher–student distillation under partial observability, discuss why they break down at learning how to explore in asymmetric settings, and motivate ASTEROID as an iterative on-policy distillation method for learning in-context exploration.

## Naive asymmetric student–teacher distillation cannot learn adaptive exploration.

A natural approach to train partially observed student policies is via behavior-cloning trajectories generated solely by a privileged policy [22, 54]. But there is a conflict: the privileged teacher policy $\pi^{*}(\cdot|s_{t})$ solves the task without exploration, whereas the unprivileged student policy $\pi_{\theta}$ must gather information through exploration before exploiting for task success [28]. Following the three-door example from Section 3, privileged experts observe $z$ , while the student only receives partial observations $o_{t}$ . At $t=0$ , $o_{0}$ is identical for all values of $z$ . Here, a student policy acting on partial observation $o_{0}$ cannot distinguish between actions provided for the three goals and learns the marginal expert behavior induced by the training data ${d}_{\pi^{*}}$ , i.e., choosing a door uniformly at random. Thus,

Naive asymmetric distillation from expert trajectories learns i.i.d. exploration, but fails to adaptively exploit sequences of environment rewards and feedback.

## In-context learning via Decision-Pretrained Transformer (DPT) [42] can learn exploration.

Recent work [42] has shown that asymmetric student–teacher distillation can learn exploration when the training dataset is constructed with specific design choices.
Lee et al. [42] introduce DPT, an in-context learning framework that constructs a dataset of contexts, observations and target actions: $\mathcal{D}^{\text{DPT}}=\{(h_{t},o_{t},a^{*}_{t})^{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}$ for supervised learning via random sampling. Here, $d_{\mathcal{D}}$ denotes the empirical distribution of histories and query observations in the dataset $\mathcal{D}$ . DPT generates its offline histories with an independent behavior policy.
Further, it labels randomly sampled query observations $o_{t}\in\mathcal{O}$ with the privileged expert $a^{*}_{t}\sim\pi^{*}(\cdot|o_{t},z)$ . The history $h_{t}$ provides context about the underlying hidden parameter, which the policy learns to use at the query observation $o_{t}$ to predict actions. DPT trains a causal transformer policy maximizing action likelihood over this dataset:

 $\mathcal{L}(\theta)\;=\;\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{(h_{t},o_{t},a^{*}_{t})\sim{\mathcal{D}}}\left[-\log\pi_{\theta}\!\left(a_{t}^{*}\mid o_{t},h_{t}\right)\right].$ 

(1)

Under coverage assumptions, DPT provably converges to posterior sampling: it uses $h_{t}$ to form an implicit posterior over the latent state, and acts according to the expert policy averaged under this posterior, i.e., $\pi(a_{t}|o_{t},h_{t})=\int\pi^{*}(a_{t}|o_{t},z)\;\mathrm{p}(z|o_{t},h_{t})\;dz$ .

Let $\mathcal{H}_{t}=(\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{R})^{t}\times\mathcal{O}$ denote the space of length- $t$ history and observation tuples $(h_{t},o_{t})$ .

The primary limitation of DPT is the reliance on a full-coverage assumption: the dataset must cover the combinatorial space of arbitrary contexts and query observations, i.e., we require

 $\mathop{\bigcup}\limits_{t=0}^{H}{\mathcal{H}_{t}}\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(d_{\mathcal{D}}),$ 

which scales exponentially with the interaction horizon $H$ .
