conclusion:
In this work, we propose ASTEROID, an iterative asymmetric distillation framework for learning in-context exploration. The key idea is to train a history-conditioned policy using supervised targets from a privileged expert, while collecting the histories on-policy from the student. This directly addresses two bottlenecks for exploration: (i) privileged teachers do not demonstrate information-gathering behavior, and (ii) offline or randomly collected histories may not match the distribution the student will encounter at deployment. While the need for history-conditioned exploration policies is well established, we show that on-policy distillation from privileged teachers, without RL or latent regression, is sufficient to learn exploration scalably across diverse simulated and real-world tasks. We believe that as robots and AI agents are deployed in the wild, acting as web assistants or robot butlers, in-context exploration learned via simple and scalable online training is key to enabling truly autonomous behavior.

A limitation is that the approach relies on a strong privileged expert, though it is agnostic to how the expert is generated. An interesting direction is to remove this reliance and train experts from offline demonstrations. We note that posterior sampling exploration is not Bayes-optimal, i.e., it trades off some exploration efficiency for tractability and strong regret guarantees. This motivates future extensions that combine our approach with optimistic exploration. Another limitation is that this exploration relies on inferring hidden states from the overall expert support. When the hidden information can only be gathered outside this support, the student cannot reduce its uncertainty. A promising future direction is to learn a residual policy on top of this student to learn off-support information-gathering behavior. Additionally, the student policy is trained to imitate expert actions, but may produce unsafe exploration. Therefore, an important direction is to enforce safety via explicit constraints and safety filters.

body_start:
Abstract

Despite recent advances, current AI systems remain highly susceptible to domain shifts, particularly in biomedical imaging, where images are usually acquired under substantially different experimental conditions. Although recent domain adaptation methods have made substantial progress, significant performance gaps under domain shift persist. To measure progress in this regard, we introduce BatchBench, a leaderboard that evaluates and compares the robustness of AI systems on biomedical images from unseen experimental batches and data sources. BatchBench is built on JUMP-CP, one of the largest publicly available biomedical imaging datasets. Generated using the Cell Painting assay, JUMP-CP exhibits pronounced batch effects and domain shifts, making it a challenging testbed for evaluating robustness to distributional changes.

Keywords: biomedical imaging, domain-adaptation, test-time-adaptation, cell-painting, jump-cp, microscopy, distribution-shift

## 1 Introduction

Figure 1: Source-level split of the BatchBench leaderboard. Nine
sources of JUMP-CP-2k are public (eight for training, source 2 for
validation). Sources 4, 6, 9, and 13 are held out as the private
test set, so that every leaderboard entry is evaluated on unseen
data-generating sources.

## Vulnerability of AI systems under domain shift and batch effects.

Deep learning methods often assume that training and test data are sampled from the same underlying distribution. However, in practice, biological images are acquired across experimental batches, plates, and sites, which introduces non-biological variation known as batch effects. These effects shift the distribution of the input images, such that a model that performs well on its training distribution can fail on images from a new experimental batch or laboratory. This limits
the use of AI in applications such as drug discovery, where new data
are generated continuously and under changing conditions.

## JUMP-CP and CellPainting.

High-content screening data obtained with the Cell Painting assay 1 provide a clear example of this problem. The JUMP Cell Painting dataset (JUMP-CP) 2, one of the largest public biomedical imaging datasets, was obtained from 13 data-generating centers (sources) using different microscopes and laboratory workflows. As a result, JUMP-CP exhibits substantial batch effects across multiple levels of its data hierarchy. Because every image is annotated with its source, experimental batch, and plate, JUMP-CP provides a exceptional setting in which domain shifts are both pronounced and explicitly annotated at multiple levels.

## Domain adaptation (DA)

methods address domain shift either by learning
domain-invariant representations during training or by adapting the
model to unlabeled target data at inference time, i.e. test-time adaptation (TTA) 9, 8, 3, 5, 11, 7. These methods have substantially improved robustness on natural
images. Nevertheless, their effectiveness on biomedical images from unseen experimental conditionsremains poorly characterized, and results reported on different subsets, splits, and metrics are rarely
comparable.

## The BatchBench Leaderboard.

We introduce the BatchBench leaderboard, an open benchmark for comparing AI models on the identification of chemical perturbations in Cell Painting images acquired from sources not seen during training. The leaderboard is designed to be used by several research communities:

• 

Domain adaptation and test-time adaptation. BatchBench evaluates multi-source adaptation to unseen target domains under combined covariate and label shift. Methods that adapt to unlabeled test images, as well as methods that do not perform test-time adaptation, can be submitted through a common \codeadapt()/\codepredict() interface.

• 

Biomedical imaging and foundation models. BatchBench evaluates whether pretrained image encoders and specialized architectures generalize to unseen imaging sites, an important requirement for deployment that is not captured by in-distribution evaluation.

• 

Cell Painting and JUMP-CP.
BatchBench provides a standardized source-level evaluation of image-based compound profiling on JUMP-CP using fixed splits and a private test set.

The leaderboard presents three components: (i) JUMP-CP-2k, a
curated subset of JUMP-CP covering 2,000 compounds, with nine public
sources and four sources held out as a private test set
(Section 2); (ii) a containerized
submission protocol that keeps the test data private and supports
both conventional and test-time adaptation methods
(Section 3); and (iii) six baseline entries
covering standard supervised training, domain-invariant training,
test-time adaptation, and meta-learning (Sections 5
and 6). The baseline entries show that test-time
adaptation reduces the domain gap but does not close it. For compounds
with few training images, every current entry remains close to chance
level. The leaderboard is open for submissions on
Hugging
Face.

## 2 The BatchBench leaderboard

## Problem setting.

Let $\mathcal{D}^{(1)},\ldots,\mathcal{D}^{(S)}$ denote labeled
data from $S$ training sources, where each sample consists of an
image $\boldsymbol{x}$ , its compound label $y\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$ ,
and its domain metadata $\boldsymbol{d}=(\text{source},\text{batch},\text{plate})$ . At test time, a submission receives the
unlabeled images $\{\boldsymbol{x}_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N}$ and their metadata
 $\{\boldsymbol{d}_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N}$ from sources that do not occur in the
training data. It may adapt to these images before predicting their
labels. The leaderboard thus evaluates multi-source domain
adaptation to unseen target domains. The setting covers domain
generalization (no adaptation), test-time adaptation, and in-context
adaptation as special cases. As the the domain metadata are
hierarchical, submissions can define domains at the level of
sources, experimental batches, or plates.

## Task.

Each input is a single five-channel Cell Painting image (DNA, RNA, ER,
AGP, and Mito). The task is to identify which of the $K=2{,}000$ 
compounds the imaged cells were treated with. Test images come
exclusively from held-out sources, so every test image also originates
from an unseen experimental batch and an unseen plate.

## Compound selection and sampling.

JUMP-CP comprises images from 13 sources and more than 100,000 compound
and genetic perturbations 2. We used the dataset cpg0016 2, available from the Cell Painting Gallery 10 on the Registry of Open Data on AWS (https://registry.opendata.aws/cellpainting-gallery/). To obtain a dataset that is
practical to download and train on, we selected the 2,000 most frequent
compounds, retained all wells treated with these compounds, and sampled
one image (field of view) per well uniformly at random.

## Domain metadata and controls.

Each sample is annotated with its source, experimental batch, and plate
identifiers. Submissions may use these identifiers as domain labels
during training and to group test images at inference. Images of
negative-control wells (DMSO-treated, unperturbed cells) from the
training sources are provided as a separate file. They can be used,
for example, for control-based normalization 7.

## Preprocessing.

From each original image we extract a $500\times 500$ pixel center crop.
We then apply illumination correction by clipping the top 0.01% of
pixel intensities in each channel.

## Splits.

Sources 4, 6, 9, and 13 form the private test set of the leaderboard
and are never released (Figure 1). The
remaining nine sources are public. Source 2 serves as the validation
set for model selection, and the other eight sources form the training
set.

## Evaluation subsets.

Compounds differ greatly in their number of training images and in the
strength of their phenotypes. In addition to the overall accuracy, the
leaderboard therefore reports accuracy on three subsets of
the test set:

• 

POSCON: the eight positive-control compounds, present
on every plate, usually at fixed well positions. They have many
training images and strong,
well-characterized phenotypes.

• 

TARGET: 293 compounds from the JUMP-Target
collection, a reference library chosen to cover diverse biological
targets and mechanisms of action.

• 

REST: all remaining compounds, each represented by
few images (about 12 per compound in the public split).

The three subsets correspond to increasingly difficult regimes:
abundant data with strong phenotypes (POSCON), a curated
mechanism-of-action reference set (TARGET), and a long tail
of rare classes (REST).

## Label shift.

In addition to the source shift, the class distribution differs
between the public and the test split. POSCON images make up
51% of the public split but 36% of the test set; TARGET
images increase from 25% to 55%; REST images decrease from
24% to 9% (Table 1). The leaderboard therefore
evaluates adaptation under combined covariate and label shift, a
setting in which many TTA methods are known to
degrade 6, 12.

## Research questions.

The leaderboard is designed to answer questions that are open in each
of the communities above, for example:

• 

Do domain adaptation and TTA methods developed on natural-image
benchmarks transfer to biological domain shift?

• 

At which level of the domain hierarchy (source, batch, or
plate) should adaptation be performed?

• 

Do pretrained microscopy foundation models generalize to unseen
imaging sources better than models trained from scratch?

• 

Can models identify compounds with weak phenotypes and few
training images (TARGET, REST) on unseen sources?

## 3 Submitting to the leaderboard

## Submission format.

A leaderboard submission is a public Git repository together with a
commit hash. The repository must contain the training code and a
Dockerfile from which the evaluation server builds a container image.
Submissions are therefore independent of the deep learning framework
and model architecture. The image must provide a
\codeSubmission class that implements two methods, \codeadapt() and
\codepredict(). Ready-to-run example submissions for all baseline
entries are available in our
baseline
repository and can serve as templates.

## Evaluation.

The evaluation server passes the private test images, as an array of
shape $(N,H,W,5)$ , together with a metadata list containing the
source, batch, and plate identifier of every image, to both
\codeadapt() and \codepredict(). No labels are provided.
\codeadapt() may update the model using the unlabeled test images
and their metadata, which permits test-time adaptation. Methods that
do not adapt should implement it as a no-op. \codepredict() must return one
prediction per image, in the original order.

## Metric and ranking.

Leaderboard entries are ranked by overall accuracy, i.e., the fraction
of correctly classified images in the entire test set. Because
POSCON and TARGET together contain over 90% of the
test images, this metric is dominated by these two subsets. The
leaderboard therefore additionally reports accuracy on
POSCON, TARGET, and REST separately, so
that progress on rare compounds remains visible. Scores are published
on the leaderboard once the manual evaluation finishes.

## Rules.

Submissions may not use any data from the held-out sources (4, 6, 9,
and 13) for training, pre-training, or model selection. This also
applies to pretrained models whose pre-training data include these
sources. Test-time adaptation on the unlabeled test images through
\codeadapt() is permitted.

## 4 Development datasets

To lower the entry barrier and enable fast prototyping before a
leaderboard submission, we release two smaller variants of
JUMP-CP-2k:

• 

JUMP-CP-MNIST contains only the eight
positive-control compounds. Its images are downsampled to
 $200\times 200$ pixels, and the five imaging channels (DNA, RNA, ER,
AGP, and Mito) are combined into three channels, so that standard
RGB architectures and pretrained models can be applied without
modification.

• 

JUMP-CP-2k-200 contains all 2,000 compounds of
JUMP-CP-2k at the reduced resolution of $200\times 200$ pixels, with
all five channels.

Both variants use the same source-level split as JUMP-CP-2k.
Leaderboard rankings are computed on the full-resolution private
test set.

## 5 Baseline entries

The leaderboard is initialized with six baseline entries that
represent the main strategies for handling domain shift. All use a
ResNet18 4 backbone whose first convolution takes five
input channels.

• 

No adaptation (ResNet18). A classifier trained with
standard empirical risk minimization on the training sources and
applied to the test sources unchanged.

• 

Domain-invariant training: DANN 3 and
deepCORAL 8. Both methods encourage representations
that do not depend on the domain during training, adversarially
(DANN) or by aligning second-order feature statistics (deepCORAL).
We use the source identifier as the domain label.

• 

Test-time adaptation: AdaBN 5 and
TENT 9. Both use the trained ResNet18 baseline and adapt
it only at inference. AdaBN replaces the BatchNorm statistics with
statistics computed on the test images. TENT additionally updates
the BatchNorm affine parameters by minimizing the entropy of the
predictions. For both methods, test images are grouped by plate, so
that each plate is adapted separately.

• 

Meta-learning: ARM-BN 11. and CS-ARM-BN 7 ARM-BN trains
the model episodically to classify images using BatchNorm
statistics computed from an unlabeled context batch of the same
domain. At test time, the statistics are computed in the same way
from the unlabeled test images.

Hyperparameters were tuned with Bayesian optimization, and for every
method the model with the highest accuracy on source 2 was
selected. The code of all baseline entries is available in our
GitHub repository.

## 6 Results

Table 2 reports the current leaderboard entries.

## Test-time adaptation reduces the domain gap.

Without adaptation, ResNet18 reaches an average overall accuracy of 0.175.
Re-estimating the BatchNorm statistics on each test plate (AdaBN)
raises this to 0.244. Most of this gain comes from POSCON,
where accuracy increases from 0.465 to 0.646. TENT’s additional
entropy minimization yields a higher performance in the POSCON group, but no improvement in TARGET or REST. Domain-invariant training does not improve over the
non-adapted baseline: DANN reaches 0.170.

## The domain gap remains for compounds with few images.

Performance on POSCON is substantially higher than on TARGET and REST, consistent with the much larger number of training images per compound, lower number of classes and strong phenotypes. These factors are absent for most TARGET and REST compounds, and none of the current entries compensates for them. Identifying compounds with weak phenotypes and few training images on unseen sources is therefore the main open problem posed by the leaderboard.

title: Differentially Private Sparse Reward Estimation with Preference Feedback
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) has become a central paradigm for aligning Large Language Models with human values. However, the reliance on sensitive preference data necessitates rigorous differential privacy (DP) guarantees to prevent user information leakage. Existing private alignment methods typically assume dense reward parameterizations, resulting in estimation error bounds that scale polynomially with the ambient {model size $d$}. Such dependence is prohibitive in modern {overparameterized models} where $d$ is vast. In this work, we study \emph{Private Sparse RLHF} problem to address this limitation, assuming that human preferences (reward model) are governed by a subset of $s^* \ll d$ relevant features. We provide the first comprehensive theoretical framework for differentially private sparse reward estimation from pairwise preference feedback under the Bradley-Terry-Luce model, and introduce efficient algorithms for both Sample-DP and Label-DP settings. Theoretically, under the squared $\ell_2$ parameter estimation error, we establish upper bounds of $\widetilde{O}(s^*/n + {s^*}^2/n^2\varepsilon^2)$ for $(\varepsilon,δ)$-Sample-DP and $\widetilde{O}(s^*/n + s^*/n\varepsilon^2)$ for $\varepsilon$-Label-DP based on randomized response, where $n$ is the training data size. For the lower bounds, we show that the Sample-DP rate is nearly optimal, and that the guarantee for our Label-DP method cannot be further improved within the randomized-response framework. We also provide a general lower bound for the problem with Label-DP. Empirically, our framework demonstrates superior efficacy over dense baselines across sentiment generation and safety alignment benchmarks, offering a significantly more favorable privacy-utility trade-off.

body_start:
Abstract

Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) has become a central paradigm for aligning Large Language Models with human values. However, the reliance on sensitive preference data necessitates rigorous differential privacy (DP) guarantees to prevent user information leakage. Existing private alignment methods typically assume dense reward parameterizations, resulting in estimation error bounds that scale polynomially with the ambient model size $d$ . Such dependence is prohibitive in modern overparameterized models where $d$ is vast.
In this work, we study Private Sparse RLHF problem to address this limitation, assuming that human preferences (reward model) are governed by a subset of $s^{*}\ll d$ relevant features.
We provide the first comprehensive theoretical framework for differentially private sparse reward estimation from pairwise preference feedback under the Bradley-Terry-Luce model, and introduce efficient algorithms for both Sample-DP and Label-DP settings.
Theoretically, under the squared $\ell_{2}$ parameter estimation error, we establish upper bounds of $\widetilde{O}(s^{*}/n+{s^{*}}^{2}/n^{2}\varepsilon^{2})$ for $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ -Sample-DP and $\widetilde{O}(s^{*}/n+s^{*}/n\varepsilon^{2})$ for $\varepsilon$ -Label-DP based on randomized response, where $n$ is the training data size. For the lower bounds, we show that the Sample-DP rate is nearly optimal, and that the guarantee for our Label-DP method cannot be further improved within the randomized-response framework. We also provide a general lower bound for the problem with Label-DP.
Empirically, our framework demonstrates superior efficacy over dense baselines across sentiment generation and safety alignment benchmarks, offering a significantly more favorable privacy-utility trade-off.

## 1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in generalization and reasoning, yet their pre-training on vast, unfiltered corpora often results in behaviors that are misaligned with harmful or biased content. To address this, Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has emerged as the standard paradigm for steering LLMs to align pretrained models with human values and objectives [16, 41, 36, 3]. In the typical RLHF pipeline, a reward model is first trained on a dataset of pairwise human preferences (e.g., response $y_{1}$ is preferred over $y_{2}$ ) to approximate the underlying human utility function. This learned reward model then guides the optimization of the language model policy via algorithms such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) [38].

Despite its success, the reliance on human feedback introduces significant privacy vulnerabilities. The preference datasets used to train reward models often contain sensitive information, ranging from personal opinions to implicit biases, which can be memorized by the model. Consequently, deploying these models risks exposing user data through privacy attacks [8, 9, 22, 56]. To mitigate these risks, recent works have integrated Differential Privacy (DP)[23], which requires that the private trained model (or its output distribution) does not significantly change when any single entry in the training data is altered, into the alignment process [56, 15, 61, 59] (refer to Section 2 for further discussion).

However, a fundamental limitation of existing private alignment methods is their implicit treatment of the reward model as a dense parameter vector. In practice, collecting high-quality human preference data for aligning large language models is both costly and time-consuming [13, 35, 58]. For instance, aligning models with general human values often requires a substantial number of annotations from experienced annotators to reliably distinguish between “helpful” and “harmless” responses. This data scarcity becomes even more pronounced in specialized domains such as medical or legal reasoning [40, 18, 21], where preference labels must be provided by highly qualified experts. These challenges impose a strict budget on the available sample size $n$ , while the semantic richness and complexity of such domains naturally induce a feature space of extremely high dimension $d$ . Standard differentially private mechanisms require noise injection proportional to the ambient dimension (i.e., $\propto d/n$ ) to hide individual contributions [23]. When $d\gg n$ , this noise overwhelms the utility signal, rendering the high estimation error and alignment ineffective.

Moreover, recent empirical studies [2, 17] suggest that the underlying reward functions and feature representations in LLM alignment exhibit significant intrinsic sparsity. Specifically, preference signals are often governed by a small subset of salient features or tokens, rather than the full high-dimensional embedding. In parallel, foundational theoretical work on differentially private sparse learning has shown that, for problems such as linear regression, one can circumvent polynomial dependence on the ambient dimension $d$ [42, 52, 6, 20, 63, 47, 19]. By leveraging sparsity, the estimation error can be reduced to scale logarithmically with the sparsity (i.e., $\propto s^{*}/n$ ), thereby enabling accurate private estimation even in high-dimensional settings. This naturally raises the following question:

Can we design effective mechanisms for private sparse RLHF with rigorous theoretical guarantees that are not polynomial in the dimension $d$ ?

We answer this question affirmatively and summarize our contributions as follows:

• 

First Analysis of Private Sparse RLHF. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to investigate sparsity in the context of private alignment, i.e., DP Sparse RLHF. We formulate the problem under the high-dimensional Bradley-Terry model and introduce two specialized algorithms: Sample-DP-IHT, which integrates iterative hard thresholding with a private peeling mechanism to protect the entire interaction tuple, and Label-DP RR+IHT, which combines randomized response with debiased gradient estimation to protect preference labels.

• 

Minimax Optimality. As summarized in Table 1, we establish upper bounds under the squared $\ell_{2}$ parameter estimation error. Specifically, we achieve rates of $\widetilde{O}(s^{*}/n+(s^{*})^{2}/(n^{2}\varepsilon^{2}))$ for $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ -Sample-DP and $\widetilde{O}(s^{*}/n+s^{*}/(n\varepsilon^{2}))$ for $\varepsilon$ -Label-DP, where $n$ is the training data size. For the lower bounds, we show that the Sample-DP rate is nearly optimal, and that our theoretical analysis for the Label-DP method cannot be further improved. We also provide a general lower bound $\widetilde{\Omega}\!\left(\frac{s^{*}}{n}+\frac{s^{*}}{n^{2}\varepsilon^{2}}\right)$ for the problem with Label-DP.

• 

Experimental Evaluation. We empirically validate our framework on Sentiment Generation and Safety Alignment benchmarks. Our results demonstrate that exploiting sparsity consistently yields superior privacy-utility trade-offs compared to dense baselines (e.g., DP-SGD and Randomized Response), effectively mitigating the noise overhead in high-privacy regimes and achieving significantly higher reward scores and alignment rates.

## 2 Related Work

Differentially Private Reward Learning and Alignment Recent work has increasingly focused on integrating differential privacy into the alignment of LLMs. Chowdhury et al. [15] investigates differentially private reward estimation using preference feedback, while subsequent studies extend these guarantees to Direct Preference Optimization and unified offline alignment frameworks Chowdhury et al. [14], Zhou et al. [61], Chen et al. [12]. Beyond reward estimation, privacy-aware regularization has received growing attention. Wu et al. [57] analyzes offline and online KL-regularized RLHF under differential privacy, while Zhang et al. [60] shows that KL regularization itself can inherently induce differential privacy guarantees in bandit and RLHF settings. The scope of private alignment has further expanded to more complex interaction models, such as reinforcement learning with self-play [37] and user-level differential privacy in RLHF pipelines [59]. Despite these advancements, prior works largely focused on dense reward structures or general function approximation, whose the estimation errors always depend on polynomial of the dimension, leaving the sparse reward learning under privacy constraints unexplored.

Differentially Private Sparse Learning
Differentially private sparse learning builds on a broader line of work on private empirical risk minimization (ERM) and convex optimization [11, 31, 29, 51, 50, 44]. Early studies [46] investigated the stability of the Lasso estimator, clarifying the conditions required for robust feature selection under privacy constraints. Building on these foundations, Talwar et al. [42] gives near-optimal utility guarantees for differentially private Lasso, establishing sharp statistical rates (up to logarithmic factors) in sparse linear regression under central DP.
More recent work has expanded both the algorithmic toolbox and the problem settings. Wang and Gu [54] propose a knowledge-transfer framework that can improve utility for private sparse regressions. [43, 26] addressed private stochastic convex optimization under heavy-tailed gradients by robust estimation and median techniques. In parallel, sparse learning under local differential privacy, Wang and Xu [52] develops LDP iterative hard thresholding procedures, and subsequent analysis Zhu et al. [62] sharpen lower/upper bounds and provide the first non-interactive LDP algorithms for the problem. Beyond regression, privacy-preserving sparse spectral estimation has also been studied. Hu et al. [28], Hu et al. [27], Wang and Xu [53] examined the sparse generalized eigenvalue problem underlying sparse principal component analysis, canonical correlation analysis, and Fisher’s discriminant analysis.
Despite these advances, existing private sparse learning results can not straightforwardly extend to the preference-based learning setting central to RLHF, along with the non-linear Bradley-Terry-Luce model and paired data dependency.

## 3 Preliminaries

In this section, we present the formal problem setup for private alignment in RLHF from pairwise comparisons, along with the necessary definitions and assumptions.

Let $D=\{(k_{i},a_{i}^{0},a_{i}^{1},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}$ be a dataset consisting of $n$ labeled comparisons drawn i.i.d. from $\mathcal{D}$ , where $k_{i}\in\mathcal{K}$ denotes a context (e.g., a prompt or state), $a_{i}^{0},a_{i}^{1}\in\mathcal{A}$ consists of two candidate actions/responses, and the label $y_{i}\in\{0,1\}$ indicates which candidate is preferred (i.e., $y_{i}=l$ means that $a_{i}^{l}$ is chosen as the preferred response). Let $r_{\theta}:\mathcal{K}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a parametric reward model indexed by $\theta\in\Theta$ , and let $\theta^{\star}$ denote the unknown ground-truth parameter. We assume the preferences are generated according to the softmax comparison model: for each $i\in[n]$ and $l\in\{0,1\}$ ,

 $\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\theta^{\star}}\!\left[y_{i}=l\,\middle|\,k_{i},a_{i}^{0},a_{i}^{1}\right]=\frac{\exp\left(r_{\theta^{\star}}\left(k_{i},a_{i}^{l}\right)\right)}{\exp\left(r_{\theta^{\star}}\left(k_{i},a_{i}^{0}\right)\right)+\exp\left(r_{\theta^{\star}}\left(k_{i},a_{i}^{1}\right)\right)},$ 

where $r_{\theta^{*}}(\cdot,\cdot)$ denotes the reward model parameterized by $\theta^{*}$ . This model is known as the Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) model [5, 33]. In this work, we focus on the BTL model with a linear reward parameterization. Specifically, let $\phi:\mathcal{K}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$ be a known feature map and assume $r_{\theta}(k,a)=\langle\phi(k,a),\theta\rangle,\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.$ 
Define the comparison (difference) feature $x_{i}:=\phi(k_{i},a_{i}^{1})-\phi(k_{i},a_{i}^{0})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.$ 
Under this model, the conditional distribution reduces to logistic regression:

 $\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\theta^{\star}}\!\left[y_{i}=1\,\middle|\,k_{i},a_{i}^{0},a_{i}^{1}\right]=\sigma\!\left(\langle x_{i},\theta^{\star}\rangle\right),\mathbb{P}_{\theta^{\star}}\!\left[y_{i}=0\,\middle|\,k_{i},a_{i}^{0},a_{i}^{1}\right]=\sigma\!\left(-\langle x_{i},\theta^{\star}\rangle\right),$ 

where $\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$ refers to the sigmoid function.

Given $D$ , our objective is to estimate $\theta^{\star}$ (and hence the reward function $r_{\theta^{\star}}$ ) by maximizing the likelihood of the observed comparisons with privacy constraints. Formally, we seek a randomized estimator $\mathcal{M}:D\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$ that minimizes the empirical risk $\mathcal{L}_{n}(\theta)$ subject to the privacy constraint, where $\mathcal{L}_{n}(\theta)$ is defined as follows:
 $\mathcal{L}_{n}(\theta)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big(\log(1+\exp(\langle x_{i},\theta\rangle))-y_{i}\langle x_{i},\theta\rangle\Big).$ 
To account for the high-dimensional nature of the feature space ( $d\gg n$ ), we adopt the following assumptions, which are standard in the literature [39, 15, 61, 58].

Assumption 3.1 (Boundedness).

(a) $\theta^{*}$ lies in the set $\Theta_{B,s^{*}}=\left\{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\mid\|\theta\|_{2}\leq B,\|\theta\|_{0}\leq s^{*}\right\}$ . (b) Features are bounded, i.e., $\|x\|_{\infty}\leq 1,\forall x=\phi(k,a^{1})-\phi(k,a^{0})$ . (c) Let $\Sigma:=\mathbb{E}[xx^{\top}]$ , and suppose there exist constants $0<\mu\leq\gamma<\infty$ such that $\mu\leq\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\leq\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\leq\gamma$ .

Our boundedness assumptions differ from the $\ell_{2}$ feature bound used in [15]. Note that in the high dimensional setting, $\ell_{\infty}$ -boundness assumption is more reasonable than $\ell_{2}$ -norm. Such an assumption has been widely used in the existing literature on high-dimensional statistics [49]. Under an $\ell_{2}$ bound
 $\|x\|_{2}\leq L$ , one has $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\mathbb{E}\|x\|_{2}^{2}\leq L^{2},$ and hence $\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\leq\frac{L^{2}}{d}.$ 
Thus, when $L=O(1)$ , a dense design cannot have all covariance eigenvalues bounded below by a constant; the curvature parameter $\mu$ may scale as $1/d$ , leading to dimension dependence through the condition number. In our work, we assume the coordinate-wise bound $\|x\|_{\infty}\leq 1$ , which allows $\|x\|_{2}=O(\sqrt{d})$ and permits covariance eigenvalues $\mu,\gamma=\Theta(1)$ . We will provide more discussions in the later parts.

Now, we recall the definition of differential privacy [23]. Informally, it ensures that the privately trained model (or its output distribution) does not significantly change when any single entry in the training data is altered.
Depending on the scenario, there are two levels of privacy: label-DP [10, 24] and sample-DP [11, 23, 1]. We provide their formal definitions in the following.

Definition 3.2 (Differential Privacy [23]).

Let $\varepsilon\geq 0$ and $\delta\in(0,1]$ . A randomized algorithm $\mathcal{M}$ is said to satisfy $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ -differential privacy with respect to an adjacency relation $\sim$ , if for any pair of adjacent datasets $D\sim D^{\prime}$ , and for any measurable set $S$ in the output space of $\mathcal{M}$ , it holds that

 $\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{M}(D)\in S]\leq e^{\varepsilon}\cdot\mathbb{P}\left[\mathcal{M}\left(D^{\prime}\right)\in S\right]+\delta.$ 

When $\delta=0$ , we say that $\mathcal{M}$ is $\varepsilon$ -differentially private. Throughout the paper, we consider two specific types of adjacency:
1) Sample Adjacency (Sample-DP). $D$ and $D^{\prime}$ differ in exactly one sample record (i.e., replacement or addition/removal of a pair $(x_{i},y_{i})$ ). 2) Label Adjacency (Label-DP). $D$ and $D^{\prime}$ differ only in the label of a single sample (i.e., fixed features $x_{i}$ , different $y_{i}$ ).

Definition 3.2 guarantees that the trained reward model remains statistically stable regardless of variations in a single user’s data. Particularly, Label-DP ensures that an adversary cannot determine the specific preference $y_{i}$ for a fixed pair of responses. In contrast, Sample-DP provides a strictly stronger guarantee by protecting the entire interaction tuple $(k_{i},a_{i}^{0},a_{i}^{1},y_{i})$ , concealing not just the preference but also the context of the query itself. Notably, prior works on private RLHF have mainly focused on the Label-DP setting [15, 61], leaving the theoretical analysis of Sample-DP largely unexplored even under non-sparse settings.

conclusion: In this work, we studied differentially private sparse reward estimation for RLHF under the BTL preference model. By exploiting the intrinsic sparsity of human preferences, we introduced two efficient algorithms: Sample-DP-IHT and Label-DP RR+IHT. Our theory establishes nearly minimax-optimal sparse rates for Sample-DP and shows that the guarantee for RR-based Label-DP cannot be further improved within the randomized-response framework. We also provide a general lower bound for arbitrary central Label-DP mechanisms. Experiments on Sentiment Generation and Safety Alignment demonstrate that sparsity-aware private reward estimation substantially improves the privacy-utility trade-off over dense baselines in the challenging $d\gg n$ regime.

title: AtomicRL: Atomic Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown promise in robotic manipulation, but imitation learning (IL) alone often struggles to master complex long-horizon skills. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers an effective avenue for further improving VLA policies. However, existing VLA-RL methods typically suffer from delayed and biased credit assignment due to trajectory-level sparse rewards, while imbalanced subtask mastery creates bottlenecks that limit overall performance. To address these challenges, we propose AtomicRL, an RL post-training framework that leverages atomic task structures for reliable credit assignment and adaptive exploration. AtomicRL introduces Semantic-Aware Policy Optimization (SAPO), which uses semantic-aware gating to constrain TD residuals from failed atomic subtasks from propagating across task boundaries, mitigating credit contamination while preserving intra-subtask credit assignment and value bootstrapping. In addition, Bottleneck-Adaptive Target Exploration (BATE) dynamically coordinates task sampling and local exploration incentives based on the mastery of individual atomic subtasks, directing learning toward the remaining bottlenecks. Finally, we develop a Real2Sim2Real pipeline that bridges online RL in simulation with real-world deployment, facilitating practical transfer to physical robots. On LIBERO-LONG, AtomicRL achieves absolute performance gains of 3.6% and 4.0% over PPO across two VLA architectures. On CALVIN ABC-D, it improves full-task performance by up to 9.5% over PPO. Combined with the Real2Sim2Real pipeline, AtomicRL further improves real-world task performance by an average of 21.3%. These results demonstrate that AtomicRL effectively improves the learning efficiency and manipulation performance of VLA policies on long-horizon tasks.

Abstract

Vision–language–action (VLA) models have shown promise in robotic manipulation, but imitation learning (IL) alone often struggles to master complex long-horizon skills. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers an effective avenue for further improving VLA policies. However, existing VLA-RL methods typically suffer from delayed and biased credit assignment due to trajectory-level sparse rewards, while imbalanced subtask mastery creates bottlenecks that limit overall performance. To address these challenges, we propose AtomicRL, an RL post-training framework that leverages atomic task structures for reliable credit assignment and adaptive exploration. In addition, Bottleneck-Adaptive Target Exploration (BATE) dynamically coordinates task sampling and local exploration incentives based on the mastery of individual atomic subtasks, directing learning toward the remaining bottlenecks. Finally, we develop a Real2Sim2Real pipeline that bridges online RL in simulation with real-world deployment, facilitating practical transfer to physical robots. On LIBERO-LONG, AtomicRL achieves absolute performance gains of 3.6% and 4.0% over PPO across two VLA architectures. On CALVIN ABC-D, it improves full-task performance by up to 9.5% over PPO. Combined with the Real2Sim2Real pipeline, AtomicRL further improves real-world task performance by an average of 21.3%. These results demonstrate that AtomicRL effectively improves the learning efficiency and manipulation performance of VLA policies on long-horizon tasks.

## 1 Introduction

Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) (Beyer et al., 2024; Deitke et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025) have established Vision–Language–Action (VLA) (Intelligence et al., 2025b; Kim et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025b) models as a prominent paradigm for robotic manipulation. Although imitation learning (IL) from large-scale robot demonstrations enables VLA models to acquire diverse manipulation skills, its performance is inherently constrained by the coverage of the demonstration data. Reinforcement learning (RL) overcomes this limitation by directly optimizing policies with task feedback obtained through environment interaction, and recent work (Li et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026) has successfully applied RL to VLA models. However, existing VLA-RL methods still face substantial challenges in long-horizon manipulation tasks.

First, most methods rely on terminal-only success rewards. In an episode that completes the first $k$ subtasks but fails at subtask $k+1$ , the absence of a terminal success reward causes generalized advantage estimation (GAE) to propagate failure-related temporal-difference (TD) residuals backward to $t_{0}$ , suppressing the advantages of correctly executed actions. We refer to this as credit contamination, where useful behavior in failed trajectories is systematically devalued, with the effect worsening as the horizon grows.
Prior work (Chen et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026a; Tan et al., 2025; Zhai et al., 2025) mitigates reward sparsity through stage-level preference optimization or subtask-level intermediate rewards, but these approaches alter reward density without resolving credit contamination.
Second, subtask mastery is uneven, with failures increasingly concentrated in a few bottleneck subtasks during later training. Uniform task sampling and fixed exploration then waste interaction budget on saturated subtasks while providing insufficient exploration for the bottlenecks.

Figure 1: Overview of AtomicRL. Unlike previous RL methods that use standard GAE which may suffer from credit contamination, AtomicRL uses SAPO to promote more reliable credit assignment. Together with BATE and the Real2Sim2Real pipeline, AtomicRL achieves strong performance on long-horizon manipulation tasks in both simulation and the real world.

To address these challenges, we propose AtomicRL, as illustrated in Fig. 1, an RL post-training framework built around atomic task structure. Our key insight is that semantic subtasks provide a unified basis for both the propagation of learning signals and the allocation of exploration resources. AtomicRL couples Semantic-Aware Policy Optimization (SAPO) with Bottleneck-Adaptive Target Exploration (BATE), supported by a lightweight Progress–Completion Critic (PCC) that estimates atomic subtask progress and completion boundaries. PCC also provides progress estimates for constructing dense progress-based shaping rewards (PBSR).
SAPO modulates TD-residual propagation in advantage estimation with a soft gate conditioned on semantic boundaries. Within each atomic subtask, it preserves standard GAE trace decay; across subtask boundaries, it maintains propagation between successful subtasks while attenuating residuals from failed subtasks. By leaving one-step TD residuals and value bootstrapping unchanged, SAPO reduces failure interference while preserving intra-subtask credit assignment and successful subtask dependencies.
BATE tracks the mastery of each subtask via a moving average of its completion rate, jointly adjusts the sampling weight of full tasks and the strength of subtask-level entropy regularization, directing interaction and exploration resources toward bottleneck subtasks.
Finally, to support physical deployment, we develop an automated Real2Sim2Real pipeline. Given a single real-world multimodal demonstration and the required auxiliary information, the pipeline reconstructs an interactive simulation environment. It connects simulation-based RL with real-robot deployment, shifting costly physical trial-and-error to parallel simulation with reproducible resets.

We conduct extensive experiments in both simulation and the real world. On LIBERO-LONG (Liu et al., 2023) AtomicRL achieves success rates of 99.0% with $\pi_{0.5}$ (Intelligence et al., 2025b) and 98.8% with OpenVLA-OFT (Kim et al., 2025), improving over PPO by 3.6% and 4.0%. On CALVIN ABC-D (Mees et al., 2022), the average completed sequence length improves from 3.56 to 4.56, while the success rate of completing full five-subtask chain improves by 9.5% over PPO.
Combined with the Real2Sim2Real pipeline, AtomicRL further yields an average improvement of 21.3% on real-robot long-horizon tasks. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of AtomicRL for long-horizon VLA reinforcement learning. Overall, our contributions are as follows:

• 

We introduce AtomicRL, an RL post-training framework built around atomic task structure for long-horizon robotic manipulation.

• 

We propose SAPO to mitigate cross-subtask credit interference and BATE to adaptively direct task sampling and exploration toward bottleneck subtasks.

• 

We develop a Real2Sim2Real pipeline that streamlines simulation construction and RL training for efficient real-robot deployment.

• 

We validate the effectiveness of AtomicRL through extensive experiments conducted in both simulated environments and real-world robots.

## 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Reinforcement Learning for VLA Models

Reinforcement learning (RL) optimizes policies through environment interaction and task-level feedback. Recent work has explored both offline and online RL paradigms for VLA policies. Offline RL approaches leverage task feedback to enable continued policy improvement (Huang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2025a). $\pi_{0.6}^{*}$ (Intelligence et al., 2025a) integrates expert demonstrations, autonomous interaction data, and human corrections through advantage-conditioned learning. For scalable online training, VLA-RL (Lu et al., 2025) and SimpleVLA-RL (Li et al., 2026) explore frameworks for continually improving VLA policies through environment interaction, while RL4VLA (Liu et al., 2026) systematically investigates how different RL algorithms affect VLA generalization. Furthermore, Flow Q-Learning (Park et al., 2025), Flow-GRPO (Liu et al., 2025a) and $\pi_{RL}$ (Chen et al., 2026a) investigate online RL fine-tuning for flow-matching policies, addressing challenges in action likelihood computation and exploration.

RL for long-horizon manipulation introduces additional challenges due to sparse and delayed task feedback (Chen et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2025c; Dalal et al., 2024). STARE-VLA (Xu et al., 2025) exploits the semantic stage structure of trajectories to perform stage-level preference optimization and reward shaping, while IG-RFT (Su et al., 2026) combines trajectory-level and subtask-level rewards to provide intermediate guidance. However, dense reward shaping provides useful process guidance over long-horizon trajectories, but cannot eliminate the spurious interference caused by later-stage failures.
In contrast, AtomicRL gates the propagation of advantage signals at the semantic boundaries of atomic tasks to prevent cross-task interference from unreliable signals, while allocating the exploration budget to bottleneck atomic tasks to improve the efficiency of long-horizon RL.

## 2.2 Online Reinforcement Learning in Real World

Online reinforcement learning for real-world manipulation is constrained by interaction costs and safety risks. To reduce reliance on real-robot trial and error, some research focuses on learning action-conditioned world models and optimizing policies through imagined interactions (Team et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2026c; Jiang et al., 2026a). WoVR (Jiang et al., 2026b) addresses prediction errors and their accumulation to improve the reliability of model-generated rollouts for VLA reinforcement fine-tuning
, while PlayWorld (Yin et al., 2026) and RISE (Yang et al., 2026b) learn world models from autonomous robot interactions and transfers policies trained through model-based reinforcement learning to real hardware.
Although world models can effectively capture short-term dynamics, long-horizon predictions still exhibit visual distortions and action–state inconsistencies. Other studies adopt an explicit Real2Sim2Real method, combining real-scene reconstruction with physics simulation to provide interactive environments for policy optimization (Li et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2026). GSWorld (Jiang et al., 2025) integrates Gaussian-on-Mesh assets with physics engines to support visually faithful policy training, while
RialTo (Torne et al., 2024) constructs digital twins of real-world environments and uses reinforcement learning in simulation to improve policy robustness.
However, constructing environments requires coordinating scene reconstruction, physical asset preparation, and control alignment, making it complex and costly to reproduce. AtomicRL introduces an automated Real2Sim2Real pipeline that uses only a single demonstration to reconstruct a real-world manipulation scene as an interactive simulation environment for long-horizon online RL. The trained policies are then transferred to physical robots for evaluation.

Figure 2: Overall pipeline of AtomicRL. (a) Progress–Completion Critic: PCC identifies atomic task boundaries and estimates atomic task progress from interaction histories. (b) Semantic-Aware Policy Optimization: SAPO uses these signals to regulate cross-subtask advantage propagation based on subtask execution outcomes. (c) Bottleneck-Adaptive Targeted Exploration: BATE adapts task sampling and local exploration according to subtask mastery, focusing training on insufficiently mastered bottleneck subtasks. (d) Real2Sim2Real workflow: A complementary Real2Sim2Real pipeline enables parallel simulation-based training and transfer to real-world robots.

## 3 Method

## 3.1 Overview

As illustrated in Figure 2, AtomicRL integrates semantic-aware credit assignment and bottleneck-adaptive exploration for long-horizon robotic manipulation. Specifically, SAPO modulates credit propagation across atomic subtasks (Section 3.2), while bottleneck-adaptive targeted exploration adjusts full-task trajectory sampling and local exploration incentives (Section 3.3). Both components are supported by a Progress–Completion Critic (PCC), which estimates subtask progress and identifies completion boundaries (Section 3.4). For real-world tasks, we further introduce a Real2Sim2Real construction workflow to support simulation training and subsequent transfer evaluation (Section 3.5).

## 3.1.1 Problem Formulation

We consider a language-conditioned partially observable Markov decision process for long-horizon robotic manipulation. At each decision step $t$ , the robot receives an observation $o_{t}$ , which may include third-person images, wrist-camera images, and proprioceptive states, and outputs an action chunk $a_{t}=(a_{t,1},\ldots,a_{t,H_{a}})$ , where $H_{a}$ denotes the chunk length. A long-horizon instruction is decomposed into an ordered sequence of $K$ atomic subtasks, $G=(g_{1},\ldots,g_{K})$ . We denote the active subtask index by $z_{t}\in{1,\ldots,K}$ . For nonterminal transitions, the semantic-boundary indicator is defined as $b_{t}=\mathbb{I}[z_{t+1}\neq z_{t}]$ , indicating whether execution of $a_{t}$ leads to a subtask transition. Our objective is to maximize full-task success under a fixed environment-interaction budget by improving credit assignment and directing exploration toward bottleneck subtasks.

## 3.2 Semantic-Aware Policy Optimization

SAPO addresses temporal credit assignment in long-horizon tasks. It leverages semantic boundaries to selectively attenuate the contribution of TD residuals from failed subtasks to the advantage estimates of preceding actions, thereby regulating cross-subtask credit propagation.

Let $r_{t}$ denote the chunk-level reward and $d_{t}$ indicate environment termination after executing $a_{t}$ . The one-step TD residual is

 $\delta_{t}=r_{t}+\gamma(1-d_{t})V_{\phi}(s_{t+1})-V_{\phi}(s_{t}),$ 

(1)

where $\gamma$ is the discount factor and $s_{t}$ denotes the observation- and language-conditioned input representation available to the value function, rather than a privileged simulator state. For an episode containing $T$ chunk-level transitions indexed by $t=1,\ldots,T$ , the standard GAE estimate used by PPO is

 $\hat{A}^{\mathrm{PPO}}_{t}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{T-t}(\gamma\lambda)^{\ell}\delta_{t+\ell},$ 

(2)

where $\lambda\in[0,1]$ controls trace decay. This expression is evaluated within a single episode and does not span environment resets.

SAPO distinguishes semantic segmentation from environment termination and uses atomic subtask outcomes to regulate cross-boundary credit propagation. Specifically, PCC (Section 3.4) identifies semantic boundaries $b_{t}$ between atomic subtasks. Keeping the one-step TD residual unchanged, SAPO applies an outcome-aware soft gate to the recursive GAE trace:

 $\hat{A}^{\mathrm{SAPO}}_{t}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{T-t}(\gamma\lambda)^{\ell}\left[\prod_{j=0}^{\ell-1}\left(1-(1-\kappa_{t+j})b_{t+j}\right)\right]\delta_{t+\ell},\qquad\kappa_{t}\in[0,1].$ 

(3)

Within a subtask, $b_{t}=0$ , and the trace follows the standard $\gamma\lambda$ decay. At a semantic boundary, $\kappa_{t}=1$ when the subsequent subtask succeeds, preserving ordinary propagation; when it fails, we set $0<\kappa_{t}<1$ to attenuate propagation across the boundary. Thus, when subtasks $1{:}k$ succeed but subtask $k+1$ fails, residuals from the failed segment propagate normally within that segment and are additionally attenuated when entering the completed prefix. Residuals within the completed prefix retain their standard trace weights. This design preserves within-task credit propagation and connections between successfully completed subtasks while reducing the direct negative influence of downstream failures on earlier successful behavior. We use the resulting advantages for updates and construct the value targets as $V_{\phi}(s_{t})+\hat{A}^{\mathrm{SAPO}}_{t}$ before advantage normalization. By making credit propagation sensitive to semantic boundaries and local outcomes, SAPO improves credit assignment and interaction-data efficiency in long-horizon tasks.

## 3.3 Bottleneck-Adaptive Targeted Exploration

During the early stages of RL, broad exploration provides informative samples for most atomic subtasks. As training approaches saturation, failures may concentrate in a few bottleneck subtasks, making persistent aggressive exploration less effective and potentially disruptive to acquired skills. BATE adapts task sampling and local exploration incentives according to atomic subtask mastery.

We estimate the mastery level of each atomic-task category using an exponential moving average of its completion rate:

 $\mu_{k}^{(n)}=\beta\mu_{k}^{(n-1)}+(1-\beta)\hat{s}_{k}^{(n)},\qquad\beta\in[0,1),$ 

(4)

where $n$ indexes statistics updates and $\hat{s}_{k}^{(n)}$ is the fraction of successful outcomes among subtask attempts whose outcomes are resolved during the update.

The competence gap, $1-\mu_{k}$ , guides both full-task sampling and local exploration.

 $w_{i}=1+\rho\left[\max_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{i}}(1-\mu_{k})\right]^{\eta},\qquad P_{\mathrm{task}}(i)=\frac{w_{i}}{\sum_{j}w_{j}},$ 

(5)

where $\mathcal{K}_{i}$ contains the subtasks of full task $i$ , $\eta>0$ controls sensitivity to the competence gap, and $\rho\geq 0$ limits sampling redistribution. The baseline weight of $1$ preserves coverage of mastered tasks to monitor forgetting.

Within each trajectory, mastery-dependent entropy regularization adjusts local exploration:

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{explore}}=-\alpha_{H}\mathbb{E}_{t}\left[f_{\mathrm{exp}}\!\left(1-\mu_{z_{t}}^{(n)}\right)\mathcal{H}_{\theta,t}\right],$ 

(6)

where $\alpha_{H}$ is the base entropy coefficient, $\mathcal{H}_{\theta,t}$ denotes policy entropy, and $f_{\mathrm{exp}}$ is a bounded exploration weight for t
conclusion: In this work, we introduce AtomicRL, a VLA RL post-training framework for long-horizon robotic manipulation centered on atomic task structure. To address temporal credit interference and imbalanced atomic subtask mastery, AtomicRL uses PCC to estimate task progress and completion boundaries, SAPO to regulate the cross-boundary propagation of TD residuals based on subtask execution outcomes, and BATE to shift task sampling and local exploration toward insufficiently mastered bottleneck subtasks. We further develop a Real2Sim2Real pipeline that connects real-task reconstruction, simulation-based RL, and real-robot deployment, enabling policy improvement in simulation environments with fast parallel interactions and reproducible resets. We validate AtomicRL in both simulation and real-world settings, and the results show that it converges faster to a higher performance level, demonstrating its potential for RL-based long-horizon robotic manipulation.

title: Parallel AI Agent Collaboration as Graph-Structured Distributed Block Optimization
abstract: Parallel AI agents can produce useful local edits yet degrade a shared solution when their edits are combined. We model this coordination problem as discrete block optimization with an exactly evaluable objective and a known dependency graph. Independent sets certify compatible edits whose verified gains, measured against the same current solution, add exactly. A coordinator constructs a safe compatible candidate and can also evaluate interacting edits to capture favorable interactions. We prove that an optimal fractional coloring yields a merger that preserves a $1/χ_f(G)$ fraction of the total verified local improvement, where $χ_f(G)$ is the graph's fractional chromatic number. This guarantee is tight among mergers that select a subset of the same proposals. Under conditional local-improvement guarantees and a block error-bound condition, repeated collaboration converges geometrically in the objective gap. The rate separates task structure, agent allocation, and computation cost, yielding a linear program for agent assignment and an explicit time-cost trade-off. Code-repair experiments show that verified merging resolves conflicts between individually useful edits that cause naive merging to fail. On larger conflict-free tasks, parallel agents reduce modeled completion time at higher input-token-equivalent cost. On three public road networks, fractional integration retains 922 units of verified graph-cut improvement across 90 paired runs. For route-search agents sharing exclusive access to vehicle routes, fractional scheduling reduces measured wall time by a median of 15% across twelve paired runs, with route-cost changes varying across runs.

body_start:
Abstract.

Parallel AI agents can each produce useful local edits yet degrade a shared solution when their edits are combined. We model this coordination problem as discrete block optimization with an exactly evaluable objective and a known dependency graph. The graph certifies compatible sets of edits through its independent sets, and evaluating proposals against the same current solution yields verified gains that add exactly within any such set. A coordinator can therefore construct a safe compatible candidate while additionally evaluating interacting edits to capture favorable interactions. We prove that, using an optimal fractional coloring, the safe merger preserves a $1/\chi_{f}(G)$ fraction of the total verified local improvement, where $\chi_{f}(G)$ is the fractional chromatic number of the dependency graph. We further show that no merger restricted to selecting a subset of the same proposals can guarantee a larger fraction in general. Under conditional local-improvement guarantees and a block error-bound condition, repeated collaboration converges geometrically in the objective gap, separating the effects of task structure, agent allocation, and computation cost. The resulting rate gives a linear program for agent assignment and an explicit time–cost trade-off. We complement the analysis with experiments on solution quality and the cost of parallel coordination. Code-repair experiments show that verified merging resolves conflicts between individually useful edits that cause naive merging to fail. On larger conflict-free tasks, parallel agents reduce modeled completion time at higher input-token-equivalent cost. On three public road networks, fractional integration retains 922 units of verified graph-cut improvement across 90 paired runs. For route-search agents sharing exclusive access to vehicle routes, fractional scheduling reduces measured wall time by a median of 15% across twelve paired runs, with route-cost changes varying across runs.

Keywords: 
multi-agent systems, generative AI agents, coordination, combinatorial optimization, resource and task allocation, distributed block optimization, fractional graph coloring

## 1. Introduction

Many tasks handled by AI agents can be decomposed into components that are worked on in parallel.
This can reduce latency and distribute work across components, but it also creates a coordination problem.
An edit that improves one component in isolation may interact with edits to other components once they are combined.
Program repair provides a concrete example: agents may modify different modules in parallel, yet their changes can still interfere through shared functionality or interfaces.
The central question is therefore not only how to generate useful local edits, but also how to decide which of them can be safely integrated into the shared solution.

For example, suppose a program must apply a discount exactly once, and either the pricing module or the checkout module can implement the required transformation.
Starting from a version that does not apply the discount, an edit to either module improves the program on its own.
If both edits are applied, however, the discount is applied twice.
Thus, individually useful edits to different modules need not be compatible.

The example exposes a broader coordination problem in parallel agent work.
A proposed edit can be evaluated in isolation against the current artifact, yet its value may change when other edits are applied alongside it.
We therefore separate proposal generation from proposal integration.
Agents work concurrently from the same artifact on distinct blocks, while a coordinator uses an evaluator and dependency information to decide which returned edits to combine.
Our goal is to determine how much of the verified local improvement can be guaranteed to be retained after integration.

We call this problem verified proposal integration.
The coordinator observes black-box block proposals, their verified singleton gains against a common base artifact, and a dependency certificate identifying subsets whose gains add exactly.
It need not know how the proposals were generated or model their joint effects beyond this certificate.
We ask how much of the verified local improvement a coordinator can always preserve using only this information.
Our main result is a tight worst-case bound for integrating fixed proposals. We extend the analysis to convergence and agent allocation under additional assumptions. Experiments examine the integration mechanism and its cost.

## Contributions.

• 

We formulate verified proposal integration for black-box agent edits and characterize its exact worst-case retention factor.
Given verified singleton gains and a dependency certificate, a coordinator can always preserve a $1/\chi_{f}(G)$ fraction of the total verified local improvement.
This guarantee is tight: in the worst case, no coordinator that forms its update by selecting a subset of the submitted proposals can guarantee a larger fraction (Sections 2–3).

• 

Under explicit assumptions on agent capability, assignment coverage, and task structure, we establish geometric convergence of repeated verified integration.
The convergence rate separates the effects of these three factors and yields a principled formulation for agent assignment and explicit time–cost trade-offs (Sections 4–5).

• 

We test proposal integration and its costs with language-model agents and use controlled examples to clarify the guarantees.
The experiments examine conflict resolution among individually useful edits, performance on held-out multi-round tasks, and the time–cost trade-off of parallel execution. A road-network diagnostic evaluates exact-factor merging on naturally occurring block interactions and compares fractional integration with fixed and adaptive ordinary coloring (Section 6).

## Related work.

Our formulation builds on ideas from parallel and distributed optimization, where multiple components are updated concurrently while accounting for their interactions.
In particular, it is closely related to parallel block coordinate descent and arbitrary sampling, which study how subsets of coordinates can be updated simultaneously (Richtárik and Takáč, 2016; Qu and Richtárik, 2016).
Within this line of work, Bradley et al. (2011) analyze interference among parallel coordinate updates using a spectral measure.
A complementary perspective appears in GenCD, which separates coordinate descent into selection, proposal, acceptance, and update stages and includes a coloring-based variant (Scherrer et al., 2012).
Our setting differs in two important ways.
First, proposals may be arbitrary discrete edits rather than gradient-based coordinate updates.
Second, the coordinator observes verified singleton gains and a dependency certificate without requiring a smooth model of their joint effects.

Distributed constraint optimization (DCOP) coordinates agents that control different variables to optimize a shared objective expressed through local functions (Modi et al., 2005; Fioretto et al., 2018; Troullinos et al., 2025).
This is closely related in spirit to our use of localized dependencies, but the coordination problem is different.
In DCOP, agents coordinate the choice of variable assignments themselves.
In our setting, agents have already generated candidate edits, and the coordinator decides which submitted proposals to combine using their verified singleton gains and a dependency certificate.
Our focus is therefore on verified integration of independently generated proposals rather than distributed search over the solution space.

Language-model agents have increasingly been applied to software development and repair.
MetaGPT and ChatDev organize software development through structured roles and multi-agent collaboration (Hong et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2024).
MAGIS and MASAI decompose repository-level software tasks across specialized agents (Tao et al., 2024; Arora et al., 2024).
RepairAgent instead focuses on autonomous program repair through tool use and iterative validation (Bouzenia et al., 2025), while a recent survey reviews the broader use of multi-agent systems across the software-development lifecycle (He et al., 2025).
These works focus primarily on how software agents generate, coordinate, and refine solutions.
We instead isolate the integration step, where independently generated edits must be reconciled into a single shared artifact.

A separate line of work studies how collaboration structures among agents should be designed or adapted.
GPTSwarm represents agent systems as optimizable computational graphs (Zhuge et al., 2024), while DyLAN dynamically selects agents and communication structures (Liu et al., 2024).
Hyperagent uses hypergraphs for the topology of multi-agent communication (Zhang et al., 2026).
These methods focus on structuring how agents interact during problem solving.
By contrast, our dependency graph represents interactions among components of the shared artifact rather than communication links among agents.
It identifies subsets of proposed edits whose verified gains add exactly and thereby supports their certified integration.

## 2. Problem Formulation

## Blocks and objective.

We represent the current shared artifact as $x=(x_{b})_{b=1}^{m}$ , where each block $x_{b}$ corresponds to one component of the solution, such as a program module.
For $b\in[m]\coloneqq\{1,\ldots,m\}$ , let $\mathcal{X}_{b}$ be the nonempty finite set of admissible values for block $b$ .
The resulting search space is $\mathcal{X}=\prod_{b=1}^{m}\mathcal{X}_{b}$ .

We evaluate an artifact using a known loss function $F:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}$ , where smaller values are better.
For example, in program repair, $F$ may count failed checks or combine penalties derived from an explicit evaluation rubric.
For $y\in\mathcal{X}_{b}$ , we write $(x_{-b},y)$ for the artifact obtained by replacing $x_{b}$ with $y$ while leaving all other blocks unchanged.
We define

(1)

 $\begin{gathered}F^{\star}\coloneqq\min_{x\in\mathcal{X}}F(x),\quad\Delta(x)\coloneqq F(x)-F^{\star},\\
D_{b}(x)\coloneqq F(x)-\min_{y\in\mathcal{X}_{b}}F(x_{-b},y).\end{gathered}$ 

Here $\Delta(x)$ is the global objective gap, while $D_{b}(x)$ is the largest improvement obtainable by modifying block $b$ alone.

## Dependency structure.

The loss need not separate across blocks, since edits to different blocks may affect the same part of the objective.
We capture these interactions through a factorization with known block dependencies.

Assumption 1 (Dependency Structure).

The objective admits a decomposition

(2)

 $F(x)=\sum_{a=1}^{M}\ell_{a}(x_{N(a)}),$ 

where $M$ is the number of objective factors and each factor $\ell_{a}$ depends only on the blocks indexed by the known set $N(a)\subseteq[m]$ .

This factorization induces a dependency graph $G$ whose vertices correspond to the blocks.
Two blocks $b$ and $c$ are connected by an edge whenever some factor depends on both.
An independent set in $G$ therefore contains blocks that never appear together in the same objective factor.
Edits to blocks in an independent set are compatible in the sense that no factor is affected by more than one of them.

We refer to the known factor scopes, or any graph that conservatively encodes them, as a dependency certificate.
Such a certificate ensures that blocks in the same independent set do not affect a common objective factor.
In program repair, it may be obtained from declared test–module scopes, interface dependencies, or conservative static analysis.
What matters is shared dependence in the objective rather than physical overlap between the edited components.
Adding extra edges to $G$ preserves the validity of the certificate but may weaken the resulting guarantee.
Omitting a true dependency, however, may incorrectly classify interacting edits as compatible.

For the pricing and checkout example from the introduction, let $x_{1},x_{2}\in\{0,1\}$ indicate whether the pricing and checkout modules apply the discount, and let $x_{3}\in\{0,1\}$ indicate whether an independent receipt defect is repaired.
Consider

(3)

 $F(x)=2(1-x_{1}-x_{2})^{2}+(1-x_{3}).$ 

The first term depends jointly on blocks $1$ and $2$ , while the second depends only on block $3$ .
The resulting dependency graph therefore contains only the edge $1$ – $2$ .
One valid coloring has color classes $\{1,3\}$ and $\{2\}$ , as shown in Figure 2.

## Assignments and verified proposals.

Suppose $n\geq 1$ agents are available, indexed by $[n]\coloneqq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ .
Given a current artifact $x$ , an assignment $\mathcal{M}\subseteq[n]\times[m]$ matches each agent to at most one block and each block to at most one agent.
Each assigned agent receives $x$ together with its designated block, works independently for a time budget $h>0$ , and returns a proposed replacement for that block.

Before combining any proposals, the evaluator tests each one separately against the same base artifact $x$ , leaving all other blocks unchanged.
A proposal is retained only if it is valid, returned within the time budget, and reduces $F$ .
Otherwise, the original block value is retained.
For each assigned pair $(i,b)\in\mathcal{M}$ , let $Y_{ib}$ denote the resulting value of block $b$ after this filtering step.
Its verified singleton gain is

(4)

 $g_{ib}\coloneqq F(x)-F(x_{-b},Y_{ib})\geq 0.$ 

We call this separate evaluation of each proposal against the common base artifact singleton verification.

## 3. Verified Proposal Integration

Singleton verification ensures that every retained proposal improves the common base when applied alone, but it does not determine how those proposals should be combined.

In the running example (3), start from $(0,0,0)$ with loss $3$ and let each agent propose setting its block to one.
The three verified singleton gains are $2$ , $2$ , and $1$ .
Applying all three proposals gives $(1,1,1)$ with loss $2$ , while applying only blocks $1$ and $3$ gives loss $0$ .
Thus, even accepting the full union whenever it improves $F$ can miss a substantially better compatible subset.

## Certified integration.

Let $\mathcal{I}(G)$ denote the collection of independent sets of $G$ .
A fractional coloring $\lambda$ assigns a nonnegative weight $\lambda_{I}$ to each independent set $I\in\mathcal{I}(G)$ so that every block is covered by independent sets with total weight at least one.
This fractional-cover view connects to classical work on fractional coloring and covers (Lovász, 1975; Alon et al., 1997); distributed algorithms for fractional coloring are studied by Bousquet et al. (2021).
The total weight of $\lambda$ is $\Lambda(\lambda)$ , and the fractional chromatic number $\chi_{f}(G)$ is the minimum such weight:

(5)

 $\displaystyle\Lambda(\lambda)$ 
 $\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{I\in\mathcal{I}(G)}\lambda_{I},$ 

 $\displaystyle\chi_{f}(G)$ 
 $\displaystyle\coloneqq\min_{\lambda}\Lambda(\lambda)$ 

 $\displaystyle\text{s.t.}\qquad\lambda_{I}$ 
 $\displaystyle\geq 0,\qquad I\in\mathcal{I}(G),$ 

 $\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}I\in\mathcal{I}(G)\\
b\in I\end{subarray}}\lambda_{I}$ 
 $\displaystyle\geq 1,\qquad b\in[m].$ 

To state the integration rule over repeated rounds, we index collaboration rounds by $k$ .
At the beginning of round $k$ , let $x^{k}$ denote the common base artifact, let $\mathcal{M}_{k}$ denote the assignment, and let $g_{ib}^{k}$ denote the verified singleton gain of proposal $(i,b)\in\mathcal{M}_{k}$ as defined above.

Fix any feasible fractional coloring $\lambda$ and write $\Lambda=\Lambda(\lambda)$ .
Only independent sets with $\lambda_{I}>0$ need to be considered in the merge rule.
For each such set $I$ , let $x^{k,I}$ denote the candidate obtained from $x^{k}$ by applying the retained proposals whose blocks belong to $I$ .
Because $I$ is independent, these proposals are compatible and their verified singleton gains add exactly.
We therefore score $I$ by

(6)

 $W_{I}^{k}\coloneqq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(i,b)\in\mathcal{M}_{k}\\
b\in I\end{subarray}}g_{ib}^{k}.$ 

The coordinator then selects a highest-scoring independent set among those with $\lambda_{I}>0$ and applies its proposals:

(7)

 $I_{k}\in\argmax_{I:\lambda_{I}>0}W_{I}^{k},\qquad x^{k,\mathrm{safe}}\coloneqq x^{k,I_{k}}.$ 

Ties in the choice of $I_{k}$ are broken by a fixed rule.
The following theorem shows that this rule guarantees a fixed fraction of the total verified singleton gain for every realized collection of agent proposals, regardless of how those proposals were generated.

Theorem 1 (Certified gain retention).

Let $\lambda$ be any feasible fractional coloring with total weight $\Lambda=\Lambda(\lambda)$ .
Under Assumption 1, for every realization of the agent proposals,

(8)

 $F(x^{k})-F(x^{k,\mathrm{safe}})\geq\frac{1}{\Lambda}\sum_{(i,b)\in\mathcal{M}_{k}}g_{ib}^{k}\geq 0.$ 

In particular, an optimal fractional coloring gives $\Lambda=\chi_{f}(G)$ and therefore retains at least a $1/\chi_{f}(G)$ fraction of the total verified singleton gain.

Proof.

For readability, suppress the round index $k$ and write $x=x^{k}$ , $\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{M}_{k}$ , $g_{ib}=g_{ib}^{k}$ , and $W_{I}=W_{I}^{k}$ .
Fix any $I\in\mathcal{I}(G)$ with $\lambda_{I}>0$ .

conclusion:
We formulate parallel agent collaboration as verified proposal integration. Evaluating proposals against a common artifact yields local gains, while the dependency graph identifies compatible sets whose gains add exactly. Fractional coloring gives the tight worst-case retention factor $1/\chi_{f}(G)$ , and evaluating the full union allows the coordinator to capture favorable interactions. Under the local-improvement and block error-bound assumptions, repeated integration converges geometrically. The rate separates task structure, agent allocation, and proposal integration, providing a basis for choosing assignments and balancing progress against time and cost.

The experiments show how compatibility shapes both the quality and cost of parallel work. Selecting compatible proposals resolves conflicts between individually useful repairs and improves retained gain over a fixed coloring on road-network objectives. Adaptive ordinary coloring matches the latter result, linking the improvement to the compatible sets considered. Parallel execution reduces modeled completion time on larger compatible repair tasks at higher input cost, while fractional scheduling shortens measured route-search time under exclusive route access. These results connect the integration of local edits and the scheduling of parallel work through their shared dependency structure.

title: From Reasoning to Action: Benchmarking Frontier AI Models on LIBERO-10 Robot Manipulation Tasks
abstract: Recent advances in frontier AI models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, planning, and tool use, raising the possibility of using general-purpose AI models for robot manipulation without task-specific training. However, their manipulation capabilities have not been systematically evaluated on standardized robotics benchmarks. In this report, we present a unified closed-loop manipulation framework for evaluating frontier AI models on the LIBERO-10 benchmark. Our framework enables models to control a robot directly through visual observations, robot proprioception, and structured tool calls, primarily by specifying target end-effector poses and gripper commands, without task-specific fine-tuning or pretrained manipulation skills. We evaluate six frontier AI models, including GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini-4 Argon, across three reasoning effort levels, resulting in 18 configurations and 1,800 evaluation episodes. Our results show that GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest success rate of 44%, followed by Gemini-4 Argon at 43%. Increasing reasoning effort generally improves manipulation performance, but the benefits vary across models and come at additional inference cost. We also observe substantial differences across tasks, with models performing relatively well on object placement tasks but struggling with precise spatial arrangements and complex multi-step interactions. These findings demonstrate both the potential and limitations of frontier AI models for robot manipulation, highlighting the challenges of translating reasoning capabilities into reliable physical actions. We release our evaluation framework and experimental results to support reproducible benchmarking and future research on reasoning-based robot manipulation.
