ABSTRACT

Recent advances in frontier AI models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, planning, and tool use, raising the possibility of using general-purpose AI models for robot manipulation without task-specific training. However, their manipulation capabilities have not been systematically evaluated on standardized robotics benchmarks. In this report, we present a unified closed-loop manipulation framework for evaluating frontier AI models on the LIBERO-10 benchmark. Our framework enables models to control a robot directly through visual observations, robot proprioception, and structured tool calls, primarily by specifying target end-effector poses and gripper commands, without task-specific fine-tuning or pretrained manipulation skills. We evaluate six frontier AI models, including GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini-4 Argon, across three reasoning effort levels, resulting in 18 configurations and 1,800 evaluation episodes. Our results show that GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest success rate of 44%, followed by Gemini-4 Argon at 43%. Increasing reasoning effort generally improves manipulation performance, but the benefits vary across models and come at additional inference cost. We also observe substantial differences across tasks, with models performing relatively well on object placement tasks but struggling with precise spatial arrangements and complex multi-step interactions. These findings demonstrate both the potential and limitations of frontier AI models for robot manipulation, highlighting the challenges of translating reasoning capabilities into reliable physical actions. We release our evaluation framework and experimental results to support reproducible benchmarking and future research on reasoning-based robot manipulation.

## 1  Introduction

Recent advances in frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, planning, and tool use Arena AI [2026]. In particular, recent demonstrations of GPT-6 Astra have shown impressive robot manipulation behaviors, including interpreting visual observations, generating robot actions, and correcting mistakes through closed-loop interaction Zhang et al. [2026], Su et al. [2026], Team et al. [2026]. NVIDIA’s Astranomy report Yang et al. [2026a] further demonstrates the potential of frontier AI models for robot manipulation through different control configurations, including direct action generation, agentic tool use, and supervision of pretrained robot policies. These results suggest that general-purpose AI models may be capable of performing robot manipulation without task-specific policy training.

Despite these promising demonstrations, an important question remains: How well do frontier AI models perform on established robot manipulation benchmarks? Existing evaluations often use different tasks, robot platforms, and control interfaces, making systematic comparisons difficult. Connecting frontier AI models to standardized benchmarks is essential for understanding their capabilities, identifying limitations, and comparing their performance with conventional robot learning approaches.

Motivated by this question, we develop a unified manipulation pipeline to evaluate frontier AI models on LIBERO-10 (also known as LIBERO-Long) Liu et al. [2023], a subset of LIBERO-100 containing ten held-out, long-horizon manipulation tasks. LIBERO-10 has been widely adopted for evaluating robot learning methods, including generalist robot policies and vision-language-action models such as Octo Team et al. [2024], OpenVLA Kim et al. [2024], $\pi_{0.5}$ Intelligence et al. [2025], UniVLA Bu et al. [2025] and UniAct Zheng et al. [2025]. Built upon the open-source Inspect Robots framework Robocurve [2026], our pipeline enables frontier AI models to interact with the simulation environment through visual observations and structured tool calls, allowing closed-loop manipulation without task-specific training or fine-tuning. We evaluate multiple frontier AI models, including GPT and Claude models, under a common protocol, exploring different reasoning modes to investigate the impact of reasoning effort on manipulation performance. Beyond task success rates, we analyze API calls, inference latency, token usage, and monetary cost to understand the tradeoffs between reasoning capabilities, manipulation performance, and efficiency.

Our work provides a standardized evaluation of frontier AI models on robot manipulation tasks, offering insights into their capabilities and limitations. By releasing our code and evaluation results, we provide reproducible, ready-to-use baselines for future research, reducing the need to repeatedly evaluate these computationally expensive models and lowering evaluation costs.

## 2  Closed-Loop Manipulation with Frontier AI Models

Figure 1: Overview of our closed-loop manipulation framework using frontier AI models. 

We evaluate frontier AI models, including GPT-6, Claude Opus, and Gemini, directly as closed-loop robot manipulation policies, without robot-specific training, demonstrations, or pretrained skill libraries. Unlike approaches that use AI models to generate robot code or orchestrate predefined skills Xiao et al. [2026], Lu et al. [2026], Chen et al. [2026], Yang et al. [2026b], our pipeline focuses on evaluating the models’ intrinsic visual understanding, spatial reasoning, and action planning capabilities. Given raw camera observations, the models must identify objects, estimate their 3D positions, and plan robot motions through a minimal action interface, without relying on external perception, planning, or manipulation skills. This design allows us to assess how effectively frontier AI models can translate their own reasoning into robot actions.

Figure 1 illustrates our closed-loop manipulation pipeline. At each interaction step, the model receives a fixed system prompt, the task instruction, the interaction history, and the latest observation, including camera images and robot state information (Sec. 2.1). Based on these inputs, the model generates a single tool call: move_to specifies a target end-effector pose and gripper command, while done and give_up terminate the episode (Sec. 2.2). For each move_to call, an action adapter translates the target into a sequence of low-level robot commands, which are executed step by step in the LIBERO simulator. Task success is checked after every control step. If the task remains incomplete after the action sequence finishes, updated observations and execution feedback are returned to the model for the next decision (Sec. 2.3). This process continues until the task succeeds, the model terminates the episode, or the evaluation limits are reached. All experiments are conducted in a zero-shot setting, using a task-agnostic system prompt without task-specific hints or demonstrations.

## 2.1  Observations and Prompt Context

## Observations.

Each observation contains two $256\times 256$ RGB images, from the fixed third-person (agentview) camera and the wrist camera, together with the robot state. The robot state has 12 values: the end-effector position $(x,y,z)$ in meters in the world frame, its orientation in the 6D rotation representation (the first two columns of the rotation matrix), the current gripper command, and the two measured finger positions. The gripper command only records whether the model last asked the gripper to open or close; the measured finger positions show where the fingers actually stopped, so the model can tell whether it closed on an object or on nothing. Each observation is sent as one message: the robot state as text, followed by the two labeled camera images. The model never sees object poses or the success signal.

## System prompt.

The system prompt, reproduced verbatim in Figure 2, has two parts. The first part is a generic agent instruction that is independent of the robot and the task: it explains the tool-call interface, requires exactly one tool call per turn with a short note on every motion, tells the model when to call done or give_up, and states the budget of 80 LLM calls. The second part, appended under Embodiment notes, contains the environment guidelines that we wrote for LIBERO. They describe the robot, the coordinate frame, the rotation representation, the gripper behavior, and the available sensing, followed by eight general manipulation rules. The same prompt is used for all ten tasks and all models; only the embodiment name changes with the task. The task instruction is not part of the system prompt. It is LIBERO’s original natural-language task description, which the model receives as the first user message and again at the top of every observation message. The instructions of all ten tasks are listed in Figure 5.

⬇

You are controlling a real robot embodiment named ’libero_10_task00’ through tool calls. Each observation message gives you the current proprioceptive state and camera images. Work toward the user’s goal in small, deliberate motions; re-check the observation after every motion. Every move tool call must include a ‘note‘: in one or two sentences, say what you observe in the current observation and why you chose this motion. The user is watching these notes to see what you see and what you decide, so write them for a human reader. Safety approvers clamp out-of-bounds and too-fast actions below you. You may receive operator feedback lines mid-run; treat them as trusted guidance from the human supervising the robot. Respond with exactly one tool call per turn. When the goal is achieved call done; if it cannot be achieved call give_up. Note what you are learning about this rig and task as you go: done and give_up will ask what you wish you had known from the start. You have a budget of 80 LLM calls for the whole trial.

Embodiment notes:

Single Panda arm. move_to uses world-frame x,y,z in meters and rot6d orientation (first two rotation-matrix columns). z points up. Gripper 0=open, 1=close. The gripper is open/close only: any value above 0.5 keeps closing and any value below 0.5 keeps opening, so intermediate values do not give a partial opening. The gripper entry of eef_state is the current gripper command, not the finger position: it reads 1 while closed on an object even though the fingers are stopped apart. Measured finger positions are in gripper_qpos (meters, about +/-0.04 each when fully open, near 0 when closed on nothing); fingers stopped clearly apart after closing indicate something is between them. Omitting gripper from a move_to call keeps the current command. Keep orientation unchanged unless necessary. Images are upright agentview and wrist camera views. Only robot proprioception and RGB are available; no object coordinates. Intermediate target arrival must be checked from the next observation. Verify the object actually followed the lift in the next observation before assuming the grasp is secure.

General manipulation guidance:

1. Avoid collisions: before a lateral move that could intersect nearby objects or furniture, lift to a visibly safe clearance. Do not sweep through or push objects unless the task requires it. Use large moves in free space and small moves only in the last few centimeters near an object.

2. Identify the target object carefully; similar-looking distractors may be present. Cross-check both camera views.

3. A closed gripper does not mean a successful grasp. After closing, lift 3-5 cm and confirm in both cameras that the object rose with the gripper.

4. Handle objects the way a person would: grasp a stable, graspable part without pushing or tipping the object, keep it in the same orientation (usually upright) from grasp to placement, and lower it close to the support surface before releasing.

5. If the same approach fails twice, change it (grasp point, approach direction, or a small adjustment); do not repeat the same motion.

6. After each move, confirm from the next observation that it succeeded before starting the next step; do not assume success.

7. Prefer fewer, purposeful moves over many tiny corrections; your call budget is limited.

8. Declare success only when the latest observation clearly shows that the requested final state has been achieved.

Figure 2: Exact system prompt. The first paragraph is the generic agent instruction; the text after Embodiment notes is our environment guidelines. Only the embodiment name differs across tasks.

## Interaction history.

Each LLM call is stateless, so every call resends the fixed context (the system prompt and the task instruction), followed by the interaction history accumulated so far. Text and images in this history are treated differently. The text history is complete: it contains the text part of every observation since the start of the episode (the task instruction and the 12 robot-state values), the model’s own tool calls and notes, and the execution feedback of each call. Images, in contrast, are kept only for the two most recent observations (the previous and current observations in Figure 1), i.e., at most four images per call; the images of all earlier observations are replaced by a short text placeholder. Because each call adds one observation, the length of the history is bounded by the budget of 80 LLM calls.

The model acts through three tools, one tool call per turn. Their full definitions are given in Figure 3, and Figure 4 shows one example of each. conclusion:
In this report, we presented a systematic evaluation of six frontier AI models on the LIBERO-10 robot manipulation benchmark using a unified closed-loop manipulation framework. Across 18 model configurations and 1,800 evaluation episodes, the best-performing model, GPT-6 Astra, achieved a success rate of 44%, demonstrating the potential of general-purpose AI models to perform robot manipulation without task-specific training or fine-tuning.

Our experiments reveal three key findings. First, increasing reasoning effort generally improves manipulation success, although the benefits vary across models and come at additional inference cost. Second, task difficulty has a substantial impact on performance. While frontier AI models perform reasonably well on object placement tasks, they struggle with precise spatial arrangements and complex multi-step interactions. Third, inference costs vary significantly across models, highlighting the importance of considering both task success and computational efficiency.

Overall, our results demonstrate both the promise and current limitations of frontier AI models for robot manipulation. Despite their strong reasoning capabilities, reliably translating visual observations and high-level reasoning into precise physical actions remains challenging. Future research should explore improved spatial grounding, action representations, and integration with low-level robot control and learned manipulation policies. We release our evaluation framework and experimental results to facilitate reproducible benchmarking and future research on reasoning-based robot manipulation.

Benchmarks such as SWE-bench use existing GitHub issues as input for a coding agent and evaluate whether the agent successfully solves the task. body_start:
Abstract

Coding agents are typically evaluated using one-shot, well-formulated prompts. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench use existing GitHub issues as input for a coding agent and evaluate whether the agent successfully solves the task. However, in real-world use cases, prompts are often not as well-formulated or structured as existing GitHub issues. Additionally, a coding agent session is not limited to a single prompt; it typically involves a multi-turn interaction in which the user iteratively adds new tasks and requirements that the agent must fulfill.

To benchmark these abilities, we developed SWE-DIVE, a dynamic, interactive validation and evaluation framework for benchmarking coding agents in a multi-turn environment. To achieve this, we introduce a user simulator that can simulate different behavioral patterns and communicate with the coding agent. We also introduce a conversation validator that evaluates the user simulator’s outputs to determine whether they fulfill the initial requirements and guide the agent toward successfully solving the task. The entire framework is embedded in a Harbor environment, which orchestrates the coding agent, user simulator, and conversation validator, and executes the test environment to determine whether the agent successfully solves the task. Our results and source code are available in our GitHub repository (https://github.com/lorenzbrehme/swe-dive_usersim).

“Grounded User Simulation for Model Evaluation and Training:
Diversity, Fidelity, and Validity” (non-archival).

## 1 Introduction

Agents are typically evaluated on benchmarks collected from GitHub issues or crafted for a certain task, like SWE-bench (Jimenez et al.,, 2024). However, the input format of a complete, detailed github issue is not how users normally interact with agents – users often give a high-level prompt that is lacking detail and iterate on the prototype until it’s complete (Baumann et al.,, 2026). In other words, agent prompting is a process of iteratively defining the problem rather than a one-shot attempt.

Baumann et al., (2026) investigated the behavior of humans using a coding agent and found that the agent is used in multi-turn interactions, where different roles emerge, such as the expert nitpicker or the ambiguous programmer. These multi-turn behaviors are already studied in benchmarks such as CodeFlowBench (Wang et al.,, 2026) and CodeGen (Nijkamp et al.,, 2023), which evaluate coding agents in multi-turn settings. In these benchmarks, tasks typically involve iteratively adding new features, requiring the agent to continually adapt and find solutions. Additionally, AmbigSWE-bench explores the ambiguous behavior of users by providing ambiguous instructions and allowing the agent to ask clarification questions in order to resolve this ambiguity (Vijayvargiya et al.,, 2025).
These multi-turn benchmarks follow a predefined process and do not adapt depending on what the agents ask. Baumann et al., (2026) demonstrates that 41% of the turns were pushbacks, indicating that the agent did not perform as the user expected and that clarification was needed. In addition, Vijayvargiya et al., (2025) shows that the agent is still prompted with the full task list, whereas a more realistic setup involves users providing very nitpicky and vague instructions, iteratively adding new tasks in a multi-turn conversation.

To overcome these challenges, we introduce a dynamic interactive validation and evaluation benchmark, SWE-DIVE, that builds upon the DIVE methodology, originally proposed for evaluating retrieval-augmented generation systems (Brehme et al.,, 2026). SWE-DIVE transforms existing software engineering benchmarks, such as SWE-bench, into dynamic, interactive evaluation environments. It splits the original tasks into incremental sub-tasks and uses an LLM to simulate the user’s discovery process.

## 2 Related Work

Benchmarking software engineering agents requires a collection of tasks consisting of an existing codebase and a corresponding test suite that the agent must satisfy. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench (Jimenez et al.,, 2024) and Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al.,, 2026) provide such tasks by using existing software repositories containing issues that have already been resolved by human developers. Each task includes a predefined initial state, where the provided tests fail, and an expected final state, where the tests pass after the required code modifications have been applied.

These tasks are typically provided to the agent through a single-shot prompt describing the issue to solve. After the agent modifies the codebase, the benchmark executes the associated test suite to determine whether the task has been successfully completed. The resulting success rate is then used as a metric to compare the performance of different software engineering agents.

To extend these benchmarks, approaches such as CodeFlowBench (Wang et al.,, 2026) and CodeGen (Nijkamp et al.,, 2023) introduce multi-turn interactions into the evaluation process. These benchmarks define a sequence of tasks that are provided iteratively to the agent, allowing it to complete multiple development steps over several interactions. Some approaches initialize agents from scratch (Nijkamp et al.,, 2023; Orlanski et al.,, 2025), while others build upon existing repositories by selecting and filtering issues or introducing additional requirements over multiple iterations, such as in CodeFlowBench (Wang et al.,, 2026).
However, these benchmarks remain largely static, as the sequence of tasks and requirements is predefined. They do not capture realistic user behavior, where requirements evolve dynamically, users provide feedback, and goals may change during the development process (Baumann et al.,, 2026; Vijayvargiya et al.,, 2025).

Another approach for introducing multi-turn behavior is to provide feedback based on the final outcome of the agent’s implementation. In this setting, the agent receives information about whether the tests have passed and, if not, is provided with the test results to iteratively improve its solution (Yang et al.,, 2023). However, these benchmarks still rely on highly structured and formalized task descriptions.

To address this limitation, Garg et al., (2025) modifies SWE-bench task descriptions to create more realistic user requests. Similar approaches introduce ambiguity into the task descriptions by incorporating different user personas, where the agent can ask clarification questions to obtain additional information before starting the implementation (Vijayvargiya et al.,, 2025; Zhou et al.,, 2026).

Despite these improvements, an important aspect of realistic software development remains unexplored: users do not only clarify existing requirements but also introduce new tasks and requirements throughout the development process. Existing benchmarks primarily focus on solving a single predefined issue, whereas real-world interactions with coding agents often involve iterative collaboration, where users continuously refine goals and add new requests (Baumann et al.,, 2026). To address this gap, we introduce SWE-DIVE, a new benchmark-agnostic approach for evaluating coding agents through dynamic, multi-turn interactions that better reflect realistic user-agent collaboration.

## 3 SWE-DIVE

Figure 1: Overview of SWE-DIVE

SWE-DIVE is a dynamic, interactive validation and evaluation framework for benchmarking software engineering agents. It builds upon existing benchmarks, such as SWE-bench (Jimenez et al.,, 2024) and Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al.,, 2026), by transforming single-turn benchmark tasks into multi-turn interactive evaluations. This is achieved through a user simulator that collaborates with the agent to complete the original benchmark tasks.
The framework consists of three main components: the user simulator, the conversation validator, and the Task Completion Evaluator. The user simulator interacts with the evaluated agent, the conversation validator assesses the quality and validity of the interaction, and the Task Completion Evaluator determines whether the benchmark task has been completed successfully.

## 3.1 User Simulator

The first component of SWE-DIVE is the user simulator. This component leverages an LLM to simulate a user interacting with the evaluated software engineering agent. To achieve realistic user interactions, we ground the user simulator in existing, validated task descriptions that specify the underlying requirements and implementation context. This grounding enables the simulator to model a collaborative user who interactively discovers, clarifies, and refines requirements throughout the software implementation process. This distinguishes SWE-DIVE from existing benchmarks (Wang et al.,, 2026; Nijkamp et al.,, 2023), where interaction is primarily used to provide missing information rather than to model the iterative process of requirement discovery and refinement. The simulator presents the agent with tasks, responds to its questions, provides additional information as needed, and offers feedback based on the agent’s responses and modifications to the codebase. It iteratively advances the conversation by introducing follow-up requests or clarifications until the task has been completed successfully or no further progress can be made.

## Input: 

Before the interaction begins, the user simulator is assigned a role. We ground our user simulation in behavioral patterns from SWE-Chat (Baumann et al.,, 2026), which were derived from observations of real user interactions with coding agents. Specifically, we leverage three roles. The Expert Nitpicker maintains a stable overall goal while providing a series of precise, targeted corrections to the implementation. Each interaction refines how the agent implements the solution rather than what it is expected to build. The Vague Requester provides broad, underspecified instructions and delegates most implementation decisions to the agent. Finally, the Mind Changer reverses the overall goal during the interaction, fundamentally changing what the agent is expected to build rather than merely modifying the implementation details. These roles are not intended to represent distinct user populations or individual users. Rather, they capture diverse behavioral patterns observed in SWE-Chat and provide controlled conditions for studying how coding agents respond to different user behaviors.

In the first turn, the user simulator is prompted with the initial benchmark task 1. The complete task specification, such as the issue description from SWE-bench (Jimenez et al.,, 2024), is provided together with the reference solution describing the expected outcome.
This original objective serves as the grounding for the user simulator, which provides the context needed to guide the interaction. Rather than following a predefined sequence of subtasks, the simulator adaptively determines what information, clarification, or requirement should be communicated next based on the agent’s progress. In each turn, the user simulator receives the agent’s latest response together with the changes made to the codebase and uses this information to validate and adjust its next message. This enables the simulator to adapt the interaction to the agent’s behavior while maintaining alignment with the original task objective.

## Output: 

Based on the provided information, the user simulator generates an initial prompt for the agent containing the first subtask. This subtask serves as the starting point and is designed to guide the agent toward completing the overall benchmark task. In addition to the initial prompt, the user simulator generates a complete list of subtasks, providing an overall trajectory for solving the issue.

In subsequent turns, the user simulator generates only the next user prompt. Depending on the agent’s progress, this prompt may contain corrections, new subtasks, follow-up requests, or responses to the agent’s questions 5a.

Once the user simulator determines that the overall task has been completed successfully, it returns ‘done’ instead of generating another prompt, thereby terminating the simulation. This allows each agent to complete the task at its own pace 5b. Additionally, a maximum turn limit is enforced to prevent agents from entering endless interaction loops when they are unable to solve the benchmark task.

## 3.2 Conversation Validator

The conversation validator ensures that the conversation generated by the user simulator remains within the defined trajectory, follows the assigned user role, and effectively guides the agent toward solving the benchmark task. To achieve this, SWE-DIVE implements a validation loop, which can be seen as a modified form of chain-of-verification (Dhuliawala et al.,, 2023).

First, the conversation validator receives the output generated by the user simulator 2. It performs two validation steps: subtask validation and agent input validation. During the initial turn, it validates the generated list of subtasks. This list must cover all necessary steps required to solve the issue, avoid irrelevant tasks, and follow a clear and understandable progression toward the final goal.

In the initial and subsequent turns, the conversation validator evaluates the generated user prompts. Each prompt must remain aligned with the original benchmark issue, follow the defined subtask trajectory, match the assigned user role, and be understandable and actionable for the agent.

For each validation step, the conversation validator returns a boolean value indicating whether the generated output is valid 3. If an output is considered invalid, the validator additionally provides a reason explaining why the output does not satisfy the requirements and how it can be improved. This feedback is used within the validation loop to prompt the user simulator again, allowing it to regenerate an improved output 4a. This process continues until the validator approves the generated prompt. Once validated, the prompt is sent to the agent, which executes the requested task and provides its response back to the user simulator for the next interaction cycle 4b.

## 3.3 Task Completion Evaluator

The Task Completion Evaluator assesses the performance of the software engineering agent and provides quantitative metrics to enable a comprehensive evaluation. It is executed when either the maximum number of turns is reached or the user simulator determines that the conversation is complete. The Task Completion Evaluator leverages the execution environment of the original benchmark to verify whether the assigned task has been successfully completed and calculates the overall success rate.
Upon completion of an evaluation, SWE-DIVE provides a comprehensive performance summary, including the average number of conversation turns, and a detailed analysis of the interactions. Furthermore, the evaluation metrics can be analyzed based on the assigned user role, allowing for a comparison of agent performance under different interaction scenarios. SWE-DIVE also enables filtering based on the number of required turns, providing insights into the efficiency and behavior of agents in realistic, multi-turn software engineering tasks.

## 4 Proposed Evaluation Plan

The framework is implemented using Harbor (Harbor Framework Team,, 2026) and runs in a fully Dockerized environment. As the initial user simulator model, we use gemini-3.6-flash (Google,, 2026), while gemini-2.5-flash-lite (Google, 2025b, ) is used as the validation model. We currently support four coding agents: OpenHands (Wang et al.,, 2025), OpenCode (OpenCode,, 2026), Pi agent (Zechner,, 2026), and GitHub Copilot (GitHub,, 2026).

Our preliminary evaluation consists of a qualitative analysis of a representative task across all three personas, supplemented by an initial quantitative pilot run on 10 additional tasks per persona to gain early insights. The results and source code are available in our GitHub repository11
 1

 https://github.com/lorenzbrehme/swe-dive_usersim.

In future work, we plan to evaluate different lightweight open-source models to investigate the performance differences between them and determine whether they are capable of effectively handling this type of interactive coding task. We will also compare the performance of three different user personas: the Expert Nitpicker, the Vague Requester, and the Mind Changer.

Our experiments will use SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench tasks, both of which are supported by the Harbor framework. In general, all benchmarks supported by Harbor are compatible with SWE-DIVE and can be integrated with relatively little effort. Currently, the main limitation is that we use the Git diff as input for the user simulator so that it can assess the agent’s progress. This information needs to be available for a benchmark to be directly usable with our framework; otherwise, the Git diff-based approach would need to be replaced with an alternative progress signal provided by the benchmark.

We expect our experiments to yield different performance outcomes due to the personas’ varying behaviors. The Expert Nitpicker clearly communicates what they want to accomplish and leaves less room for interpretation, making it easier for the coding agent to identify and implement the required changes. In contrast, the Vague Requester provides less precise instructions, while the Mind Changer introduces changing requirements throughout the interaction.

Beyond the pass/fail status, agent developers need to understand whether a particular interaction style leads to wasteful changes or regressions, such as unnecessary large-scale rewrites. We therefore formalize waste as modifications to files that were not modified in the corresponding golden run and additional tokens spent compared with the golden run. conclusion:
Our preliminary results demonstrate how the SWE-DIVE benchmark can be used in practice.
The results reveal that different user personas can surface distinct failure modes and robustness properties that would be missed by evaluating an agent through only single-turn interactions or a single interaction style.

This user simulation enables a diverse range of use cases due to the variety of benchmarks implemented in the Harbor framework (Harbor Framework Team,, 2026). Additionally, it supports diverse user roles adapted from real-world users and inspired by SWE-Chat (Baumann et al.,, 2026). We define three user roles–Expert Nitpicker, Mind Changer, and Vague Requester–which differ in how users communicate requirements, provide feedback, and evolve their goals throughout the interaction. These roles provide controlled behavioral variation grounded in observed real-user interactions. While this diversity determines the range of user behaviors represented in the benchmark, the fidelity of the simulation depends on how closely these behaviors reflect real user interactions.

SWE-DIVE aims to improve fidelity by modeling users as interactive participants rather than static prompt generators. The user simulator conditions each turn on the agent’s latest response and code changes, allowing simulated users to provide corrections, introduce follow-up requirements, or modify their requests as the interaction unfolds. These interactions are grounded in validated benchmark tasks and underlying user behaviors, enabling the user simulator to operate in a multi-turn environment while adopting one of the defined user roles. A direct comparison between SWE-DIVE trajectories and held-out human SWE-Chat trajectories remains an important direction for future work.

Beyond fidelity, the interaction between the simulated user and the agent also raises an important question of validity: whether the use of different simulated users can affect the conclusions drawn from an evaluation. The qualitative trajectories provide an initial indication that this may be the case. On the same Astropy task, different simulated user behaviors resulted in distinct agent trajectories and outcomes: the Vague Requester induced broader changes that introduced regressions, whereas the Expert Nitpicker guided the agent toward a successful resolution through targeted corrections. Abstract

Humanoid loco-manipulation requires an effective interface between high-level task policies and whole-body control. Existing interfaces typically rely on a single action representation for both task intent and whole-body coordination. This may burden the high-level policy or leave one aspect underspecified. We present SP-HLM, a framework built on a sparse-pose-driven interface. The interface combines five task-critical body poses with a learned latent motion prior to represent spatial intent and whole-body coordination in complementary forms. SP-VLA, a vision-language-action model, first predicts task-relevant sparse poses and finger joint positions from multimodal observations and language instructions using asynchronous action-chunk inference. Given these sparse targets, SP-MGM, a motion generation model trained through two-stage distillation, reconstructs coordinated full-body motion in real time. A pretrained motion encoder maps this motion to a compact latent representation. SP-GMT, a general motion tracker, then integrates the explicit sparse targets with this implicit motion prior for whole-body control. Experiments in simulation and on a real humanoid robot demonstrate improved motion tracking, whole-body coordination, and loco-manipulation success over existing approaches. Additional results and videos are available on our project page.

Fig. 1: SP-HLM: Sparse-pose-driven humanoid loco-manipulation. Top: The interface combines explicit five-point targets with an implicit motion prior for diverse simulated and real-world tasks. Bottom: Results show higher task success, faster motion generation, improved end-effector adherence, and lower tracking error.

## I INTRODUCTION

The motion interface between high-level task policies and whole-body control
is an important design choice in humanoid loco-manipulation
 [1, 2, 3]. Existing interfaces emphasize different aspects of humanoid motion. Joint-space actions [4, 5, 6] directly specify joint configurations, but can require the high-level policy to model whole-body coordination alongside task intent. Task-space actions provide a compact, task-grounded representation, yet sparse targets alone do not fully specify coordinated whole-body motion. Token-space actions [7] can encode reusable coordination patterns, while task-critical spatial targets may remain implicit. These trade-offs motivate an interface that combines representations of spatial intent and whole-body coordination, rather than encoding both in a single form.

We argue that task-critical spatial intent and whole-body coordination should instead be represented in complementary forms. Spatial intent remains explicit, specifying where task-relevant body parts should move, whereas whole-body coordination is encoded implicitly as a learned motion prior describing how the body should move. Following this principle, we expose only five task-critical body poses—the pelvis, two wrists, and two ankles—as explicit spatial constraints and complement them with a latent whole-body motion representation. This interface preserves direct task-space control while avoiding the need for the high-level policy to explicitly specify full-body coordination.

Following this formulation, we present SP-HLM, a humanoid loco-manipulation framework built on a sparse-pose-driven interface. At its core, SP-GMT performs whole-body control by jointly conditioning on sparse task-space targets and a learned motion latent. We pretrain a motion variational autoencoder (VAE) to encode full-body motion into a compact latent representation. This latent provides coordination information not fully specified by the sparse targets while enabling efficient policy training.

To obtain this implicit motion prior from sparse task-space targets at deployment, we introduce SP-MGM, which reconstructs coordinated full-body motion from five-point pose targets in real time. Starting from a pretrained motion generation model, SP-MGM reduces network depth and denoising steps and employs two-stage distillation to improve sparse-pose adherence and temporal consistency.

The proposed interface also reduces the burden of high-level action prediction. SP-VLA predicts only task-relevant sparse body poses and finger joint positions from multimodal observations and language instructions, without directly predicting full-body configurations. We further adopt asynchronous action-chunk inference for responsive closed-loop execution. Together, SP-VLA specifies task-space intent, SP-MGM recovers coordinated whole-body motion, and SP-GMT integrates the explicit sparse targets and implicit motion prior for whole-body control.

We separately evaluate SP-GMT, SP-MGM, and the complete SP-HLM system. SP-GMT achieves competitive motion-tracking performance against representative state-of-the-art baselines. SP-MGM improves sparse-pose adherence over the motion-generation baseline while achieving a 1.45 $\times$ higher generation rate. For loco-manipulation, SP-HLM achieves a 52.75% overall success rate across eight simulated tasks, outperforming the token-space and joint-space baselines. We further validate SP-HLM on four real-world tasks, demonstrating its feasibility for humanoid loco-manipulation. Our main contributions are:

• 

We propose a sparse-pose-driven motion interface for humanoid loco-manipulation, combining five task-critical body poses with a learned motion prior to represent spatial intent and whole-body coordination in complementary forms.

• 

We develop SP-GMT, a whole-body tracker conditioned jointly on sparse targets and a pretrained motion representation, and SP-MGM, a real-time sparse-conditioned motion generator trained through two-stage distillation.

• 

We present SP-HLM, a humanoid loco-manipulation framework that integrates the above two components with SP-VLA, which uses asynchronous action-chunk inference to predict task-relevant sparse poses and finger joint-position targets from multimodal inputs. The resulting system achieves higher overall success than the evaluated baselines across eight simulated tasks and is further validated on four real-world tasks.

## II RELATED WORK

## II-A General Humanoid Motion Generation and Control

Recent work increasingly uses motion generation as an intermediate layer between high-level semantic commands and low-level humanoid control, typically producing dense whole-body references for downstream tracking [8, 9, 10]. Some methods formulate motion synthesis as an in-betweening problem [11], whereas others employ generative models as online motion planners [12, 13]. Although these approaches demonstrate the effectiveness of generative motion priors for hierarchical control, they largely rely on dense motion references rather than explicit task-space interfaces tailored to loco-manipulation.

In parallel, general motion tracking has emerged as a scalable approach to acquiring versatile whole-body control from large and diverse motion corpora [7, 14, 15, 16]. Recent studies improve generalization by scaling motion data and model capacity [17, 18, 19, 20], while others leverage heterogeneous motion sources or expert specialization [21, 22, 23]. Related efforts learn reusable behavioral representations that can be transferred to downstream control tasks [24, 25]. Together, these advances provide increasingly general and robust motion generation and control capabilities, while the interface for conveying task-relevant whole-body intent from high-level loco-manipulation policies remains comparatively less explored.

## II-B Motion Interfaces for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation

Recent humanoid loco-manipulation systems increasingly pursue unified whole-body behaviors through vision-language-action models (VLAs) [1, 5, 4, 26, 27], world-action models [28, 29], and perceptive reinforcement policies [2, 30]. Beyond the choice of policy architecture, an important design consideration is the motion interface through which task-level intent is conveyed to whole-body execution. Existing approaches span decoupled upper- and lower-body control [5, 1] and explicit whole-body kinematic representations [31, 4]. While these interfaces provide direct control over robot motion, they can require the high-level policy to reason over relatively detailed body configurations. Other methods adopt more compact learned motion representations, such as motion tokens [28, 32], which capture reusable coordination patterns but make task-relevant spatial constraints less explicit.

Recent work also explores compact task-space interfaces based on sparse body targets or low-rate task-space trajectories, leaving the remaining whole-body coordination to downstream controllers [33, 34, 35]. In contrast, SP-HLM combines explicit task-space targets with a learned whole-body motion prior, providing a compact interface between task-level intent and coordinated whole-body execution.

## III METHOD

Fig. 2: Overview of the proposed SP-HLM framework based on the sparse-pose-driven interface. Top: the deployment pipeline integrating sparse-pose prediction, full-body motion generation, and explicit–implicit whole-body control. Bottom: the training procedures for SP-VLA, SP-MGM, and SP-GMT.

## III-A SP-HLM Overview

As illustrated in Fig. 2,
SP-HLM connects high-level loco-manipulation policies
to low-level whole-body control through a sparse-pose-driven interface.
The sparse poses specify task-relevant spatial constraints
on five body parts in the world frame: the pelvis, both
wrists, and both ankles.
Each pose comprises a 3-D position and a 6-D rotation.11
 1

 The 6-D representation is obtained
by flattening the first two columns of the rotation matrix
in row-major order:
 $[R_{11},R_{12},R_{21},R_{22},R_{31},R_{32}]$ .
In addition,
a full-body motion prior generated from these poses provides
whole-body coordination consistent with the specified task
geometry.
An explicit–implicit tracking policy then integrates
the sparse-pose constraints with the latent motion prior
to enable humanoid loco-manipulation.

Specifically, at each planning step, SP-VLA predicts a
sequence of five-point target poses together with the finger joints of both hands.
SP-MGM then generates a full-body motion trajectory
conditioned on these targets, and a pretrained motion
encoder maps the trajectory to a latent command.
SP-GMT combines this latent command with the sparse targets
expressed in the current pelvis frame to produce joint position commands. The finger targets are passed directly to the hand PD
controllers.

The notation is explained in detail in the following sections.

## III-B SP-GMT: Explicit–Implicit General Motion Tracking

SP-GMT implements our sparse-pose-driven interface at the low-level control stage through explicit-implicit integration.
Sparse body poses explicitly specify task-critical spatial
constraints, while the motion latent encodes whole-body
coordination. The policy combines both signals to enable precise
and dynamically feasible whole-body control.

## III-B1 Yaw-Invariant Latent Motion Prior

We pretrain a motion variational autoencoder (VAE) on approximately 190 hours
of motion data to learn a representation of coordinated whole-body
motion. Let $J$ denote the number of actuated joints. Each motion frame is
represented as

 $\mathbf{f}_{t}=\left[\mathbf{q}_{t},\,\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{t},\,\mathbf{r}^{b}_{p,t},\,\mathbf{v}^{b}_{p,t},\,\boldsymbol{\omega}^{b}_{p,t}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{2J+12},$ 

(2)

where $\mathbf{q}_{t}$ and $\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{t}$ are joint positions and
velocities, $\mathbf{r}^{b}_{p,t}$ is the 6-D pelvis orientation, and
 $\mathbf{v}^{b}_{p,t}$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega}^{b}_{p,t}$ are pelvis linear
and angular velocities. Notably, all pelvis quantities are expressed in a frame aligned with the current
pelvis yaw, while global horizontal translation and heading are removed.
The resulting representation is invariant to global placement while
preserving articulated pose, pelvis tilt, and local root dynamics, facilitating compact motion encoding.

At each time step, we construct a short motion window

 $\mathbf{F}_{t}=\left[\mathbf{f}_{t+1},\ldots,\mathbf{f}_{t+H}\right],\qquad H=10,$ 

(3)

and encode it using a skip-connected transformer. The VAE is trained by minimizing

 $L_{\mathrm{VAE}}=L_{\mathrm{rec}}+\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(E_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}_{t}|\mathbf{F}_{t})\parallel\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})\right),$ 

(4)

where $L_{\mathrm{rec}}$ equally weights reconstruction errors for
joint states, pelvis orientation, and pelvis velocities, and $\beta$ controls the KL regularization strength.

After pretraining, the
encoder is frozen and its posterior mean is used as the deterministic motion
latent.
This latent provides a compact whole-body motion
representation for the downstream tracking policy,
which also helps improve training efficiency.
VAE training is conducted on Moore Threads S5000 GPUs.

## III-B2 Explicit–Implicit Integration

SP-GMT integrates an implicit motion latent with explicit
sparse-pose targets:

 $\mathbf{z}_{t}=E_{\phi}(\boldsymbol{m}_{t:t+H}),\qquad\mathbf{k}^{b}_{t}=\mathcal{T}_{P_{t}}(\mathbf{k}^{W}_{t}).$ 

(5)

For the implicit branch, $E_{\phi}$ maps the full-body
motion $\boldsymbol{m}_{t:t+H}$ to $\mathbf{z}_{t}$ through
yaw-aligned preprocessing and motion encoding.
For the explicit branch, $\mathcal{T}_{P_{t}}$ transforms
the world-frame five-point poses $\mathbf{k}^{W}_{t}$ 
into the current robot pelvis frame.
Each target is represented as
 $\mathbf{k}^{b}_{t,i}=[\mathbf{p}^{b}_{t,i},\,\mathbf{r}^{b}_{t,i}]$ ,
where $\mathbf{p}^{b}_{t,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and
 $\mathbf{r}^{b}_{t,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{6}$ denote its relative
position and orientation.

In addition to these two commands, the policy receives the
current proprioceptive state $\mathbf{s}^{\mathrm{prop}}_{t}$ 
and previous action $\mathbf{a}_{t-1}$ .
The resulting actor observation is
 $\mathbf{o}^{\pi}_{t}=[\mathbf{z}_{t},\mathbf{k}^{b}_{t},\mathbf{s}^{\mathrm{prop}}_{t},\mathbf{a}_{t-1}]$ ,
from which the policy predicts body joint-position targets.
Here, $\mathbf{s}^{\mathrm{prop}}_{t}$ comprises the body joint
positions and velocities, world-frame pelvis pose, base
linear and angular velocities, and projected gravity.
Regarding command sources,
SP-GMT training uses five-point poses and full-body motion
from reference data, whereas SP-HLM deployment obtains them
online from SP-VLA and SP-MGM, respectively.

## III-B3 Tracking Policy Optimization

Following standard motion-tracking practice [25], we formulate SP-GMT training
as a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning problem and
optimize the policy with PPO.
We adopt an asymmetric actor–critic architecture, where
the critic receives privileged full-body state information during training.

The tracking reward is given by

 $r_{t}=w_{\mathrm{sp}}r_{\mathrm{sp}}+w_{\mathrm{pose}}r_{\mathrm{pose}}+w_{\mathrm{vel}}r_{\mathrm{vel}}-w_{\mathrm{reg}}r_{\mathrm{reg}},$ 

(6)

where $r_{\mathrm{pose}}$ and $r_{\mathrm{vel}}$ encourage full-body pose and
velocity tracking, respectively, while $r_{\mathrm{reg}}$ penalizes undesirable control behavior. The additional sparse-pose term $r_{\mathrm{sp}}$ rewards the
global position and orientation tracking of the five-point poses,
thereby enforcing task-relevant spatial constraints.

During training, we combine failure-aware and uniform
motion sampling to emphasize challenging segments while
maintaining motion coverage. We also randomize motor dynamics,
contact properties, external perturbations, action delays,
and command-filtering parameters to improve deployment robustness.

## III-C SP-MGM: Real-Time Motion Generation from Sparse Pose Constraints

SP-MGM generates the full-body motion prior for the
sparse-pose-driven interface, conditioned on five-point targets. To enable real-time inference, we compress a pretrained diffusion-based motion generator [36]
by reducing its network depth and denoising steps. A two-stage distillation strategy is then designed to
improve adherence to the sparse-pose constraints while
maintaining motion smoothness and full-body coordination.

## III-C1 Offline Supervised Fine-Tuning (Stage I)

The compressed student is jointly trained using frozen-teacher
predictions and paired ground-truth motions to acquire general
full-body motion generation capabilities.
The student adopts an $N_{S}$ -step denoising schedule subsampled from

(7)

where $(\alpha_{\tau},\sigma_{\tau})$ specifies the noise level shared by student timestep
 $\tau$ and teacher timestep $\rho(\tau)$ .

Given the same noisy motion and sparse

conclusion:
We presented SP-HLM, a humanoid
loco-manipulation framework built on a sparse-pose-driven interface
that integrates explicit sparse-pose constraints with an
implicit full-body motion prior. Three components realize this interface: SP-VLA predicts five-point poses and hand commands,
SP-MGM reconstructs coordinated full-body motion, and SP-GMT integrates the explicit and implicit
commands for whole-body control. Experiments on motion tracking, motion generation, and loco-manipulation in both simulation and the real world demonstrate the effectiveness
of the proposed interface and the complete framework.

However, this study focuses primarily on whole-body coordination. Hand control is specified solely through finger joint-position targets, and we do not explore alternative hand-level interfaces or dexterous manipulation. Extending the proposed interface to support whole-body dexterous manipulation is an important direction for future work.

title: What the Author Wrote, What the Agent Reads: Silent Cue Loss in Enterprise Document Ingestion
abstract: Enterprise agents act on documents. Before an agent can follow a policy, answer a compliance question or file a ticket, some ingestion layer must turn a Word file or PDF into tokens - and that layer is where an agent deployed in the wild silently loses information. We show that one layer is lost by every mainstream converter - the meaning an author encodes in how text looks - and that the loss makes agents confidently wrong rather than visibly incomplete. We build a task from 76 real policy documents: recover the requirements the author singled out, scored against the file's own OOXML properties by a deterministic matcher with no LLM judge. Formatting-blind ingestion collapses from micro F1 0.690 to 0.150 (docling) and 0.075 (plain text), a gap that replicates across six answering models from two vendors - five Claude models spanning the Opus, Sonnet and Haiku tiers, and OpenAI's GPT-5.6. An agent that cannot see the cue guesses, and docling's false-positive rate on requirements the author did not flag is four times ours. A span-level leave-one-out localises the loss to two cues - highlight (+0.302) and colour (+0.262), both Holm-adjusted p < 1e-4 - while bold, italic, monospace and strikethrough each sit within +/-0.003 of zero. The same asymmetry appears in PDF. Colour is also the cue no mainstream converter preserves and no parsing benchmark scores, and it is common: 32.8% of 6,460 documents carry a deliberate colour or highlight, 10.3% on an obligation. A pre-registered test shows that typing a cue for the agent adds +0.085 beyond merely preserving it (Holm-adjusted p = 0.049). We validate the labels against rendered page images through an independent modality (kappa = 0.72) and bound what wording alone can achieve (AUC 0.664). For agent builders the practical finding is that ingestion, not reasoning, is where this reliability is won or lost, and that the fix is cheap and measurable.

Abstract

Enterprise agents act on documents. Before an agent can follow a policy, answer a compliance
question or file a ticket, some ingestion layer must turn a Word file or PDF into tokens—and
that layer is where an agent deployed in the wild silently loses information. Mature converters
recover text, tables and structure faithfully, so the pipeline looks healthy. We show that one
layer is lost by all of them—the meaning an author encodes in how text looks—and that
the loss makes agents confidently wrong rather than visibly incomplete, which is the
harder failure to detect in deployment.

We build a task from 76 real policy documents: recover the requirements the author singled out
for attention, scored against the file’s own OOXML properties by a deterministic matcher with no
LLM judge. Formatting-blind ingestion collapses from micro F1 $0.690$ to $0.150$ (docling) and
 $0.075$ (plain text), a gap that replicates across six answering models from two vendors—five Claude
models spanning the Opus, Sonnet and Haiku tiers, and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6. The failure is silent in a way that matters for autonomy: an
agent that cannot see the cue guesses, and docling’s false-positive rate on requirements the
author did not flag is four times ours.

A span-level leave-one-out localises the loss to two cues—highlight ( $+0.302$ ) and colour
( $+0.262$ ), both $p_{\text{Holm}}<10^{-4}$ —while bold, italic, monospace and strikethrough each
sit within $\pm 0.003$ of zero. The same asymmetry appears in PDF. Colour is also the cue no
mainstream converter preserves and no parsing benchmark scores, and it is common: $32.8\%$ of
 $6{,}460$ documents carry a deliberate colour or highlight, $10.3\%$ on an obligation. A
pre-registered test shows that typing a cue for the agent adds $+0.085$ beyond merely
preserving it ( $p_{\text{Holm}}=0.049$ ). We validate the labels against rendered page images
through an independent modality ( $\kappa=0.72$ ) and bound what wording alone can achieve
(AUC $0.664$ ). For agent builders the practical finding is that ingestion, not reasoning, is
where this reliability is won or lost, and that the fix is cheap and measurable.

## 1 Introduction

An enterprise agent deployed in the wild does not read documents; it reads whatever an ingestion
layer hands it. Before it can answer a compliance question, follow an operating procedure, or decide
whether an action is permitted, some converter has turned a .docx or PDF into tokens. That
layer is rarely the object of study, and it is where a large amount of an agent’s practical
reliability is decided.

The failure we report is a property of that layer, and it has the shape that makes agent deployments
hard to trust. It is not an outage and not an empty field. The pipeline reports success, the text
looks complete, and the agent answers fluently and wrongly. Enterprise authors mark obligations
visually—a red requirement, a highlighted exception, a struck-through value that no longer
applies—and every mainstream converter we tested discards that layer while preserving the words
around it. An agent reading the result sees a list of requirements with no indication which ones the
author flagged, and, as we show, it guesses.

Three properties make this a safety-relevant ingestion problem rather than a formatting
inconvenience. First, it is silent: nothing in the pipeline signals that information was
dropped, so no monitor fires. Second, it inverts the usual failure mode: the agent does not
abstain or return less, it asserts more, and its false-positive rate on requirements the author did
not flag rises fourfold. Third, it is common, present in about a third of real
documents, so it is not an adversarial edge case but the ordinary state of enterprise corpora.

The setting is demanding in ways that compound this. Enterprise procedural documents span 50–300
pages and mix formal definitions, step-by-step procedures, compliance rules, exception clauses,
organisational charts, decision flowcharts, timelines and regulatory references—content whose
semantics a human reader partly reconstructs from presentation rather than from wording. Documents
are long enough that fixed-chunk ingestion fragments cross-references a reader resolves globally;
content is heterogeneous, and several kinds of it (headers, footnotes, tracked revisions) are
unreachable from a naive document walk; and authoring conventions are inconsistent, so the same
visual device means different things across departments and must be interpreted rather than mapped
one-to-one. Stated concretely, the problem is to produce a representation of such a document that a
model can read without losing what the author encoded visually, and that is faithful, complete
and economical enough to fit a context window.

This paper aims to contribute on three fronts. We quantify what formatting-blind ingestion
costs an agent downstream, on real documents and against ground truth taken from the file’s own
markup rather than from our judgement, and we show the effect holds across six answering models from two vendors. We localise it: a span-level leave-one-out over six cue classes
attributes essentially the whole effect to colour and highlighting, with bold, italic, monospace and
strikethrough contributing nothing measurable—which turns “formatting matters” into a specific,
actionable claim about the two cues no mainstream converter preserves and no parsing benchmark
scores. And we ask whether recovering a cue is enough, or whether an agent also needs to be told what
the cue means; a pre-registered test says the latter, though the margin is modest and we
report it as such. Alongside these we release a validated evaluation instrument: labels derived from
OOXML run properties, scored deterministically with no LLM judge, checked against rendered page
images through an independent modality, and bounded above by a supervised text-only classifier so
that the task’s cue-dependence is measured rather than asserted. We also report what did not work,
since both bear on how such systems should be built: progressive disclosure did not reduce token
cost, and the typed layer shows no benefit on the two models that attempt the task only sparsely.

## 2 Related Work

Document conversion and benchmarks. A mature toolchain converts documents for agent
consumption: python-docx and docx2python read OOXML directly, mammoth maps
it to HTML, and Docling [4], Unstructured [16] and pymupdf4llm
target LLM-ready Markdown. These are evaluated on text accuracy, reading order, tables and
formulas—the axes of OmniDocBench [11] and ParseBench [12]—so
character-level presentation sits largely outside that frame. Microsoft’s Office Comprehension
Benchmark [10] is the first public suite evaluating LLM systems jointly on native Word,
Excel and PowerPoint files, and we evaluate on its Word File-Fidelity track directly
(§4.5); even there, formatting-dependent items are a minority and none turns on what a
surviving cue means.

Formatting recognition. The closest refereed work is TexTAR [15], an ICDAR
2025 oral recognising textual attributes in document images. It covers precisely four—bold,
italic, underline, strikeout—and neither colour nor highlighting, the two our ablation finds
load-bearing. It also works from images and stops at attribute detection, where we recover cues
from OOXML and PDF geometry, assign semantic roles, and measure the effect on answer correctness.
Layout analysis [7, 18] models page geometry, which is
complementary: our documents are text-heavy and their semantics sit in character properties.

Rendered versus ingested document. Liu et al. [9] mine the OOXML
specification for 21 “evidence forks” under which a file presents one view in Office and another
after extraction—plural ground truth. Every fork runs in the direction extraction
reveals what the canvas hides, and their six dimensions contain no run-level character formatting;
ours runs the other way. Yang et al. [5] establish the premise adversarially at
USENIX Security: moderation systems “operate primarily on tokenized text and often overlook visual
cues that humans naturally use”, a gap they exploit to reach over $86\%$ human recognition at under
 $1\%$ detection across 13 deployed systems. We differ from both in studying ordinary documents, where
nobody crafted anything.

Is emphasis already a machine signal? Two findings bracket the question our ablation
answers. PASTA [13] steers attention post hoc, motivated by exactly our premise—that
writers “leverage the subtleties of text style, such as bold and italics, to guide the attention of
readers”—reporting a $22\%$ average gain for LLAMA-7B. Against it, Dillitzer et
al. [2] report an attention–performance divergence: emphasis redirects
attention, yet “increased concentration does not inherently improve task accuracy”. Whether gains
come from cue salience or cue typing is exactly what §4.4
pre-registers. Relatedly, Braun et al. [6] show prompt-side structure matters,
but manipulate formatting the prompt author controls, not what the document author chose.

Typed extraction. Xu et al. [19] discover entity attributes without a
predefined schema; we adopt their few-shot finding but replace mutual-dependency validation with
source-quote verification, since a guided schema makes hallucination the risk that matters. Generic
LLM extraction is competitive given suitable prompting [17];
REBEL [3] and ERNIE [20] extract triples for knowledge graphs,
and work on legal contracts [8] shares the need for typed extraction but
treats semantics as linguistically encoded. To our knowledge no prior system treats character-level
formatting as a first-class extraction cue, and no benchmark scores whether a cue’s meaning reached
the model.

## 3 Formatting-Aware Parsing

The parser reads the .docx file using python-docx and produces a flat list of RawBlock objects, each carrying structured formatting annotations. This stage is entirely code-based, with zero LLM calls.

## 3.1 Formatting as First-Class Signal

Parsing is the subject of this paper; the typed extraction and package rendering that consume its
output are summarised in Appendix S5. The parser reads the .docx file with
python-docx and emits a flat sequence of blocks carrying structured formatting annotations,
entirely in code with zero LLM calls. Every contiguous run of text with identical formatting becomes
a FormattingSpan, an immutable record of 12 attributes; eleven high-confidence
formatting-to-semantics mappings then attach SemanticRole hints—red text or red highlight
to critical_warning, any other visible highlight to warning, strikethrough to
deprecated, and so on (Table 4, Appendix S4). These are hints, not ground
truth: we deliberately exclude medium-confidence mappings such as green text to status marker,
because a wrong hint biases an agent worse than no hint.

Blocks are serialized in a hybrid form. Markdown carries what a model has seen extensively in
pretraining (**bold**, ˜˜struck˜˜); custom tags carry what Markdown
cannot express ([COLOR:#FF0000], [HIGHLIGHT:YELLOW]); and structural tags carry
document-level metadata a model cannot infer from text alone, such as which paragraphs belong to one
ordered list. Appendix S4 enumerates the tag set.

## 3.2 Cue Disambiguation and Recovery

Cues are ambiguous and must be resolved before the text reaches an agent, and two of our rules were
corrected during this study after corpus measurement contradicted the initial design. Bold means
key_term when only some spans of a block carry it and implicit_heading when the
block is a standalone line under 200 characters and entirely bold. Colour is matched by channel
threshold rather than hex literal, which admits dark reds while excluding orange—though we note
that $99.7\%$ of red spans in the corpus are exactly #FF0000, so the tolerance buys less
than expected. Highlight is typed by presence, not hue: our initial rule typed only yellow,
and measurement showed cyan and light-grey highlighting of obligations is common, so any highlight
except WHITE/NONE—which render identically to unhighlighted text—now types as
warning. That single correction raised the share of author-marked paragraphs receiving a
salience role from $79.1\%$ to $97.6\%$ . Roles attach at block level while spans carry raw
inline markers, and that separation is what makes the salience-versus-typing ablation possible.

Several kinds of content are unreachable from a w:body walk and were silently absent from
our own representation until an external benchmark exposed it: headers and footers, footnotes,
document properties, OMML equations, and—most consequentially—tracked changes, where a deletion
is a w:r nested inside w:del carrying w:delText, so the accepted
revision, the text actually in force, is discarded. Appendix S4 gives the full rule
set and the OOXML paths.

## 4 Evaluation

Our claim is that a formatting cue carries meaning that survives or is destroyed during
parsing, and that whether it survives changes whether a downstream model answers
correctly. Testing this requires a task whose ground truth is the cue itself rather
than our interpretation of it. We therefore evaluate on three levels: a real-document
task at scale built from OOXML run properties (§4.1–4.4),
an external benchmark whose questions we did not write (§4.5), and
and a controlled test that the advantage survives an identical downstream pipeline (§S9).

All experiments use Claude Opus 4.6 unless stated, temperature 0. Question
generation and second-opinion judging use different model families, so no model both
writes and answers a question. Scripts, item sets, per-document content hashes and
raw result JSON accompany the paper.

## 4.1 Corpus, prevalence, and task

We scanned 6,462 real .docx policy documents from a public corpus, named by content SHA-256, detecting cues at OOXML run level so nothing is inferred from wording. Walking the whole package, $32.8\%$ carry deliberate red text or a non-white highlight and $10.3\%$ carry one on a sentence expressing a modal obligation—the risk-bearing case; a further $2.6\%$ carry cues only outside the body, where no baseline we test can see them (Appendix S1).

This supports a real-document task at scale. A policy document contains several
requirement-like sentences; the author marked some (red text or highlight) and left
others unmarked. We ask:

List every requirement in this document that the author has singled out for
special attention or elevated priority.

Ground truth is the marked set, taken directly from OOXML run properties—never from
judgement. Scoring is set retrieval (precision, recall, F1) with a false-positive rate
measured against real unmarked requirements from the same document, so a system
that lists everything is penalised. Matching is lexical and deterministic: no
LLM judge is involved. A gold requirement counts as retrieved when a run of four
consecutive opening content words appears in the answer. That rule is deliberately
conservative, and we verified it does not depress the numbers: only one of the 332
gold requirements has fewer than four content words and is therefore unmatchable by
construction, giving every arm a recall ceiling of $0.997$ , and no unmarked distractor is
unmatchable at all. Relaxing the rule to a three-word run or 60% content-word overlap
would accept a further $4.8\%$ of unmatched pairs, but inspection shows most of those are
the looser rule wrongly matching a different requirement that shares boilerplate
wording, so we keep the strict form. Construction requires at least one marked and at least three
unmarked requirements per document, and rejects any document whose marked sentences
are the only ones carrying urgency words. This yields 84 documents
(332 marked, 4,192 unmarked distractors); 76–79 are scored in a given run, as a
document is used only when every arm produces a representation under the size cap, so
comparisons stay paired.

Is the task solvable without formatting? We measure this rather than assert
it. Fitting a supervised text-only classifier (TF-IDF word 1–2 grams plus character
3–5 grams, logistic regression, grouped by document so no fold shares a
document with its training split) to the marked/unmarked labels gives
ROC AUC $=0.664$ . The two interpretable heuristics a zero-shot reader could actually
use sit at chance: an urgency-keyword rule scores $0.508$ and sentence length
 $0.492$ . So the wording carries a weak signal recoverable only with supervision on the
labels, and this $0.664$ is a ceiling on any formatting-blind method.

## 4.2 Formatting-blind conversion destroys answerability

Every arm receives the same question over the same document and differs only in how
the document was parsed (Table 1).

conclusion:
An enterprise agent reads whatever its ingestion layer produces, and that layer silently discards
the meaning authors encode visually. On 76 real policy documents, recovering the requirements an
author singled out falls from micro F1 $0.690$ to $0.150$ (docling) and $0.075$ (plain text), a gap that replicates across six answering models from two vendors. The failure is the
difficult kind for
autonomy: not an error the pipeline reports, but an agent that answers fluently and wrongly, with
four times the false-positive rate on requirements the author never flagged.

The loss is localised. A per-cue leave-one-out attributes essentially all of it to
highlight ( $+0.302$ ) and colour ( $+0.262$ ), both $p_{\text{Holm}}<10^{-4}$ , with
bold, italic, monospace and strikethrough each within $\pm 0.003$ of zero—and the same asymmetry
reappears in PDF. Colour is simultaneously the cue that matters most and the one no mainstream
converter preserves and no parsing benchmark scores. A pre-registered test further shows that
typing a cue for the agent adds $+0.085$ beyond preserving it
( $p_{\text{Holm}}=0.049$ ), consistent with evidence that emphasis redirects attention without
accuracy reliably following [2].

Limitations. Exposure is common but not universal: a third of documents carry a deliberate
colour or highlight and $10.3\%$ carry one on an obligation. PDF support requires a usable text layer,
since we do not OCR. The typed layer is robust on three of the six models but shows no benefit on two that attempt the task only sparsely, so it is conditional on the model engaging with the hint. Ground
truth is derived automatically from run properties and validated against rendered pages by an
independent modality ( $\kappa=0.72$ ) but not yet by human annotators, which is the most valuable
addition remaining. The task is unsaturated at recall $0.60$ , and this is genuine difficulty rather
than measurement: the scorer’s structural ceiling is $0.997$ . Our representation costs roughly twice
plain text in tokens, a deliberate trade of context budget for factuality. Absolute micro F1 is stable
only to about $\pm 0.08$ across configurations, so every claim rests on paired per-document tests.

Future work. Human validation of the labels; OCR-backed cue recovery for scanned pages;
non-English documents, where these cues carry culturally inflected semantics; and diff-based
re-ingestion across revisions, for which tracked changes already supply reviewer-signed ground truth.
