headings: Stationarity Constraints Improve Both Energies and Densities
body_start:
Abstract

Empirical exchange-correlation functionals are fitted on fixed orbitals but used self-consistently, so better energies often come with worse densities. We show that the Brillouin residual of a trained functional on the Kohn-Sham orbitals of an accurate density controls, to first order, both the self-consistent density shift and the gap between fitted and self-consistent energies. Penalizing it requires no self-consistent-field solution during training. Trained on 6 energies and 11 CCSD densities, a neural meta-GGA surpasses SCAN in both atomization energies and densities of unseen molecules.

Kohn-Sham density functional theory (KS-DFT) [1, 2] is the most widely used electronic-structure method in chemistry and materials science, and its accuracy is set by the approximation to the exchange-correlation (XC) energy. The most accurate approximations for molecular thermochemistry contain tens of empirical parameters [3, 4, 5, 6] or, as machine-learned functionals, thousands or more [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12]. These parameters are fixed almost exclusively by reference energies; the electron density, which by the Hohenberg-Kohn theorem determines all ground-state properties, does not enter the fit. Medvedev et al. found that functionals with more empirical parameters tend to give worse atomic densities [13], suggesting that part of the energetic gain comes from error cancellation rather than from approaching the exact functional [13, 14, 15].

A concrete but rarely discussed mechanism underlies this trend: a functional is not used in the state in which it is fitted. Its parameters are fitted to energies on fixed orbitals, but the functional is solved self-consistently. A parameter change that lowers the fixed-orbital energy error also changes the XC potential, so the self-consistent-field (SCF) solution relaxes away from the fitted orbitals—and an energy-only loss does not penalize this relaxation, even when the fixed orbitals come from the exact density. In the language of density-corrected DFT [16, 17], energy fitting controls the functional-driven error but leaves the density-driven error unconstrained. Accuracy reached in the fit therefore need not survive self-consistency, let alone transfer to new molecules.

Two routes bring information beyond energies into the fit. One fits XC potentials obtained by density inversion [18, 19], as in the TH, HCTH, and B97-2 functionals [20, 21, 22, 23, 24], or learns the density-to-potential map directly [25, 26]; but finite-basis inversion is ill-conditioned and fixes the potential only up to a constant [27, 28, 29, 30], so pointwise fitting imports numerical noise into the target. The other is differentiable DFT [31, 32, 33], which places the SCF cycle inside automatic differentiation so that self-consistent densities and energies enter the loss directly. It is effective, but every training step must converge the SCF and backpropagate through it, which is costly and fragile for hard-to-converge systems; alternating training with SCF [34] likewise requires repeated SCF solutions.

In this Letter we expand about the KS orbitals of an accurate reference density and constrain how the trained functional behaves there. Our key observation is that a single quantity—the Brillouin residual of the trained functional on the reference orbitals, i.e., the occupied-virtual block of its Fock matrix—controls, to first order, both the self-consistent density shift and the gap between fitted and self-consistent energies. Penalizing it yields a stationarity loss and a first-order density loss (Fig. 1) with three properties: their target is exact self-consistency at the reference orbitals; they see only the part of the potential error that rotates occupied orbitals, so the constant and ill-determined components that plague inversion drop out; and they need one Fock build per system, with no SCF solved or differentiated during training. Trained on 6 reference energies and the coupled-cluster (CCSD) densities of 11 atoms, ions, and diatomics, and tested fully self-consistently on 103 molecules, many with elements and bonds absent from training, the same network reproduces the trend of Ref. [13] under energy-only training—densities worse than those of the base functional—and reverses it with the two constraints: the resulting meta-GGA surpasses SCAN in both energies and densities.

Figure 1: Training XC functionals on fixed orbitals.
(a) Wu-Yang inversion of the CCSD density gives fixed KS orbitals, on which the occupied-virtual Fock block $F_{ai}$ of the trained functional yields the predicted SCF rotation $\kappa_{ai}$ (stationarity loss $\mathcal{L}_{G}$ ) and the first-order density change $\delta n$ (density loss $\mathcal{L}_{D}$ ); the energy loss $\mathcal{L}_{E}$ uses the same orbitals. One Fock build per system gives the parameter gradient, with no SCF.
(b) Energy along one occupied-virtual rotation. Energy-only training (E) matches the reference energy at $\kappa=0$ , but the orbital gradient $2F_{ai}$ drives the SCF solution to $\kappa^{*}=-F_{ai}/\Delta_{ai}$ , causing an energy error $\Delta_{ai}\kappa^{*2}$ and a density shift $\delta n$ . EGD makes the reference orbitals stationary.

Self-consistent mismatch on fixed orbitals.—Let $\{\bar{\phi}_{p\sigma},\bar{\epsilon}_{p\sigma}\}$ be the KS orbitals and orbital energies obtained from the CCSD reference density $n^{\mathrm{ref}}$ by Wu-Yang inversion [19], i.e., eigenstates of a local-potential Hamiltonian $\hat{h}^{\mathrm{ref}}_{\sigma}$ . For a functional with parameters $\Theta$ , the energy of system $m$ on these fixed orbitals is

 $E_{m}(\Theta)=E_{m}^{0}+E_{\mathrm{xc}}^{\Theta}[\bar{\Phi}_{m}],$ 

(1)

where $E_{m}^{0}$ collects the kinetic, external, Hartree, and nuclear-repulsion energies and is independent of $\Theta$ . Conventional energy-only fitting (hereafter E) makes reaction energies assembled from Eq. (1) reproduce reference values. Because Eq. (1) is evaluated on orbitals of the reference density, E fitting does not lack density information; it lacks information on whether the functional’s self-consistent solution stays on these orbitals.

Writing a real occupied-virtual rotation as $\phi_{i\sigma}=\bar{\phi}_{i\sigma}+\sum_{a}\kappa^{\sigma}_{ai}\bar{\phi}_{a\sigma}+O(\kappa^{2})$ and expanding to second order about $\kappa=0$ gives

 $E_{m}(\Theta;\kappa)\simeq E_{m}(\Theta)+\sum_{\sigma ai}\Big[2F^{\sigma}_{ai}(\Theta)\,\kappa^{\sigma}_{ai}+\Delta^{\sigma}_{ai}\big(\kappa^{\sigma}_{ai}\big)^{2}\Big],$ 

(2)

where $F^{\sigma}_{ai}(\Theta)=\langle\bar{\phi}_{a\sigma}|\hat{F}^{\sigma}[\bar{\Phi};\Theta]|\bar{\phi}_{i\sigma}\rangle$ is the occupied-virtual block of the trained functional’s Fock matrix on the reference orbitals and $2F^{\sigma}_{ai}$ the orbital gradient (unit occupation per spin orbital). We take the uncoupled diagonal orbital Hessian $\Delta^{\sigma}_{ai}=\max(\bar{\epsilon}_{a\sigma}-\bar{\epsilon}_{i\sigma},\Delta_{\min})$ , where $\Delta_{\min}=0.05\,E_{h}$ keeps near-degenerate pairs from dominating. Minimizing Eq. (2) gives the first-order SCF relaxation

 $\kappa^{\sigma}_{ai}(\Theta)=-F^{\sigma}_{ai}(\Theta)/\Delta^{\sigma}_{ai}$ 

(3)

and its two observable consequences,

 $\displaystyle E^{\mathrm{SCF}}_{m}(\Theta)$ 
 $\displaystyle\simeq E_{m}(\Theta)-\sum_{\sigma ai}\Delta^{\sigma}_{ai}\big(\kappa^{\sigma}_{ai}\big)^{2},$ 

(4)

 $\displaystyle\delta n_{m}(\mathbf{r};\Theta)$ 
 $\displaystyle\simeq 2\sum_{\sigma ai}\bar{\phi}_{a\sigma}(\mathbf{r})\,\bar{\phi}_{i\sigma}(\mathbf{r})\,\kappa^{\sigma}_{ai}(\Theta).$ 

(5)

Equation (4) shows that the fixed-orbital energy targeted by E fitting differs from the self-consistent energy by a term quadratic in $F$ —the density-driven error relative to the reference density [16, 17]—and Eq. (5) that the SCF density shift is first order in $F$ . Neither is a target of E fitting, and both vanish only when $F^{\sigma}_{ai}=0$ , i.e., when the reference determinant satisfies the Brillouin condition [35] of the trained functional. Importantly, this target is exact: $F^{\sigma}_{ai}=0$ for all pairs if and only if the reference orbitals are a self-consistent solution of the trained functional in the given basis, so the uncoupled Hessian affects only how deviations from stationarity are weighted. A positive-definite Hartree-XC kernel (the Hartree part usually dominates) screens orbital relaxation, in which case Eq. (4) bounds the energy relaxation from above.

Relation to potential fitting.—Because the reference orbitals are eigenstates of $\hat{h}^{\mathrm{ref}}$ ,

 $F^{\sigma}_{ai}=\langle\bar{\phi}_{a\sigma}|\,\Delta\hat{v}_{\sigma}\,|\bar{\phi}_{i\sigma}\rangle,\qquad\Delta\hat{v}_{\sigma}=\hat{v}^{\Theta}_{\mathrm{xc},\sigma}-v^{\mathrm{ref}}_{\mathrm{xc},\sigma},$ 

(6)

where $v^{\mathrm{ref}}_{\mathrm{xc}}$ is the inverted local XC potential and, for a meta-GGA, $\hat{v}^{\Theta}_{\mathrm{xc}}$ includes the nonmultiplicative generalized-KS term $-\tfrac{1}{2}\nabla\cdot[(\partial e_{\mathrm{xc}}/\partial\tau_{\sigma})\nabla]$ [36, 37]. Equations (3) and (5) are thus the uncoupled first-order orbital rotation and KS density response induced by $\Delta\hat{v}$ . Unlike pointwise potential fitting, only the occupied-virtual block of $\Delta\hat{v}$ enters: a constant shift cancels ( $\langle\bar{\phi}_{a}|c|\bar{\phi}_{i}\rangle=0$ ), and components with a vanishing occupied-virtual block—which leave the density unchanged to first order and are precisely those that finite-basis inversion cannot determine—are excluded. The constraint retains exactly the potential information that the reference density carries.

Figure 2: Absolute errors of self-consistent atomization and ionization energies on the test sets. Boxes: interquartile range; bars: medians; diamonds: MAEs. “Energy loss only” denotes E training; the other NN functionals use the full loss, Eq. (9) (EGD). The stationarity and density terms lower the errors of both NN functionals on all atomization-energy sets, most strongly for new bond pairs. CCSD uses the aug-cc-pVTZ basis.

Stationarity and first-order density constraints.—The stationarity loss is the squared norm of the predicted rotation,

 $\mathcal{L}_{G}(\Theta)=\sum_{m\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{\sigma ai}\big[\kappa^{\sigma}_{ai}(\Theta)\big]^{2}.$ 

(7)

By Eq. (4), the energy gap $\sum\Delta^{\sigma}_{ai}(\kappa^{\sigma}_{ai})^{2}\leq\max\Delta^{\sigma}_{ai}\cdot\sum(\kappa^{\sigma}_{ai})^{2}$ , so $\mathcal{L}_{G}$ also controls it; relative to the gap ( $\propto F^{2}/\Delta$ ), $\mathcal{L}_{G}$ ( $\propto F^{2}/\Delta^{2}$ ) emphasizes small-gap pairs, which relax most easily. The first-order density loss compares the predicted SCF density directly with the CCSD density,

 $\mathcal{L}_{D}(\Theta)=\frac{1}{N_{\mathcal{S}}}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{S}}\big\|\bar{n}_{m}+\delta n_{m}(\Theta)-n^{\mathrm{ref}}_{m}\big\|^{2},$ 

(8)

where $\|f\|^{2}=\int f(\mathbf{r})^{2}d\mathbf{r}$ , $\bar{n}_{m}$ is the density of the reference orbitals, and $\mathcal{S}$ is the set of $N_{\mathcal{S}}$ training systems with density data.

The two losses are complementary. $\mathcal{L}_{D}$ targets the observable $n^{\mathrm{ref}}_{m}$ itself, so $\delta n_{m}$ can also absorb the part of the inversion residual $d_{m}=\bar{n}_{m}-n^{\mathrm{ref}}_{m}\neq 0$ that orbital rotations can represent. $\mathcal{L}_{G}$ acts on the orbitals: rotations that barely change the density still change a meta-GGA energy through the kinetic-energy density $\tau$ , and $\mathcal{L}_{G}$ keeps the predicted rotations small, so the first-order prediction behind $\mathcal{L}_{D}$ stays valid.

Training objective.—The total loss is

 $\mathcal{L}(\Theta)=\lambda_{E}\,\mathcal{L}_{E}(\Theta)+\lambda_{G}\,\mathcal{L}_{G}(\Theta)+\lambda_{D}\,\mathcal{L}_{D}(\Theta),$ 

(9)

where $\mathcal{L}_{E}$ is the root-mean-square error (in hartree) of six reference reaction energies assembled from Eq. (1). We compare E ( $\lambda_{G}=\lambda_{D}=0$ ) and EGD ( $\lambda_{E}=\lambda_{G}=50$ , $\lambda_{D}=500$ ), which share reference orbitals, energy term, optimizer, and checkpoint selection and differ only by Eqs. (7) and (8). Each training step needs one occupied-virtual Fock block per system, and the gradient with respect to $\Theta$ follows from a single adjoint pass; no SCF is solved or implicitly differentiated. Training uses only the first-order response, but every energy and density reported below is fully self-consistent and thus measures the functional in actual use. Derivations and numerical details are in the Supplemental Material (SM) [38].

Figure 3: (a) GGA and (b) meta-GGA functionals in the plane of AE103 atomization-energy MAE and DP99 density error. Open circles: conventional functionals; filled blue circles: Pareto-optimal conventional functionals; blue line: Pareto front; red diamonds: NN functionals trained with $L=E$ or $L=EGD$ . The two constraints move both NN functionals from the interior to the low-density-error end of the front. Values for all functionals are in the SM [38].

Models and data.—To test two rungs of Jacob’s ladder [39], we train a PBE-based NN-GGA and a SCAN-based NN-mGGA [40, 41] of the form

 $\displaystyle E^{\Theta}_{\mathrm{xc}}[n]=\alpha\,E^{\rm base}_{\mathrm{xc}}[n]+\beta\int n(\mathbf{r})\,f_{\theta}\big(\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{r})\big)\,d\mathbf{r},$ 

(10)

 $\displaystyle\mathbf{z}^{\rm GGA}=\big(\ln(1+n),\,\zeta,\,\ln(1+s)\big),$ 

 $\displaystyle\mathbf{z}^{\rm mGGA}=\big(\mathbf{z}^{\rm GGA},\,\ln(1+a_{\tau})\big),$ 

(11)

where $E^{\rm base}_{\mathrm{xc}}$ is PBE or SCAN, $\zeta$ the spin polarization, $s$ the reduced density gradient, $a_{\tau}=(\tau-\tau_{W})/\tau_{\rm unif}$ the kinetic-energy-density indicator, and $f_{\theta}$ a fully connected network. All of $\Theta=(\alpha,\beta,\theta)$ are trained, starting from the base functional ( $\alpha=1$ , $\beta=0$ ), so E and EGD compare directly with PBE or SCAN. NN-GGA and NN-mGGA have 2274 and 2306 parameters (architectures and hyperparameters in the SM [38]).

Table 1: Training and validation systems. Density systems use CCSD $\Lambda$ densities and their Wu-Yang orbitals, entering $\mathcal{L}_{G}$ and $\mathcal{L}_{D}$ (training) or the density error (validation). Atomic energies of C and O needed for atomization energies are evaluated on fixed orbitals but do not enter $\mathcal{L}_{G}$ or $\mathcal{L}_{D}$ . The partition follows Ref. [32], with O+ and Ne+ added to the density set.

The energy term uses six data (Table 1): atomization energies of H2, LiH, O2, and CO from W4-11 [42] and experimental first ionization energies of O and Ne [43]. The stationarity and density terms use 11 atoms, ions, and diatomics, with all-electron UCCSD ( $\Lambda$ -equation) one-particle density matrices [44, 45] (UHF reference, aug-cc-pVTZ basis [46, 47], PySCF level-6 grid [48]); the Wu-Yang orbitals of these densities stay fixed during training. Checkpoints are selected by fully self-consistent validation calculations that include atoms absent from training (N, F), using a weighted sum of the SCF root-mean-square energy errors (kcal/mol) and the mean density error. E and EGD share this score, so their differences stem from the training objective alone. The data set is comparable to the smallest used for machine-learned functionals [7, 32] and orders of magnitude smaller than those of recent large-scale models [9, 12].

The test set AE103 comprises 103 molecules with 2–14 atoms from the first three rows of the periodic table; it and the 18 atomic ionization energies of IP18 (H–Ar) are taken from the data set of Ref. [32]. Because training covers only atoms, ions, and diatomics of H–Ne, we also report two extrapolation subsets: molecules with elements absent from training (“new elements,” 37) and with bonded atom pairs absent from training (“new bond pairs,” 53). We further test 99 density records for 98 molecules (DP99), with the density error ${\rm DP}=\int(n^{\mathrm{SCF}}-n^{\mathrm{ref}})^{2}d\mathbf{r}$ evaluated against CCSD/aug-cc-pVTZ reference densities, averaged over records, and reported in units of $10^{-3}$ a.u. Full lists are in the SM [38].

Same network, same data, different objective.—Comparing E with EGD isolates the effect of Eqs. (7) and (8) (Fig. 2). For NN-GGA, EGD lowers the AE103 mean absolute error (MAE) from 11.6 to 5.6 kcal/mol, 2.6 times below its base PBE (14.6 kcal/mol). For NN-mGGA, EGD lowers the MAE from 7.1 to 3.3 kcal/mol, below SCAN (3.7 kcal/mol).

The gain is largest outside the training distribution. On new elements, NN-GGA(E) is worse than PBE (11.2 vs 9.1 kcal/mol): the fixed-orbital error reduced in the fit does not carry over to self-consistent prediction, consistent with Eq. (4). EGD lowers this MAE to 6.2 kcal/mol, and that of NN-mGGA from 5.1 to 4.4 kcal/mol. On new bond pairs, EGD lowers the NN-GGA MAE from 12.0 to 5.0 kcal/mol (PBE: 17.5 kcal/mol) and the NN-mGGA MAE from 9.1 to 2.5 kcal/mol, a factor of 3.6. On IP18, where all methods lie within 2.7–4.3 kcal/mol, EGD again removes the degradation caused by energy-only training (NN-GGA: 4.3 to 3.2 kcal/mol; PBE: 3.6 kcal/mol).

Both EGD functionals are also more accurate than CCSD on all three atomization-energy sets (9.5 kcal/mol on AE103), although CCSD supplies their reference densities. The energy term fits W4 and experimental values, whereas CCSD densities enter only through the occupied-virtual block of the potential; the energy accuracy of the trained functional is therefore not capped by the method that generates its reference densities.

title: Code Comprehensor: Hierarchical Documentation and Cross-Modal Retrieval for Large Repositories
abstract: Understanding large, complex, and rapidly evolving code bases remains a core challenge for software engineering at scale, hindering onboarding, maintenance, refactoring, and impact analysis. Providing this information to a Large-Language Model (LLM) is another hurdle, as the LLM must understand not only the required code method but also its associated methods in the grand scheme of the repository. We propose Code Comprehensor, a hybrid retrieval-reasoning framework combining (i) a code dependency callgraph, (ii) CodeScribe, which uses code-aware LLMs to generate hierarchical documentation across repository call graphs, and (iii) CodeContrast, a CLIP-style dual-encoder model trained on CodeScribe output to learn aligned text-code embeddings. CodeContrast enables fast, semantically precise retrieval of relevant code-context neighborhoods, which serve as grounded evidence for an MCP-based LLM orchestrator answering domain-specific queries. Evaluation on OpenCV and a proprietary 5M-LOC repository shows that CodeScribe-derived supervision significantly improves cross-modal retrieval in text-to-code accuracy over baseline approaches. Richer textual supervision (hierarchical documentation, parent/sibling context, and LLM-generated synthetic questions) consistently enhances performance across both repositories. LLM-as-a-judge evaluation using the popular RAGAS of the Code Comprehensor output yields above 90% faithfulness scores.
comment: Accepted at 42nd International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution

Abstract

Understanding large, complex, and rapidly evolving code bases remains a core challenge for software engineering at scale, hindering onboarding, maintenance, refactoring, and impact analysis. Providing this information to a Large-Language Model (LLM) is another hurdle, as the LLM must understand not only the required code method but also its associated methods in the grand scheme of the repository.
We propose Code Comprehensor, a hybrid retrieval–reasoning framework combining (i) a code dependency callgraph, (ii) CodeScribe, which uses code-aware LLMs to generate hierarchical documentation across repository call graphs, and (iii) CodeContrast, a CLIP-style dual-encoder model trained on CodeScribe output to learn aligned text-code embeddings. CodeContrast enables fast, semantically precise retrieval of relevant code-context neighborhoods, which serve as grounded evidence for an MCP-based LLM orchestrator answering domain-specific queries.
Evaluation on OpenCV and a proprietary 5M-LOC repository shows that CodeScribe-derived supervision significantly improves cross-modal retrieval in text-to-code accuracy over baseline approaches. Richer textual supervision (hierarchical documentation, parent/sibling context, and LLM-generated synthetic questions) consistently enhances performance across both repositories.
LLM-as-a-judge evaluation using the popular RAGAS of the Code Comprehensor output yields above 90% faithfulness scores.

Index Terms: 
Large Language Models (LLMs),
Code comprehension,
Semantic code retrieval,
Contrastive learning,
CLIP-style encoders,
Software repository analysis,
Program analysis,
Hybrid retrieval‑reasoning frameworks

## I Introduction

Enterprises typically have large code repositories that have been developed and maintained over the years. The ability to document and understand such complex repositories has been a challenge [1, 2]. Code complexity creates dependencies on senior engineers’ expertise to understand and navigate such repositories, and introduces inefficiencies in the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) [3]. The growth of Large Language Models (LLM) in recent years and their ability to understand and explain code introduce the possibility of making this process more efficient [4]. This growth will lead to greater productivity in developing new features and maintaining and debugging existing ones.

However, the ability to use LLMs to document and understand large repositories in a reliable, replicable fashion requires careful design and consideration. Despite the large context window of many modern LLMs [5], code repositories often will consume a much larger number of tokens. For example, [6] gives Lines of Code (LOC) for some public repositories, and token sizes will be much larger. Proprietary code repositories are often large in terms of LOC. For example, one of the repositories mentioned in this paper is larger than most listed in [6]. More importantly, just because an LLM can process a large number of tokens does not mean an LLM should access the entire repository for every question. In addition to cost implications, large context sizes are known to give poorer results [7, 8].

Additionally, code repositories often contain identical or very similar files, methods, and variables across different parts of the code base, and using probabilistic machinery like an LLM is unlikely to be reliable or replicable. In view of this, it is important to design systems that enable LLMs to navigate code repositories more consistently and deterministically. Regarding this issue, some studies discuss using the inherent structure of code, as captured in the call graph, to drive documentation. Work by [9] discusses using a static-analysis-based call tree to generate documentation for large-scale repositories recursively. A similar approach to generate initial and incremental documentation has been followed by other works [10]. A hierarchical engine for document generation and querying has also been studied [11]. Recently, Google released a repository to document code [12]; however, to the best of our knowledge, the system’s design has not been disclosed. The common aspect of these repositories is the use of either the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) [13] or the call-graph. However, if one wants to build more than just static documentation, a broader and more comprehensive approach is needed. Previous work [14, 15] has looked at cross-modal contrastive learning for code search; however, without deep domain-level documentation mapping methods to domain and code structure, the effectiveness of such cross-modal retrieval on large, complex repositories is limited.

Fig. 1: Overview of the Code Comprehensor architecture. CodeGraph is created through static analysis and consumed by CodeScribe to generate structured technical descriptions. These descriptions are used by the contrastive model for text and code retrieval. An agentic layer built on the Model Context Protocol coordinates CodeGraph traversal, CodeScribe based retrieval, and contrastive model queries for interactive use.

## I-A Proposed Solution

We present Code Comprehensor, an end-to-end system that combines four main components: (i) CodeGraph, a call graph generated via static analysis and exposed through API endpoints for traversal and chunking; (ii) CodeScribe, a hierarchical documentation engine that recursively processes directory-structured code, supports multiple documentation chapters and custom prompts per directory, and outputs PlantUML diagrams; (iii) a custom data processing module that parses CodeScribe output into relational records linking methods to parent/sibling context; and (iv) CodeContrast, a CLIP-based dual-encoder contrastive model using InfoNCE loss for asymmetric text-to-code and code-to-text retrieval with multi-positive learning support.

CodeScribe operates on a repository directory structure with configurable chapter-based perspectives (e.g., code description, algorithms, data flow). For each start method (in-degree zero in the method subgraph), CodeScribe retrieves the Depth-First-Search (DFS) traversal tree via CodeGraph, chunks it if necessary using post-order traversal to preserve hierarchy, and generates documentation. CodeScribe supports both full and incremental (git-commit-driven) documentation runs.

CodeContrast leverages the structured training data from CodeScribe parsing to train a retrieval model. We adopt CLIP’s dual-encoder architecture for efficient pre-computed embeddings and asymmetric modalities. The InfoNCE objective learns well-separated embedding spaces and extends naturally to multi-positive scenarios.

Finally, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) based orchestration layer integrates CodeGraph, CodeScribe, and CodeContrast into an agentic system accessible via an Integrated Development Environment (IDE). This Master Agent invokes specialized agents (RAG over CodeScribe output, CodeGraph traversal, CodeContrast retrieval) to answer domain-specific queries on code repositories.

The core contributions of this paper are as follows:

• 

A post-order chunking algorithm that enables LLM documentation of arbitrarily large call trees while preserving structural hierarchy.

• 

A multi-granularity training data construction pipeline that leverages parent-sibling relationships from documentation structure and LLM-generated synthetic questions for enhanced retrieval performance.

• 

Code Comprehensor: an integrated end-to-end system combining CodeGraph, CodeScribe, and CodeContrast components for large-scale repository understanding and retrieval.

• 

Empirical evidence that hierarchical documentation-derived supervision improves cross-modal code retrieval by at least 9% Top-1 accuracy over baseline approaches.

The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. We briefly summarize previous work in Section II. We discuss the System Architecture in Section III, the detailed methodology in Section IV, and present results in Section V. We conclude with a discussion, threats to validity, and future works in Sections VI, VII, and VIII, respectively.

## II Related Work

## II-A Code Search and Retrieval

Code search and retrieval has been an active area of research for understanding large repositories. Recent work has focused on neural approaches combining text and code embeddings. Sun et al. [16] presented context-aware code translation for code search, while Chai et al. [17] explored cross-domain deep code search using meta-learning techniques. Mathew and Stolee [18] investigated cross-language code search, and Mao et al. [19] proposed self-supervised query reformulation for improved retrieval. More recently, Wang et al. [20] examined fusion of multiple code searchers, and Shi et al. [21] introduced CoCoSoDa for effective contrastive learning on code search tasks. Large-scale contrastive pre-training for code retrieval has been explored by Li et al. [22], who developed CodeRetriever. Comprehensive surveys on code search have been provided by Di Grazia and Pradel [23] and Sun et al. [24].

## II-B Repository-Level Documentation Generation

Documentation generation at repository scale has emerged as a critical need for understanding complex systems. Luo et al. [25] introduced RepoAgent, which combines static analysis with LLM-driven documentation. Hoang et al. [26] developed CodeWiki, a framework for generating hierarchical documentation. Sounthiraraj et al. [27] proposed a hierarchical engine for structured document generation and querying.

## II-C Contrastive Learning for Code

Contrastive learning has proven effective for learning aligned embeddings of code and text. Neelakantan et al. [28] introduced text and code embeddings using contrastive methods. Li et al. [22] leveraged contrastive learning in CodeRetriever for large-scale pre-training. Shi et al. [21] proposed CoCoSoDa with a momentum encoder design.

## II-D Differentiation from Prior Work

Code Comprehensor extends prior work in three key ways. First, unlike code search methods that operate on isolated code snippets (e.g., CodeRetriever, CoCoSoDa), our system first generates hierarchical documentation that captures inter-method relationships through call graph analysis and multi-perspective documentation generation, then trains a contrastive model on this enriched representation. Prior work on code retrieval has focused primarily on Python and Java; CodeRetriever and CoCoSoDa lack publicly available implementations for C/C++ repositories, limiting direct empirical comparison on the systems programming domain where our work is evaluated. Second, unlike RepoAgent, which focuses solely on documentation generation, our system uses the generated documentation as a structured training signal for a retrieval model, enabling efficient inference-time retrieval without requiring LLM calls per query. Third, we employ a post-order chunking algorithm to handle arbitrarily large call trees while preserving structural hierarchy, enabling scalable documentation and retrieval on repositories exceeding 5M lines of code.

## III System Architecture

Figure 1 shows the overall system architecture for Code Comprehensor. Git repositories are first cloned into our system, and the CodeGraph is generated using static analysis. This CodeGraph is then consumed in CodeScribe, which uses two additional external information sources: prompts and configuration files. These are discussed in detail in Section IV-B. The output of CodeScribe, called “Synthesized Technical Descriptions” (SynTD), is consumed by CodeContrast. CodeScribe uses recursive synthesis (shown as “S” in Figure 1) indicated by the self-loop. To enable an end user (or an external system/agent) to interact with the documentation, multiple custom agents are built. The end user interacts with the Master Agent (MA) via an MCP gateway. The MA is an LLM-based orchestrator that calls multiple specialized agents. The CodeScribe Agent is an RAG-based system on the SynTD. There is a CodeContrast agent that can invoke API calls on the trained contrastive model. The CodeGraph agent can perform custom traversals on the CodeGraph via an exposed API.

Given a natural-language question from the user (an Engineer in this example), the MA retrieves relevant code blocks from the CodeContrast agent using Text $\rightarrow$ Code-based retrieval. The MA retrieves the hierarchy of the relevant methods from the CodeGraph agent and obtains their documentation using the CodeScribe Agent. Finally, the MA composes a natural-language response to the end user and adds relevant diagrams and code blocks to provide a more comprehensive answer. The end user can interact further with the MA with follow-up questions. The Engineer can also ask questions, such as explanations of specific files, methods, or classes, and their relevance to the overall system. In such a case, MA uses the Code $\rightarrow$ Text retrieval from the CM agent. It also identifies the method or file hierarchy from the CodeGraph agent and the documentation from the CodeScribe Agent. The MA decides which type of retrieval to invoke from the CodeContrast agent. This system allows for seamless end-to-end navigation and interpretation of the repository.

## IV Methodology

## IV-A CodeGraph Creation

To create the CodeGraph, a static analysis of the code repository is first performed. Static analysis identifies all code files and their corresponding methods.
Dependencies are resolved via compile commands or, if unavailable, with reasonable heuristics. Node types are files and methods, and in object-oriented languages, other node types, such as classes, are added. Comments written by the developer for the methods are also extracted as attributes for the method nodes in CodeGraph, along with the method signatures. For methods without a developer-written comment, an LLM is prompted to generate one. The actual method body is also available as an attribute on the method. Since the same method can appear in multiple files, nodes are named “method_name:::file_name” where “:::” is chosen as the separator since it is unlikely to appear elsewhere. In object-oriented languages, nodes are named “method_name:::file_name::::line_number” to handle operator overloading. Method names include the namespace and class name, where relevant, as fully qualified names. The Tree-Sitter library [29] is used for parsing, though other approaches can be used. The CodeGraph generation, of course, needs (programming) language-specific parsing. The CodeGraph structure is generic, and the rest of the processing in the entire system is language-agnostic.

The CodeGraph is saved as a Python Networkx [30] library object. This CodeGraph is also exposed through a FastAPI service [31]. Several endpoints are exposed via the FastAPI service. Most are standard endpoints for graph traversal, e.g., Breadth-First-Search (BFS) and Depth-First-Search (DFS), along with the “invokes” edge in both forward and reverse directions. The resultant CodeGraph and the endpoints are used to generate the documents using CodeScribe.

## IV-B CodeScribe

CodeScribe documentation is driven by the repository’s directory structure because that is the natural way developers navigate it. The output of CodeScribe is Markdown files in a directory structure that replicates the code repository’s directories. CodeScribe has configuration files that allow one to exclude irrelevant directories and include only file name extensions that are present. Every directory can have one or more perspectives to document the code, called “chapters” (e.g., code description, algorithms, data flow, interfaces). For each chapter, a custom prompt is generated, with flexibility to customize per directory. CodeScribe can also consume configuration information, such as abbreviation lists for specialized domains.

The system prompts are designed with three key principles: (1) LLM output is constrained to generate documents at hierarchical levels of abstraction, summarizing at appropriate semantic boundaries; (2) quoted code segments are marked with metadata (method name, file path, language) to enable downstream parsing and tracing back to source; (3) consistency across documentation perspectives ensures coherent multi-chapter views of the same code units. These design choices are critical for downstream parsing and contrastive model training.

When processing any directory, CodeScribe invokes CodeGraph to find all files in the directory and the methods they contain. Next, among the methods it identifies, start methods are those with an in-degree of zero in the method-only subgraph (a subgraph consisting only of methods). These methods are invoked by the external system (outside the scope of the current module graph). For each start method, the DFS traversal tree is retrieved via an endpoint on the CodeGraph API. The DFS traversal endpoint generates a key for each element in the DFS walk, and this information is included in the LLM’s context. The context also includes the method definitions in the DFS tree. Thus, there is one Markdown output file per chapter and per start method. The documents for each start method are then combined for a summarized document at the directory level. Optionally, via a configuration file, summarizations for directory hierarchies are also done.

However, in large repositories, it is common to find trees that exceed the allowable context window, especially since method definitions are included. It is important to note that context sizes include output tokens, and there must be a reasonable allowance left for the LLM to generate sufficiently detailed documentation. This requires that the DFS walk trees be properly chunked. Hence, we build a chunking process that allows customizable chunk sizes. To handle such large trees, we implement an algorithm that uses recursive post-order traversal to process the DFS tree. For each node, we first process all children recursively,
conclusion:
The results across both repositories demonstrate the nuanced benefits of incorporating CodeScribe-generated information into the CodeContrast pipeline. In Table I, the Top-1 accuracy overall for OpenCV is 66.05% for D2 and is 80.64% for D3, showing an improvement of 14.59%. Similarly, for Repo-A, we get 8.72% improvement (67.6% for D2 and 76.18% for D3). In Table II, for non-synthetic tests on human-authored descriptions, D2 achieves superior performance: on OpenCV’s doc_brief_merged category, D2 achieves Top-1 accuracy of 96.43% while D3 achieves 93.94%. This indicates that adding parent/sibling context and synthetic QA can reduce performance when evaluating against developer-authored comments.

However, for synthetic test queries, D3 demonstrates consistent improvements over D2 across all Top- $K$ values for complex query categories (qa_doc_gen, qa_doc_raw, qa_self, qa_parent, qa_sibling). This improvement compensates for the drop in accuracy in doc_brief_merged discussed earlier.
To ensure that function names in synthetic questions do not lead to data leakage, we remove function-name tokens from questions - the results in Table II are using these post-processed questions.

The larger architecture explains these complementary benefits. CodeScribe introduces a structured way of summarizing code at different levels of abstraction through call graph traversal, recursive document synthesis, and chapter-based documentation prompts. The parsing pipeline converts these hierarchical documents into structured records that preserve parent and sibling relationships. These relational signals help the contrastive model learn contextual relationships between methods. D2 excels when queries closely match human-authored documentation, while D3 provides benefits for high-variability or indirectly-specified queries that require broader semantic reasoning.

In practice, the expected query distribution should inform configuration selection: D2 is recommended for applications where queries directly correspond to method documentation (e.g., documentation search), while D3 is better suited for diverse developer queries requiring understanding of broader system context. The practical deployment should measure performance on the target query distribution.

body_start:
Abstract

LLM agents with similar success rates can follow different action sequences. An Agent Behavior Map represents LLM–harness combinations using centered action log-likelihoods on shared reference trajectories, without requiring new environment rollouts from the target agent. We derive error bounds relating squared coordinate distances to trajectory KL under explicit assumptions, and across eight cross-scored models the distances track the directly measured trajectory KL in rank order. Across 100 LLMs and four environments, ALFWorld-based coordinates support performance prediction and identify behavioral similarities. In ALFWorld, these similarities persist after controlling for success rates and model size, including across model families. As an extension, harness-component displacements approximately compose, with accuracy varying across components and environments.

## 1 Introduction

Figure 1: Agents close on the map act alike when run. (a) 100 LLMs with the BASE harness, scored on 500 ALFWorld reference trajectories (t-SNE layout; neighbors computed in the original space). $\star$ : gemma4-31b; green: its five nearest models on the map; orange rings: the five closest in parameter count. (b) Action sequences of these 11 models on one ALFWorld task. All succeed, but four of the five map neighbors share the anchor’s short route, whereas three of the five size-matched models take longer ones. (c) Effect size of the behavioral distance to the $k$ -th nearest model on the map (solid) or in parameter count (dashed), averaged over four aspects and 100 models (§3.3); positive means more similar than the average pair.

Comparing LLM agents is a matter not only of how often they succeed but also of how they act. Agents with similar success rates can differ in the tools they choose, the order of their actions, and how often they repeat an operation. Such behavior depends on the combination of the underlying LLM and the harness that manages history, planning, and reasoning (Zhang et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026; Vats and Golev, 2026; Fan et al., 2026). Running every combination in the environment reveals both performance and behavior, but each new agent to compare requires collecting new trajectories. This paper asks whether a representation that captures similarity of run-time behavior can be built without new environment runs of the target agent.

When agents are compared by their log-likelihoods on shared reference trajectories, the difficulty is that the distribution of the histories on which the likelihoods are conditioned itself depends on the agent’s policy. The histories contained in the reference trajectories need not coincide with those that an agent reaches through its own actions. Whether similarity of action probabilities measured on shared histories corresponds to similarity of trajectory distributions and behavior at run time is therefore not obvious. How much of these on-policy properties can be captured by off-policy observations on fixed reference trajectories is the central question of this work.

Language model maps, which vectorize log-likelihoods on shared texts, represent the relations between models in a common coordinate space (Oyama et al., 2025). Their extension to prompt–response distributions has examined performance prediction from conditional log-likelihoods and the approximate additivity of the coordinate displacements caused by prompt changes (Oyama et al., 2026). This paper applies the framework to agents that interact sequentially with an environment and answers the question above with theory and experiments.

An Agent Behavior Map treats each agent as a pair of an LLM and a harness. Each agent rebuilds its input with its own harness from the shared external history in the reference trajectories, namely the task, the observations, and the past actions. The recorded actions are teacher-forced under this input, and the resulting log-likelihood vector is centered to give the agent’s coordinates. Because the reference trajectories are reused, the coordinates of a new agent can be computed without collecting any additional environment trajectories from it. Figure 1 shows an example in which agents that are close in these coordinates take similar action sequences when run. We validate the representation from two angles.

• 

Theoretical and empirical relation to the trajectory distribution (§2, §3.1). Under assumptions on the locality of the two policies and on the mismatch with the reference distribution, we derive error bounds that relate squared coordinate distances to the KL divergence between trajectory distributions. The error decomposes into local approximation, reference mismatch, centering, and finite samples, and the decomposition shows how the step-level and trajectory-level representations differ in their dependence on trajectory length. In a cross-scoring experiment with eight models, we compare the coordinate distances with the directly measured trajectory KL, the target itself, and find a high rank correlation.

• 

Validation on performance and behavior (§3.2, §3.3). We apply a common harness to 100 LLMs and evaluate coordinates built from ALFWorld reference trajectories alone on ALFWorld, TextWorld, BFCL, and MiniWoB++. Besides predicting the success rates of unevaluated models from the evaluation results of the others, we ask whether neighbors on the map generate similar action sequences. In ALFWorld in particular, the similarity of action sequences remains when compared with neighbors chosen by success rate or by size, and when the candidates are restricted to models of other families. These results support the view that the coordinates carry behavioral information that neither performance level nor model family explains. The accuracy of performance prediction and the strength of behavioral similarity among neighbors, however, depend on the environment and the measure.

Finally, we represent the addition of a harness component as a displacement on the map and ask whether such displacements add up within an LLM (§4). Comparison with measured coordinates shows approximate additivity, with an accuracy that depends on the component and the environment.

## 2 Agent Behavior Maps

## 2.1 Problem: comparing agents by what they do when run

On task $x$ , an agent interacts with the environment and produces a trajectory $\tau=(x,o_{0},a_{0},o_{1},\dots,a_{T-1},o_{T})$ of observations $o_{t}$ and actions $a_{t}$ . Its length $T=T(\tau)$ varies and is capped by a known limit $T_{\max}$ . The external history before the action at time $t$ is $h_{t}=(x,o_{0},a_{0},\dots,o_{t})$ ; it excludes the generator’s internal state, such as its system prompt, reasoning, plans, and summaries. An agent $i=(\text{LLM},\text{harness})$ rebuilds its input from $h_{t}$ by its own rule $C_{i}$ (history window, retrieval, summarization) and generates text under the action grammar; $\pi_{i}(a\mid h)$ denotes the resulting probability of action $a$ (Appendix A.1 covers the grammar and tokenization). Given a task distribution $w$ , an initial observation $p_{0}$ , and environment dynamics $E_{t}=E(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t})$ shared by all agents, agent $i$ induces the trajectory distribution

 $P_{i}(\tau)=w(x)\,p_{0}(o_{0}\mid x)\prod_{t<T}\pi_{i}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})\,E_{t}.$ 

(1)

The environment terms cancel in the log-likelihood ratio of two agents. We compare agents by the trajectory KL $K_{ij}:=\mathrm{KL}(P_{i}\|P_{j})$ and its symmetrization $K_{\mathrm{sym}}:=(K_{ij}+K_{ji})/2$ . $P_{i}$ is the distribution of trajectories when agent $i$ is actually run, so the properties we care about, such as success rates and action frequencies, are functionals of $P_{i}$ : on-policy quantities.

Writing $\mathbb{E}_{i}=\mathbb{E}_{P_{i}}$ , the chain rule of KL (Cover and Thomas, 2006; Ke et al., 2020) gives

 $K_{ij}=\mathbb{E}_{i}\textstyle\sum_{t<T}\mathrm{KL}\bigl(\pi_{i}(\cdot\mid h_{t})\|\pi_{j}(\cdot\mid h_{t})\bigr),$ 

(2)

an expectation over the histories that agent $i$ visits when it runs, so measuring it directly takes $n$ rollouts and $O(n^{2})$ cross-scorings for $n$ agents. We ask how much of this quantity can be read, without running the agents, from distances between coordinates obtained by forward passes alone.

## 2.2 Scoring agents on shared reference trajectories

We prepare $N$ reference trajectories $\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{N}$ once, from an unknown reference distribution $Q$ . The distances use neither $Q(\tau)$ nor the generators or their mixing weights, so the trajectories can come from anywhere. We use four sources: logs of the agents under study (ALFWorld, Appendix C), traces published by others ( $\tau$ -bench (Yao et al., 2025) and SWE-Bench (Jimenez et al., 2024) from HAL (Kapoor et al., 2026)), rollouts of two models (the 100-model experiment, §3), and an equal-weight pool of eight scored models (§3.1). Let $T_{r}=T(\tau_{r})$ be the lengths and $M=\sum_{r}T_{r}$ the total number of steps. For each agent $i$ , teacher forcing (Williams and Zipser, 1989) reads $\ell_{i,rt}:=\log\pi_{i}(a_{rt}\mid h_{rt})$ and $A_{i,r}:=\sum_{t<T_{r}}\ell_{i,rt}$ without running the environment. Sharing the trajectories has two costs, the mismatch between $Q$ and each agent’s on-policy distribution and the finite number of trajectories, which §2.3 and §2.4 address.

## 2.3 Step and trajectory embeddings

Let $\bar{\ell}_{i}$ and $\bar{A}_{i}$ be the means of $\ell_{i,rt}$ over all $M$ steps and of $A_{i,r}$ over all $N$ trajectories. Subtracting each agent’s own mean, we define two centered embeddings

 $z^{S}_{i}:=M^{-\frac{1}{2}}(\ell_{i,rt}-\bar{\ell}_{i})_{r,t},\,z^{\tau}_{i}:=N^{-\frac{1}{2}}(A_{i,r}-\bar{A}_{i})_{r}.$ 

A step coordinate asks whether an action is natural in its situation; a trajectory coordinate asks whether a trajectory is natural from its initial state. Only existing steps $t<T_{r}$ are included. The distances are $\hat{D}_{S}=\lVert z^{S}_{i}-z^{S}_{j}\rVert$ and $\hat{D}_{\tau}=\lVert z^{\tau}_{i}-z^{\tau}_{j}\rVert$ . For a pair $(i,j)$ , let $d_{t}=\log\frac{\pi_{i}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})}{\pi_{j}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})}$ be the step log-ratio, $X=\sum_{t<T}d_{t}=\log\frac{P_{i}(\tau)}{P_{j}(\tau)}$ its sum, $\mu=\mathbb{E}_{Q}X$ its mean under the reference, and $\bar{T}=\mathbb{E}_{Q}[T]$ the mean length. The population distances are then $D^{2}_{S}=\frac{1}{\bar{T}}\mathbb{E}_{Q}\sum_{t<T}(d_{t}-\mu/\bar{T})^{2}$ and $D^{2}_{\tau}=\mathrm{Var}_{Q}(X)$ . Centering removes each agent’s overall confidence, its mean log-likelihood, from the coordinates (Appendices A.5 and B.2 treat the uncentered variants).

Distances estimate the trajectory KL.

Fix a pair $(i,j)$ . Assumption 1 (locality): for every history $h$ that occurs under $P_{i}$ , $P_{j}$ , or $Q$ , $\pi_{i}(\cdot\mid h)$ and $\pi_{j}(\cdot\mid h)$ have the same support and $\lvert\log\pi_{i}(a\mid h)/\pi_{j}(a\mid h)\rvert\leq\varepsilon$ on it. Assumption 2 (reference mismatch): $\mathrm{TV}(P_{i},Q)\leq\lambda$ and $\mathrm{TV}(P_{j},Q)\leq\lambda$ . Lengths satisfy $1\leq T\leq T_{\max}$ ; we assume neither independence across steps nor independence between $T$ and the actions.

Theorem 1 (Approximation error).

Under Assumptions 1 and 2, $\lvert K_{ij}-\tfrac{\bar{T}}{2}D^{2}_{S}\rvert\leq R_{S}$ and $\lvert K_{ij}-\tfrac{1}{2}D^{2}_{\tau}\rvert\leq R_{\tau}$ , where, up to absolute constants,

 $\displaystyle R_{S}$ 
 $\displaystyle=O\bigl(\varepsilon^{3}\mathbb{E}_{i}[T]+\lambda T_{\max}\varepsilon^{2}+\mu^{2}/\bar{T}\bigr),$ 

(3)

 $\displaystyle R_{\tau}$ 
 $\displaystyle=O\bigl(\varepsilon^{3}\mathbb{E}_{i}[T^{2}]+\lambda T_{\max}^{2}\varepsilon^{2}+\mu^{2}\bigr).$ 

(4)

Analogous bounds hold for $K_{\mathrm{sym}}$ (Appendix A.2).

The factor $T_{\max}$ on the $\lambda$ term, i.e., state-distribution mismatch accumulating over steps, is an error source that LM maps do not have (constants in Table 1, proofs in Appendix A.2).

## 2.4 Total error: approximation plus sampling

Theorem 1 concerns the population distances. In practice, $\hat{D}_{S}$ and $\hat{D}_{\tau}$ are computed from $N$ reference trajectories, so the total error adds sampling error to the approximation error. Bounding $\mathbb{E}_{i}[T]\leq T_{\max}$ and $\mathbb{E}_{i}[T^{2}]\leq T_{\max}^{2}$ in Table 1 gives the following.

Corollary 1 (Total error).

Let $\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{N}\sim Q$ be i.i.d., and let $\hat{\bar{T}}:=M/N$ , $\hat{K}_{S}:=\tfrac{\hat{\bar{T}}}{2}\hat{D}_{S}^{2}$ , $\hat{K}_{\tau}:=\tfrac{1}{2}\hat{D}_{\tau}^{2}$ , and $u_{N}:=\sqrt{\log(8/\delta)/(2N)}$ . Under Assumptions 1 and 2, with probability at least $1-\delta$ , simultaneously

 $\displaystyle\lvert K_{ij}-\hat{K}_{S}\rvert$ 
 $\displaystyle\leq T_{\max}\,\varepsilon^{2}\bigl(\tfrac{\varepsilon}{4}+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}+3u_{N}\bigr)+\tfrac{\mu^{2}}{2\bar{T}},$ 

 $\displaystyle\lvert K_{ij}-\hat{K}_{\tau}\rvert$ 
 $\displaystyle\leq T_{\max}^{2}\varepsilon^{2}\bigl(\tfrac{\varepsilon}{4}+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}+3u_{N}\bigr)+\tfrac{\mu^{2}}{2}.$ 

The trajectory bound carries an extra factor of $T$ on every term. Since $K_{ij}\leq\varepsilon^{2}\mathbb{E}_{i}[T]/2$ by Lemma 1(iii) and the chain rule, the step bound grows with $T$ like the KL it estimates, whereas the trajectory bound grows as $T^{2}$ : summing log-ratios before squaring picks up cross terms between steps (Appendix A.4). Sampling error shares the parentheses, so it keeps this factor; it decays as $N^{-1/2}$ , while the other terms do not. The proof applies Hoeffding’s inequality (Hoeffding, 1963) to four sample means (Appendix A.3).

Scope of the guarantees.

The guarantees cover only close pairs, with small $\varepsilon$ and $\lambda$ . We therefore test empirically whether distances preserve the order of the KL outside this regime (§3.1) and whether close pairs behave alike when run (§3.3).

## 3 What does the map capture about an agent?

This section fixes the harness to a standard configuration (BASE: a history window of the last four steps, no planning, direct action; §4.1) and places each LLM as one point. The question is what the coordinates capture about an agent. LM maps showed a correlation between coordinates and downstream performance (Oyama et al., 2025). We answer with three quantities: the target itself, the KL between the trajectory distributions of the agents when run (§3.1); one projection of it, the success rate (§3.2); and the behavior itself when run (§3.3).

## 3.1 Does distance track the on-policy divergence?

Theorem 1 applies only in the local regime of small $\varepsilon$ , that is, to nearly identical policies, whereas actual pairs of models may be far apart. We therefore check empirically whether the distances track the trajectory KL outside that regime, and which version, step or trajectory, tracks it better. In the bounds, the step version is favored by a factor of order $T$ (Table 1); we ask whether this advantage shows in the data. Measuring the trajectory KL directly requires rollouts of every model and $O(n^{2})$ cross-scoring, so we use eight models: each solves a common set of ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021) train tasks, every model scores every trajectory, and the cross-scoring gives $K_{\mathrm{sym}}$ for the $\binom{8}{2}=28$ pairs. The distances use the pooled trajectories of the eight models as the common reference (Appendix B.1).

Figure 2: Map estimates, step version $\tfrac{\bar{T}}{2}\hat{D}_{S}^{2}$ and trajectory version $\tfrac{1}{2}\hat{D}_{\tau}^{2}$ , against the directly measured symmetric trajectory KL $K_{\mathrm{sym}}$ : 8 models, 28 pairs, centered coordinates, log–log axes; error bars are standard errors over the 988 shared ALFWorld train tasks. Both track $K_{\mathrm{sym}}$ , the step version more closely.

Both correlate with the KL, the step version more strongly.

Figure 2 shows the result (numbers in Table 6, Appendix B.2). The centered step estimate $\tfrac{\bar{T}}{2}\hat{D}_{S}^{2}$ correlates with $K_{\mathrm{sym}}$ at Pearson $r=0.90$ and Spearman $\rho=0.95$ , and the trajectory estimate $\tfrac{1}{2}\hat{D}_{\tau}^{2}$ at $0.86$ / $0.94$ : distances measured without running the agents preserve the order of the trajectory KL measured by running them. Two trends are consistent with the bounds (Appendix B.2): the RMSE of the trajectory version is an order of magnitude larger than that of the step version, as the orders $T$ versus $T^{2}$ predict, and adding reference trajectories shrinks only the sampling error while the approximation error remains. Centering, although it adds a term to the bound, raises the correlation and lowers the RMSE for both versions. Reading the distances between the eight models from the 100-model map of §3.2 instead, with different reference trajectories and no grammar constraint, gives $r=0.86$ and $\rho=0.88$ (Appendix B.2). Both versions overestimate the measured KL in level, by a median factor of 7.5 for the step version and 74 for the trajectory version (Appendix B.2), so in what follows we use the distances only as a proxy for the order of the KL, and we use the step version.

## 3.2 Performance: predicting without running

Setup.

From here on we use 100 open-weight LLMs. The reference traject
limitations:
Locality.

Both the theoretical guarantee and the empirical correspondence are limited to close pairs. The KL can be read off the distance only for pairs in the local regime of small $\varepsilon$ and $\lambda$ , and pairs of different LLMs are not guaranteed to fall in it: the estimates exceed the measured KL by a median factor of 7.5, although their order agrees (§3.1). The correspondence with behavioral distance holds for neighbors and fades beyond about the 30th neighbor (Figure 1(c)); we have not shown that the magnitude of the distance between far-apart pairs measures how different their behavior is. The map answers who is similar to whom, not by how much.

Dependence on the reference trajectories.

Differences between policies in regions that $Q$ never visits cannot be measured, and the reference mismatch $\lambda$ remains a sensitivity parameter that the likelihood matrix alone does not determine. A general theory of the reference policy is left for future work.

Estimation of the KL.

The trajectory log-likelihood ratios in §3.1 are based on the probability of the canonical token sequence and differ from action probabilities that marginalize over all tokenizations. In environments where the candidate set can be enumerated, this can be resolved by renormalization, but in general it is a limitation.

Access to log-likelihoods.

The coordinates require the target model’s log-likelihood of a given action sequence. Models that are available only through an API that does not return the log-probabilities of given text cannot be placed on the map, so this study is limited to open-weight models.

Sample size of behavior.

The behavioral comparisons are based on one rollout per task, and the behavior of the same model varies from run to run (Bjarnason et al., 2026; Gonuguntla, 2026). We have not compared the size of this variation with the behavioral distance to neighbors.

Scope of the harness experiment.

The harnesses in §4 are limited to the 12 configurations of our own three-slot design (context management, planning, acting) and to 12 LLMs; the main additivity results are on $\tau$ -bench, and ALFWorld and SWE-Bench cover 6 LLMs. Whether the same additivity holds for other scaffolds with differently designed components has not been tested.
conclusion: Agent Behavior Maps, obtained by teacher forcing on common reference trajectories, locate agents without running them. Their coordinates predict the success rates of models that were never run, on the benchmark the map was built from and, combined with size, in other environments. Neighbors on the map take similar action sequences when run. The theory decomposes the gap between the distances and the trajectory KL into four error sources and limits the guarantee to close pairs. Harness components appear as displacements within an LLM whose sums approximate the coordinates of unscored combinations, with an accuracy that depends on the component and the environment. The map represents not only a ranking by performance but also how close agents are in what they do.

title: Building Auditable AI Text Detectors with Sparse Autoencoders
abstract: AI-generated text detectors are increasingly deployed in consequential settings---peer review, education, admissions, journalism, and content moderation---where their outputs directly affect individuals. Yet the strongest detectors are fine-tuned neural classifiers whose decisions are opaque, while transparent alternatives (stylometric and linguistic-feature classifiers) underperform them by wide margins. We present a pipeline that converts a fine-tuned neural detector into a classifier that operates on human-readable concepts. We accomplish this by training sparse autoencoders (SAEs) directly on a detector's residual stream, assigning auto-interpretation labels to each SAE feature, and retaining only features whose generated descriptions pass a global fidelity threshold. We then train a lightweight classifier on just the interpretable features. We find that our SAEs recover latent concepts that correspond to highly specific and predictive linguistic "tells" of AI-generated text. Classifiers built on these extracted features are not only highly interpretable but exhibit stronger performance on out-of-distribution texts than either neural or stylometric alternatives.

body_start:
Abstract

AI-generated text detectors are increasingly deployed in consequential settings—peer review, education, admissions, journalism, and content moderation—where their outputs directly affect individuals. Yet the strongest detectors are fine-tuned neural classifiers whose decisions are opaque, while transparent alternatives (stylometric and linguistic-feature classifiers) underperform them by wide margins. We present a pipeline that converts a fine-tuned neural detector into a classifier that operates on human-readable concepts. We accomplish this by training sparse autoencoders (SAEs) directly on a detector’s residual stream, assigning auto-interpretation labels to each SAE feature, and retaining only features whose generated descriptions pass a global fidelity threshold. We then train a lightweight classifier on just the interpretable features. We find that our SAEs recover latent concepts that correspond to highly specific and predictive linguistic “tells” of AI-generated text. Classifiers built on these extracted features are not only highly interpretable but exhibit stronger performance on out-of-distribution texts than either neural or stylometric alternatives.

## 1 Introduction

AI-generated text detection is no longer a purely academic problem. Detectors are used to flag student essays, vet peer-review submissions, screen job applications, and moderate online content. Their outputs feed into decisions that affect individuals, and in practice they are often treated as black boxes by users who cannot inspect or contest them.

Figure 1: In our work, we use Sparse Autoencoders to convert existing black box AI detectors into ones that operate on human-interpretable concepts—allowing for more auditable deployment.

In settings like these, accuracy is not the only thing that matters. What also matters is whether an auditor—a reviewer, an instructor, a compliance officer—can look inside a decision, understand what the detector is keying on, and stress-test it. Stylometric detectors (Fröhling and Zubiaga, 2021; Aityan et al., 2026) are interpretable by construction but underperform their neural counterparts. Fine-tuned neural models achieve high accuracy but operate as black boxes.
What real-world deployment needs is a performant AI detector whose decisions can be explained and grounded in specific characteristics and features of the input text.

Our work builds an interpretable AI detector in four stages. First, we fine-tune a model on the AI detection task. Then, we train sparse autoencoders on the model’s residual stream at various depths. Then, we run an auto-interpretation pipeline on the SAE features (Bills et al., 2023; Paulo et al., 2025), and keep only those features whose explanations reach a certain global simulation score threshold. Finally, we train a lightweight $L_{1}$ -regularized logistic regression classifier on the remaining features. The resulting classifier is built on automatically discovered features that each have an associated natural-language description that accurately describes their underlying activation patterns.

## 2 Background

## 2.1 Sparse Autoencoders

Individual neurons in a neural network are often polysemantic Olah et al. (2020)—firing on seemingly unrelated inputs in ways that make interpretability challenging.
Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) Cunningham et al. (2024); Bricken et al. (2023) undo this polysemanticity by converting dense neural network activations $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}$ into large sparsely-active vectors of monosemantic features $\mathbf{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{SAE}}}$ . The encoder and decoder are parameterized as

 $\displaystyle\mathbf{f}_{\text{enc}}(\mathbf{x})$ 
 $\displaystyle=\sigma(\mathbf{W}_{\text{enc}}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}_{\text{enc}})$ 

(1)

 $\displaystyle\mathbf{f}_{\text{dec}}(\mathbf{h})$ 
 $\displaystyle=\mathbf{W}_{\text{dec}}\mathbf{h}+\mathbf{b}_{\text{dec}}$ 

(2)

where $\sigma$ is a non-linear function (often ReLU). These functions are trained to reconstruct the input $\mathbf{x}$ while minimizing a sparsity penalty on $\mathbf{h}$ .

 $\mathcal{L}=||\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{\hat{x}}||_{2}^{2}+\lambda||\mathbf{h}||_{1}$ 

(3)

where $\lambda$ is a coefficient set to balance the tradeoff between sparsity and reconstruction accuracy. The resulting features are highly monosemantic and are usable in place of neurons for interpretability analysis Shu et al. (2025); Marks et al. (2025).

## 2.2 Automatically Interpreting SAE Features

Auto-interpretation Bills et al. (2023); Paulo et al. (2025) is the act of generating human-readable descriptions of SAE features given their activations on a large corpus. A typical pipeline for this is as follows: For each feature, sample a small representative set of documents from across the feature’s activation distribution. Then, provide these documents to a large language model and ask it to generate a short human-readable description of that feature (typically 10-20 tokens).

Once a description is generated, the model is then asked to validate the accuracy of the description by “simulating” the neuron—predicting on which tokens of an arbitrary input text the feature is active—given only the generated description. The resulting correlation score between the true activations and simulated activations measures how faithfully the feature’s description represents its true behavior.

## 2.3 SAEs for Hypothesis Generation

Recent work has begun to investigate SAEs not just as ways of uncovering information about the internal activations of language models but also as ways of generating hypotheses about textual classification tasks in an unsupervised manner Movva et al. (2025).

For example, say an SAE feature fires disproportionately on a particular class in a classification task. That feature may represent a semantically meaningful and predictive aspect of the class. In their work, Movva et al. (2025) found SAE features such as “mentions being surprised or shocked” that were positively predictive of news engagement and “mentions issues related to food safety” that were negatively predictive of restaurant rating.

Broadly speaking, this concept of using interpretability as a “microscope” Olah (2015) to illuminate interesting aspects of underlying data distributions is a strong undercurrent of our work. We follow this line of work by uncovering specific predictive linguistic cues of AI generated text and show that these tells create strong classifiers.

Figure 2: Our pipeline. Starting from a fine-tuned AI-text detector, we train SAEs on its residual stream at four layers, label each latent with an auto-interp explanation, mask out all features that do not meet our global threshold and train a lightweight classifier over the remaining concepts. The result is a detector that retains the strength of the original neural model while being composed of auditable and intervenable human-understandable concepts.

## 3 Related Work

## Explainable AI Detection

Early work on explainable AI detectors primarily centered around distributional analysis of linguistic features Fröhling and Zubiaga (2021); Uchendu et al. (2020); Zahid et al. (2024); Zaitsu et al. (2025). Follow-up work refined this to include discourse features Kim et al. (2024); Russell et al. (2026) dependency parses Ahmed and Hammond (2026) ngram overlaps Koike et al. (2026) and ensembles Aityan et al. (2026). However, AI detectors built on these linguistic features generally underperform black-box counterparts and are limited in their ability to generalize to adversarial or out-of-distribution inputs Schuster et al. (2020).

On the other hand, fine-tuned neural classifiers Solaiman et al. (2019), and other zero-shot likelihood-based metrics Mitchell et al. (2023); Hans et al. (2024) exhibit surprisingly strong in-distribution performance and much better generalization than their stylometric counterparts Dugan et al. (2025); Sandhan et al. (2026). Previous work used techniques like LIME Ribeiro et al. (2016) and SHAP Lundberg and Lee (2017) to interpret these neural models Shah et al. (2023); Schoenegger et al. (2026) but such explanations only give global token-level importance scores and fail to provide rationales as to why particular tokens are predictive. Our work is the first to go beyond these token-based attribution scores and create a fully interpretable AI detection system that maintains the strong performance of neural models.

## Interpretable Classifiers using SAE Features

 $L_{1}$ -regularized linear classifiers (“sparse probes”) trained on SAE features were first proposed as diagnostic tools for measuring monosemanticity Gurnee et al. (2023); Gao et al. (2025). Follow up work showed that such classifiers perform on par with (but no better than) dense linear probes Bricken et al. (2024); Kantamneni et al. (2025). Our work follows Peng et al. (2026) in claiming that interpretability, not accuracy, is the primary benefit of these classifiers.

In this vein, recent work has shown that classifiers trained on SAE features are useful as interpretable reward models Zhang et al. (2026), dense retrievers Park et al. (2025), hallucination detectors Xiong et al. (2026), and LLM-as-judge systems Wedgwood et al. (2026). However, these works all provide the full set of SAE features as input to the downstream classifiers without any explicit removal of high density or polysemantic SAE latents Sun et al. (2025); Chanin et al. (2025). The lack of such filtering undermines the faithfulness of the system-level explanations.

To combat this, Kulkarni et al. (2026) proposed to remove the $M$ least interpretable SAE features from their classifier. However, this does not guarantee that the remaining features are themselves interpretable. Our work is the first to propose a global filtering threshold based on auto-interpretability score to ensure our explanations are faithful to the underlying dynamics of our classifier.

## Using SAE Features for AI Detection

Previous work by Scher (2024) noted the potential for SAEs as a means of interpreting AI detectors. They trained a lightweight classifier on SAE features of GPT-2 Small and found that they outperformed stylometric features in AI detection. Follow-up work by Kuznetsov et al. (2025) looked at how SAE features of Gemma-2-2B co-occurred with AI generated text. However, neither of these works train their own SAE models on AI detectors, nor do they evaluate the accuracy of the provided feature descriptions. Our work is the first to train SAEs directly on AI detectors and is the first to propose using these features as an interpretable AI detector.

## 4 Methods

## 4.1 Pipeline Overview

Figure 2 shows an illustration of our full pipeline. Given a token sequence $(\mathbf{t}_{0},\ldots,\mathbf{t}_{n})$ , we extract language model activations $(\mathbf{d}_{0}^{(\ell)},\ldots,\mathbf{d}_{n}^{(\ell)})$ from the residual stream at layers $\ell\in L$ and pass them through the corresponding SAE encoder to get features $(\mathbf{h}_{0}^{(\ell)},\ldots,\mathbf{h}_{n}^{(\ell)})$ . We then max pool the resulting features along the sequence dimension and concatenate along the layer dimension to get the feature vector for our document $\mathbf{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{|L|\cdot d_{\text{SAE}}}$ .11
 1

 In our work we use $L=7,13,17,22$ following McDougall et al. (2025), but this can be modified as needed.

For our interpretability mask, we compute a simulation score $s_{i}\in[-1,1]$ for each feature $h_{i}\in\mathbf{h}$ using our auto-interpretation pipeline (§4.2). This score measures how faithfully a generated natural-language description predicts that feature’s activations on our training corpus. Given a global interpretability threshold $\tau$ , we construct a binary mask $\mathbf{m}\in\{0,1\}^{|L|\cdot d_{\text{SAE}}}$ where $m_{i}=\mathbb{I}[s_{i}\geq\tau]$ and apply this mask element-wise to obtain our masked feature vector $\mathbf{h}_{\tau}=\mathbf{h}\odot\mathbf{m}$ .

Finally, to obtain our prediction, we apply an $L_{1}$ -regularized logistic regression to the features.22
 2

 That is, given labeled data $\mathcal{D}=\{\mathbf{H}_{\tau},\mathbf{y}\}$ , we minimize
 $\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\beta},\lambda)=\frac{1}{N}\,\mathrm{BCE}\big(\mathbf{y},\,\sigma(\mathbf{H}_{\tau}\boldsymbol{\beta})\big)+\lambda\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_{1}$ where $\mathrm{BCE}$ is binary cross-entropy loss and $\sigma$ is sigmoid. The prediction for a given input is $\hat{y}=\sigma(\mathbf{h}_{\tau}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\star})$ , with $\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\star}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\beta},\lambda)$ . Since each feature $h_{i}\in\mathbf{h}_{\tau}$ has a corresponding natural-language description from our auto-interpretation pipeline, we can straightforwardly explain any given prediction by listing out the top- $k$ features with the largest net contribution to the prediction along with their descriptions.33
 3

 Full training details such as preprocessing, hyperparameters, and grid searches for both our Logistic Regression model and trained SAEs are listed in Appendix B.

## 4.2 Auto-Interpretation

## Description Generation

To generate a description for a feature $h_{i}$ , we partition the training corpus into $k$ quantile bins $\mathcal{Q}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{Q}_{k}$ based on the empirical distribution of document-level max activations of the feature, plus a bin $\mathcal{Q}_{0}$ of inactive documents. We sample a stratified group of $N$ documents across bins, crop each to a short snippet centered on the highest-activating token, and add angled-bracket highlights (e.g., <<word>>) to any token in the snippet whose activations are more than 10% of the feature’s global maximum. We then prompt gemini-3.1-flash-lite with these quantile-grouped snippets to produce a concise ( ${\leq}20$ word) description of the feature’s behavior.

## Description Validation

To validate our generated descriptions we employ a quantile-based variant of the fuzzing procedure introduced in Paulo et al. (2025). Given a generated description and a list of documents, our pipeline prompts gemini-3.1-flash-lite to predict which quantile bin (0- $k$ ) each document was sampled from. We compute the simulation score $s_{i}$ as the Spearman correlation between the predicted and true quantile assignments across all documents. In our experiments we use 10 documents for generation and 50 documents for validation. Full details including prompts, decoding strategies, and other hyperparameters are listed in Appendix D.

## 5 Experimental Setup

## 5.1 Data

## Open Domain

In this setting we train the model to detect AI generated text from an arbitrary AI model in an arbitrary domain. We train our models on the English split of the COLING shared task dataset Wang et al. (2025) a collection spanning 41 highly diverse language models paired with human texts. We use the official train and dev splits (610k and 261k documents) for training and in-distribution testing. For evaluating out-of-distribution generalization we use the official english devtest and test splits of the COLING dataset as well as the non-adversarial test split of the RAID leaderboard Dugan et al. (2024).

## Closed Domain (Paper Reviews)

For our closed setting we fine-tune models to detect AI generated academic peer reviews using the Peer Review Detection Benchmark (PRDB) Yu et al. (2026). This contains 106,413 human-written peer reviews for the NeurIPS and ICLR conferences for years 2016-2024 along with paired AI generated texts. For training we use the extended split and separate it into two sets: Human vs. GPT-4o and Human vs. Llama-3.1-70B. For evaluation we use the combined calibration and test splits, which contain held out human texts and paired generations from GPT-4o, Llama 3.1 70B, Qwen 2.5 72B, Claude Sonnet 3.5, and Gemini 1.5 Pro.

## 5.2 Baselines

##
conclusion:
In order to be able to use AI detectors in real-world high-stakes situations, they need to be auditable. It is unreasonable to expect major decisions to be made at the behest of an AI detector that cannot provide a rationale for its output. Current interpretable stylometric AI detectors underperform state-of-the-art neural AI detection methods by wide margins—making them infeasible for widespread use.

In this paper we propose a technique to take an existing black box neural AI detector and convert it into a detector that operates on human-interpretable concepts. We accomplish this by training Sparse Autoencoders on the detector’s residual stream and training a lightweight classifier over only the features that pass a given global interpretability threshold. We find that classifiers constructed in this way retain the performance and generalization properties of the underlying base model while being substantially more understandable. Extensive ablations show that our feature descriptions have high recall and high precision, faithfully representing what the features fire on and how they contribute to the final prediction.

In addition to this, we find that classifiers based on SAE decompositions of base model activations are surprisingly robust detectors of AI generated text. We find that they outperform strong well-established baselines in the AI detection literature and encourage future work to follow up with further experimentation on using internal activations of language models as input to AI detectors.

Finally, we analyze the features used by AI detectors and find that they frequently use highly specific token sequences and formatting elements which may fail to generalize to other domains and models. Our findings raise questions about which features are valid to use in an AI detection system and we encourage future work to investigate adversarial hardening techniques using this style of unsupervised concept discovery.
