Operator logs are confidential, so what the field publishes is a causal graph between alarm types rather than per-incident causes, a fixed scenario set, gated, or never released. Two recent benchmarks carry per-incident root causes at scale; neither states a download location or a licence. We give a generator rather than a dataset. It runs on real backbone topologies from the Internet Topology Zoo and records the exact root cause and the propagation path of every alarm -- a by-product of generation, not a labelling pass. Every emitted field binds to a term in NORIA-O, RFC 8632, RFC 8345 or TMF642, and an unknown term fails the run. We ship fixed configurations, splits, a scorer and nine baselines. A one-line rule -- rank the device that raised the earliest critical alarm -- takes top-1 at 0.650 against 0.575 for our own temporal method, and wins 13 of 15 runs over three backbones and five seeds. An LLM given the same view reaches 0.600, the same model allowed to query the graph 0.625, and the rule wins on real operator alarms too, at 0.773: a property of alarm streams, not of our generator. One fault class separates the table: when a site loses power its PoP reports nothing, so every method that ranks alarmed devices scores 0.000 or near it, while the two that walk the topology to a silent candidate take 1.000 and 0.833.

body_start:
Abstract

Alarm root-cause analysis is studied on data that cannot be shared. Operator logs are
confidential, so what the field publishes is a causal graph between alarm types
rather than per-incident causes, a fixed scenario set, gated, or never released. Two recent
benchmarks carry per-incident root causes at scale; neither states a download location or a
licence.

We give a generator rather than a dataset. It runs on real backbone topologies from the
Internet Topology Zoo and records the exact root cause and the propagation path of
every alarm — a by-product of generation, not a labelling pass. Every emitted
field binds to a term in NORIA-O, RFC 8632, RFC 8345 or TMF642, and an unknown term fails
the run. We ship fixed configurations, splits, a scorer and nine baselines.

A one-line rule — rank the device that raised the earliest critical alarm — takes top-1
at $0.650$ against $0.575$ for our own temporal method, and wins $13$ of $15$ runs over three
backbones and five seeds. An LLM given the same view reaches $0.600$ , the same model
allowed to query the graph $0.625$ , and the rule wins on real operator alarms
too, at $0.773$ : a property of alarm streams, not of our generator. One fault class
separates the table: when a site loses power its PoP reports nothing, so every method that
ranks alarmed devices scores $0.000$ or near it, while the two that walk the topology to a
silent candidate take $1.000$ and $0.833$ .

## 1 Introduction

A network operations centre sees a storm of alarms and must name the one resource that
caused them. Research on this problem is evaluated on data nobody else can obtain, because
an operator’s alarm log carries its customers, its topology and its failures. The
consequence is not that the work is wrong but that it is incomparable: two methods
reporting $0.7$ on two private logs have not been compared.

The resources the field has published do not close that gap, and
Section 2 goes through them one at a time. Briefly: the most-used open
alarm data gives a causal graph between alarm types, with no incident identifier and
no topology [10, 7]; the benchmarks that do carry a
cause per incident are either announced without a download [5, 6]
or gated with terms that contradict their own licence tag [8]; and the open
RCA benchmarks that are genuinely downloadable are
microservice systems, not telecom alarms [3, 2]. One paper
advertises its data at a repository that contains a single 378-byte
README [15], and is still cited as a data source five years later.

## A generator, not a dataset.

We take the other route. A generator sidesteps
confidentiality in a way no release process can, and it gives something a released log
cannot: the ground truth is not an annotation added afterwards by an expert who was not
there, it is what the generator did. That distinction matters most for the
propagation path. An annotator can reasonably name the resource that caused an
incident; reconstructing which alarm caused which other alarm, through what, is a different
task, and the largest prior benchmark states plainly that it does not have
one [6].

## The claim.

We do not claim the first per-incident root causes for telecom
alarms. Two 2025–2026 benchmarks claim that, and at a realism we cannot match — real
production networks, expert annotation, hundreds of thousands of
alarms [6, 5]. Our claim is narrower:

No downloadable, openly licensed resource gives per-incident root causes
and propagation paths for telecom alarms at scale, and no open generator exists.

Both halves were checked against the sources rather than assumed, on 2026-10-21, and the
check is published with the paper.

## Contributions.

1. 

A generator of telecom alarm storms that records the root cause and the full
propagation path of every alarm, parameterised by topology and seeded
(Section 3).

2. 

A binding of every emitted type and field to NORIA-O, RFC 8632, RFC 8345 or TMF642,
enforced at generation time (Section 4). NORIA-O itself aligns to
ITU-T X.733/X.721 and TMF638 and references neither RFC 8632 nor TMF642; the binding
to those two is ours, not inherited.

3. 

A benchmark — fixed configurations, splits, a scoring script, and baselines we did
not design (Sections 5–7).

4. 

Nine scored baselines — four one-line rules, a fitted topological Hawkes process,
personalised PageRank, a language model given the same view, the same model allowed to
query the graph, and a control that isolates what the winning rule actually uses: severity,
not time (Section 8).

5. 

A realism study against public real alarm data, including the test that decides
whether the resource is useful: the ranking of methods on generated data is the ranking on
real data (Kendall $\tau=1.0$ over four rules on $4{,}539$ real bursts), while three
realism metrics show the generated stream matches real alarms on type vocabulary and
chaining and diverges on time, arriving in burstier volleys.

## 2 Related work

from a secondary description, and the record of what was checked ships with the paper.

## The closest prior work is TeleRCA, and it is better than ours on realism.

TeleRCA [6] gives 10,922 production incidents, 485,681 alarm events and
5,621 network resources, each incident carrying an expert annotation naming the root-cause
resource. That is a real network and we do not have one. We differ on three things its own
paper establishes: it states twice that it has no ground-truth propagation graph,
and reports no graph-reconstruction metric in consequence; it publishes no topology or
inventory; and although it says four times that it is released, the paper contains no
repository, no download and no licence. TN-RCA530 [5] is closer to us on
topology — each of its 530 scenarios is a knowledge graph — and is likewise announced
without a download or a dataset licence.

## The most-used open alarm data labels types, not incidents.

The Huawei PCIC 2021
data [10] is live under MIT, though not at the URL its paper
prints [7]: 34,838 alarms, 18 alarm types, 55 devices over 243 days.
Its ground truth is an $18\times 18$ adjacency between alarm types. There is no
incident identifier, no storm grouping, no root-cause column and no topology. It is a good
realism reference and not a source of per-incident labels. The nearest open artefact to
such labels is a 49-row prior shipped with a later competition sample, whose “root cause”
is itself an alarm type.

## Availability is the field’s recurring failure, and it is the argument for a
generator.

Zhang et al. [15] states that its data and code are available at a
named repository; that repository holds one 378-byte README saying the release is going
through internal procedures. The paper is still cited as a data source. TeleRCA and
TN-RCA530 repeat the pattern. A generator is not a better dataset — it is a way of not
depending on someone else’s release process.

## Open RCA benchmarks exist, for other systems.

RCAEval [3] and
LEMMA-RCA [2] are downloadable and well constructed, and are microservice
and water-treatment systems rather than telecom alarms; LEMMA-RCA carries CC BY-ND on its
own site, which would block derived works. OpenRCA [4] has a domain named
Telecom, which invites confusion: it is cloud observability telemetry — KPIs,
traces and logs of enterprise systems — not NOC alarms, and the repository states no
licence for the data.

## No generator on the Internet Topology Zoo.

We found none that emits alarms with
labelled root causes. The closest prior work describes an optical alarm-propagation
simulator with an ITU-T G.798 rule engine producing alarm correlation trees; no code
repository was found.

## 3 The generator

Topologies are real backbones taken from the Internet Topology
Zoo [9], which is CC BY 4.0.
A backbone’s GraphML gives the PoPs and the links between them, and those are the only
real objects in the output; everything below carries synthetic: true.

## Inventory and services.

Each PoP gets two core routers, two or three
aggregation routers dual-homed to both, and six to twelve access or radio sites homed to
aggregation, then cards, then ports, then cabling. Backbone links land on core-router
ports, so the real topology constrains the synthetic one rather than sitting beside it.
Services follow the inventory: mobile data per radio site, broadband per access site, and
enterprise VPNs across PoPs with a primary and a backup path. Customers carry a market
segment and nothing else — there is no personal data to anonymise.

## Faults and propagation.

There are $7$ fault types: card, device, port and
software failure, fibre cut, site power loss, and a configuration change, which is always
preceded by a Change whose outcome is failed. What follows from a fault is
computed from the topology, not scripted: a dead card takes its ports down, the far end of
each down port loses signal, a breadth-first search from the NOC’s own PoP over surviving
links decides which devices still have a path home, and a service whose endpoint is
unreachable is out. Redundancy is what stops a failure spreading, so dual homing and two
core routers per PoP are what make most faults local and a few of them storms.

## Alarms.

Each of those states raises an alarm on the resource that would report
it, with a per-mechanism severity and a per-mechanism emission probability: the root alarm
when the root can still speak, loss of signal at the far ends, an unreachable-device alarm
after the next poll, a service alarm per lost service, neighbour-cell link failures on live
radio sites near a dead one, and congestion where traffic reroutes. The dataset uses $4$ 
X.733 event types and $21$ NORIA-O probable causes over $4$ RFC 8632 severities.

## What makes it hard is in the config, not in a script.

The root resource often
raises no alarm at all: in $50$ of $70$ faults it does, and in the rest the method has to
infer the root from what its neighbours said. A site power loss never raises one — the
PoP it kills cannot report itself, which is also why the fault model’s fifth event type,
environmentalAlarm, appears nowhere in the data. On top of that, alarms go
missing, flap through raise/clear cycles, duplicate, and carry per-device clock skew drawn
once per device, so the order alarms arrive in is not the order the faults happened in.
Background alarms arrive throughout, unrelated to any fault. Two faults can overlap inside
one PoP. Every one of those is a knob with a number in the config, which is what lets the
ablation in Section 8 say which of them the methods are actually reading.

Section 8.3 removes each of these in turn and measures what it was worth.
Alarms that never arrive are worth the most by a wide margin; mis-grouping is worth the
least, and was worth nothing at all before the arrival times were fixed.

## The distribution, not the mean.

Alarms per fault have a median of $3$ and a
90th percentile of $41.1$ , with a maximum of $103$ . Most faults are quiet and a few are
storms, so a method evaluated at the mean is evaluated at neither end.

## What is recorded.

For every injected fault the generator writes the fault, its
onset and repair, the resources it hit, the alarms it caused and the window it spans. This
is the ground truth, and it is a by-product of generation rather than a labelling pass.

## Splits.

Scenarios are split into history and eval before
generation, not after, and each scenario owns its own window, so the two never interleave
in time. A method may use everything about history — its alarms, its incidents, its
resolved tickets, its changes, and the ground truth — to fit whatever it likes. On eval
it sees the static topology and the incident’s alarms, and nothing else. The GÉANT small
configuration has $30$ history faults and $40$ eval faults in three scenario shapes:
a single fault, a storm, and two faults overlapping inside one PoP.

The split is only a split if a method cannot see across it, which is a property of the
method and not of the data. The one baseline here that fits anything — the topological
Hawkes process in Section 7 — is given a hard cutoff at the onset of
the first eval incident, and a test asserts that every alarm it was trained on falls below
that cutoff and that the cutoff excludes a non-zero number of them. A cutoff that excludes
nothing proves nothing.

## 4 Standards binding

Every emitted type and field resolves to a term in one of four published vocabularies:
NORIA-O [11], the alarm-management YANG model of RFC 8632 [14],
the network-topology model of RFC 8345 [1], and the TM Forum alarm
API TMF642 [13]. Generation fails on an unknown term rather than emitting it.
The binding is a build step rather than a convention. Each vocabulary is converted to a
graph of its own terms — an OWL/SKOS pass for NORIA-O, a YANG pass for the two RFCs, an
OpenAPI pass for TMF642 — and a catalog entry records where each build came from. The
generator then declares what it needs: for each node label, the ontology classes it claims
to be, and for each enumerated field, the vocabulary and the owning term the values must
come from. At generation time every label and every enumeration value is resolved against
those builds, $11$ labels and $4$ vocabularies in this configuration, and an unresolved
term raises rather than being emitted. The release carries binding.json: the terms
used, and the build files they came from with their sha256, so a reader can check the
vocabulary a value claims without trusting the paper.

The grounding also travels in the graph itself, as one SchemaLabel node per label
with a GROUNDED_IN edge to each ontology concept, rather than as a table in a
README. A query can therefore ask what an Alarm is in NORIA-O’s terms.

## What is ours and what is inherited.

NORIA-O’s own alarm vocabulary aligns to
ITU-T X.733/X.721 and to TMF638 Service Inventory; neither it nor its IETF
draft [12] references RFC 8632 or TMF642. Binding to those two is this
paper’s contribution rather than an alignment we inherited, and we state it so that a
reader who opens the ontology does not have to discover it.

## Licence.

NORIA-O is BSD-4-Clause, which carries an advertising clause and a
no-endorsement clause. What we ship from it is term names — $6$ class IRIs and $21$ of the
 $173$ concepts in its probable-cause scheme — and not the ontology files, so the clauses
requiring a redistribution to retain the notice do not reach the dataset; the advertising
clause does, because this paper mentions the use, and satisfying it is an acknowledgement
sentence, which the release carries. RFC 8632 and RFC 8345 are Simplified BSD; TMF642 is
Apache-2.0; Topology Zoo is CC BY 4.0.

## Acknowledgement required by NORIA-O’s licence.

This product includes software
developed by Orange. That sentence is the acknowledgement NORIA-O’s BSD-4-Clause licence
requires of material describing use of it. It is a statement about the ontology and not
about any commercial relationship, and Orange does not endorse this work.

title: HiddenLens: A Multi-Layer LLM Framework for Detecting and Resolving Hidden Assumptions in Software Requirements
abstract: Natural-language software requirements often omit assumptions about performance, operating conditions, user behaviour, and domain constraints, affecting architecture, testing, and deployment. If undiscovered until implementation, resolving them is far more costly than addressing them early. Although ambiguity and vagueness are widely studied, less attention has been given to assumptions embedded in requirements that appear clear and reasonable. We propose HiddenLens, a novel six-layer BERT-LLM pipeline and, to our knowledge, the first framework engineered to detect, classify, question, and resolve hidden assumptions rather than merely flag ambiguity. Layer 1 uses BERT attention entropy to localise unresolved spans; Layer 2 uses CoT-prompted LLM reasoning to articulate each assumption and its failure risk; Layer 3 uses fine-tuned BERT to classify assumptions into six non-functional requirement categories: performance, security, scalability, usability, reliability, and domain; Layer 4 generates ranked clarification options using FS LLM prompting; Layer 5 enables human validation through confirmation, editing, or rephrasing; and Layer 6 rewrites the requirement using the confirmed resolution, producing an explicit, testable, and traceable requirement. We also introduce the HiddenLens Corpus (HLC), comprising 312 requirements annotated with 847 hidden assumptions across six NFR categories. Inspired by PROMISE and PURE, HLC addresses the lack of annotated data for this task and is, to our knowledge, the first dataset developed specifically for it. HiddenLens outperforms keyword-based and QuARS-Adapted baselines by 71% and 61%, respectively, achieving an end-to-end F1-score of 0.79; its BERT-based NFR classifier achieves an F1-score of 0.847. These results indicate that HiddenLens can help analysts resolve hidden assumptions before they propagate through software development.

However, preparing fault-augmented scenarios for HIL testing remains largely a manual process, limiting test coverage, scalability, and efficiency. Given a baseline Scenic/CARLA scenario and a structured fault specification, FaultGene generates a fault-augmented test case that captures the effects of HIL-level fault injection. body_start:
Abstract

Reliable validation of autonomous driving cyber-physical systems requires testing not only nominal driving behavior but also failures arising from faults in sensing and embedded computation. Physical road testing provides realistic system behavior but is costly and difficult to reproduce, while simulation enables scalable evaluation but cannot fully capture hardware-dependent behavior and fault propagation. Hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) validation bridges this gap by executing the driving stack on real embedded hardware within a simulated environment. However, preparing fault-augmented scenarios for HIL testing remains largely a manual process, limiting test coverage, scalability, and efficiency.

We present FaultGene, an LLM-assisted framework for automated generation of executable fault-augmented tests for HIL fault-resilience validation. Given a baseline Scenic/CARLA scenario and a structured fault specification, FaultGene generates a fault-augmented test case that captures the effects of HIL-level fault injection. During offline refinement, semantic-consistency checks and execution-level feedback are used to correct candidates that fail to preserve the intended scenario context or produce the desired fault-induced degradation, and to construct high-quality supervision for fine-tuning. The resulting generator then produces fault-augmented tests directly at deployment time without requiring manually engineered reference executions or repeated refinement loops.

On held-out scenario–fault combinations, FaultGene improves semantic alignment and executability over one-shot LLM generation across both modular and end-to-end autonomous driving architectures. It also preserves the main sensor- and compute-fault sensitivity trends observed in HIL evaluation, capturing hardware-level fault effects beyond simulation-based verification and falsification alone. Compared with conventional manual fault-scenario engineering, FaultGene reduces estimated fault-scenario preparation time by 72×, enabling scalable HIL-based dependability validation.

## I Introduction

The rapid advancement of Automated Driving Systems (ADS) has created an urgent need for testing environments that can reliably expose safety-critical failures [1]. Road testing provides high-fidelity evaluation but is costly, time-consuming, difficult to reproduce, and limited in its ability to systematically exercise rare fault conditions. Simulation-based testing offers scalable and reproducible alternatives through controllable scenario generation using platforms such as CARLA [2]. Existing probabilistic, constraint-based, and search-based approaches [3, 4] further expand the scenario space for systematic verification. However, simulation alone cannot fully capture hardware-dependent effects, such as timing variations, scheduling jitter, and embedded computation faults, motivating hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testing, where the driving stack executes on real hardware within a simulated environment.

Despite these advantages, preparing fault-augmented scenarios for HIL testing remains a practical bottleneck. A fault-oriented test must define both the driving context and the intended sensor or compute fault while preserving scenario semantics and producing meaningful system-level effects. Manually constructing scenarios across fault types, activation times, and severities is labor-intensive and difficult to scale.

Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential solution by translating high-level specifications into executable scenario programs [5]. However, one-shot generation may produce scenarios that violate the intended context, fail to compile or execute, or fail to expose the specified fault meaningfully. These limitations motivate combining LLM-based generation with execution-guided refinement grounded in HIL behavior.

This paper presents FaultGene, an LLM-assisted framework for automated generation of fault-augmented HIL test cases. Given a baseline Scenic [3]/CARLA scenario and a structured specification of fault type, activation timing, and severity, FaultGene generates a fault-augmented test while preserving the underlying driving context. The framework integrates structured LLM generation with execution-guided refinement in the Autonomous Driving Digital Twin (ADDT) environment [6].
HIL executions provide fault-grounded reference behavior and system-level feedback that are used offline to refine generated scenarios and construct supervision for fine-tuning the generator.
After tuning, the generator produces fault-augmented tests in a single pass without reference executions or iterative refinement during deployment.

We evaluate FaultGene on held-out scenario–fault combinations across modular and end-to-end AD architectures. Experimental results show improved scenario validity and executability over one-shot LLM generation, while the generated tests reproduce the main sensor- and compute-fault sensitivity trends observed in ADDT. Compared with conventional manual fault-scenario engineering, FaultGene reduces fault-engineering effort by 72 $\times$ per fault type.

In summary, this work makes the following contributions:

• 

An LLM-assisted framework for automatically transforming baseline driving scenarios and structured fault specifications into executable fault-augmented test cases;

• 

A feedback-driven refinement and tuning mechanism that uses execution feedback as supervision to improve semantic consistency and fault-induced system behavior;

• 

An empirical evaluation showing improved scenario validity, ADDT-consistent fault trends, and higher testing efficiency compared with conventional HIL workflows.

## II Related Works

Digital-twin-based hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) validation enables controlled evaluation of autonomous driving systems under realistic sensing, compute, and communication disturbances. Digital twins model the vehicle, environment, and traffic context [7, 8], while HIL co-simulation executes perception, planning, and control on real embedded hardware, exposing timing effects, scheduling jitter, and fault propagation that simulation-only studies may miss [9, 10, 11]. Fault injection has been used to assess neural-network-based autonomous driving components: APPRAISER [12] and DNN accelerator fault-injection frameworks [13] examine model-level vulnerability, while AVFI and Kayotee [14, 15] inject faults across perception, planning, and control in simulated environments. However, these approaches generally do not jointly address fault-oriented scenario generation and realistic embedded execution.

Autonomous-driving scenario generation has explored probabilistic and constraint-based specification, systematic search, and optimization. Scenic [3] enables probabilistic and constraint-based scenario specification, while VerifAI [4] performs simulation-based verification and falsification over parameterized scenario spaces; their combination has been used to identify challenging scenarios [16], alongside optimization- and adversarial-search-based approaches [17]. Works have also explored learning scenario representations from driving videos, such as [18]. More recently, LLMs have been applied to driving-scenario description and generation. DriveGPT4 [19] and Talk2Drive [20] support language-based driving representation and interaction, vision-language approaches derive structured scenarios from driving videos [21], and DriveArena [22] and LMDrive [23] explore LLM-based scenario expansion and reasoning over traffic interactions and environmental conditions. Nevertheless, these methods typically rely on predefined scenario spaces or text-/simulation-level generation and do not directly construct fault-augmented scenarios from structured hardware-fault specifications or validate their fault-induced effects on real embedded hardware.
FaultGene addresses this gap by treating fault-augmented test generation as a program-level generation and refinement problem grounded in HIL execution.

## III HIL-Based Autonomous Driving Validation

Fig. 1: Overview of the ADDT hardware-in-the-loop setup.

In this section, we introduce the Autonomous Driving Digital Twin (ADDT) [6], the HIL validation environment used throughout this work.

## III-A Hardware-in-the-Loop Setup

As shown in Fig. 1, ADDT consists of a simulation system and an AD computing system connected through Ethernet. The simulator streams sensor data to the AD system and receives control commands, enabling closed-loop execution in the virtual environment.

## III-A1 Digital-Twin Simulation System

Software.
The simulation system is built on CARLA [2], an open-source AD simulator based on Unreal Engine [24]. OpenSCENARIO [25] and Scenic [3] specify and parameterize the traffic scenarios.

Hardware.
The simulator runs on a workstation with an Intel i7-9800X CPU and an NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti GPU.

## III-A2 AD Computing System

The AD stack (AD architectures are described in Section V) runs on an NVIDIA Jetson Xavier or Orin, processing six 480p or three 720p camera streams at 10 Hz and producing control commands at 100 Hz.

## III-A3 Testing Scenarios

(a) (1) Vehicle following.

(b) (2) Large-curvature turning.

(c) (3) Overtaking.

Fig. 2: Driving scenarios used for evaluation.

We evaluate three representative driving scenarios: vehicle following, large-curvature turning, and overtaking. Fig. 2 shows their configurations and parameters, including vehicle speeds and inter-vehicle distances.

## III-B Fault Injection Mechanism

We evaluate resilience by injecting faults into the sensing and computing paths of the HIL pipeline.

Sensor fault injection.
ADDT models temporal and spatial sensing faults:

1. 

Temporal faults:
Controlled timestamp delays are introduced into sensor streams. Delays exceeding the perception model’s out-of-order tolerance are treated as frame drops.

2. 

Spatial faults:
Position and orientation perturbations are applied to the ground-truth extrinsic parameters to emulate sensor misalignment with controllable severity.

Computing hardware fault injection.
ADDT supports closed-loop CPU and GPU fault injection for studying memory and data-path errors [26, 27]. CPU faults are injected with LLFI [28], while GPU faults are injected with NVBitFI [29]. Both tools introduce register-level bit flips at specified locations and values, allowing the resulting errors to propagate through subsequent AD computations. This approach follows prior fault-injection studies [27, 26].

## IV FaultGene: Automated Fault-Augmented Test Generation

Fig. 3: 
Overview of FaultGene.
(a) Pipeline overview showing offline refinement and deployment-time generation steps.
(b) Detailed offline refinement process, where FaultGene generates fault-augmented Scenic scenarios, compares their executions with manually engineered HIL references using ScenarioFeat, and uses the resulting feedback for refinement and fine-tuning.

FaultGene is an LLM-based framework for generating executable fault-augmented tests for autonomous-driving fault-resilience validation. An overview of the framework is shown in Fig. 3. Given a baseline Scenic/CARLA scenario and a structured fault specification, it produces constrained scenario variants that can be executed in CARLA or through a CARLA-based HIL setup, such as the ADDT HIL environment described in Section III.

FaultGene has two phases. During offline framework construction, a prompt-based generator produces candidate fault-augmented Scenic programs, while ScenarioFeat extracts semantic attributes from execution videos. Generated executions are compared with manually engineered ADDT HIL references, and detected mismatches guide prompt refinement and supervision construction. After fine-tuning, the deployed generator produces tests in one pass without accessing manually engineered references, execution feedback, or refinement loops.

## IV-A ScenarioFeat: Video-Based Scenario Feature Extraction

ScenarioFeat is a prompt-engineered module that extracts semantic features from manually engineered reference and FaultGene-generated executions. It uses Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct as its base vision-language model.

For an execution video $V$ , ScenarioFeat extracts a predefined semantic feature vector describing the driving context and safety-relevant behavior, including road environment, surrounding-object interactions, obstacle relationships, and vehicle maneuvers such as cut-in behavior:

 $C(V)=[c_{1}(V),c_{2}(V),\ldots,c_{n}(V)],$ 

(1)

where $c_{i}(V)\in[0,1]$ denotes the predicted confidence score for feature category $i$ .

ScenarioFeat is prompt-engineered using representative execution videos and expected feature annotations. It does not generate scenarios; instead, it provides a structured semantic representation for comparing generated executions with manually engineered references.

## IV-B FaultGene: Prompt-Based Scenic Generation

FaultGene is a text-only LLM, instantiated with Qwen3-14B-Instruct, that transforms a baseline Scenic scenario and structured fault specification into a fault-augmented Scenic program. Formally,

 $S_{F}=\pi_{\theta}(S_{0},F),$ 

(2)

where $S_{0}$ is the baseline scenario, $F$ is the fault specification, and $\pi_{\theta}$ is the generator.

The input includes $S_{0}$ , $F$ , and constraints requiring valid Scenic syntax and preservation of the original driving context. The fault specification defines the fault type, activation condition, and severity. FaultGene modifies the scenario while preserving its road layout, actor identities, and intended maneuver semantics. Because the output is structured Scenic code rather than free-form text, it can be syntax-checked and executed directly in CARLA or CARLA-based HIL setups such as ADDT.

## IV-C Reference-Guided Similarity and Execution Checks

Each generated scenario $S_{F}$ is executed through the HIL loop with the under-test AD system and compared with the corresponding manually fault-engineered ADDT HIL execution.
The reference provides offline HIL grounding for supervision construction and is not required at deployment.

Let $V_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and $V_{F}$ denote the reference and generated execution videos. ScenarioFeat extracts their semantic feature vectors:

 $C(V_{\mathrm{ref}})=[\ldots,c_{n}(V_{\mathrm{ref}})],\qquad C(V_{F})=[\ldots,c_{n}(V_{F})].$ 

(3)

The feature mismatch vector is defined as

 $\displaystyle\mathbf{d}_{C}(V_{\mathrm{ref}},V_{F})$ 
 $\displaystyle=[c_{1}(V_{\mathrm{ref}})-c_{1}(V_{F}),\ldots,$ 

(4)

 $\displaystyle c_{n}(V_{\mathrm{ref}})-c_{n}(V_{F})].$ 

A generated execution is semantically inconsistent if

 $|\mathbf{d}_{C}(V_{\mathrm{ref}},V_{F})_{i}|>\tau_{i}$ 

(5)

for any feature $i$ . The threshold $\tau_{i}$ controls the tradeoff between semantic preservation and scenario diversity and is used only during offline refinement.

We separately assess fault relevance using near-collision events, inter-vehicle clearance, maneuver interruption, collision outcome, and task completion.
Let $M(S_{F})$ denote the resulting metric vector. A scenario is fault-relevant if

 $M(S_{F})\in\Omega,$ 

(6)

where $\Omega$ denotes safety-relevant degradation without trivial invalidity, such as deadlock, early termination, or failure to trigger the fault.

Together, these checks determine whether the scenario preserves the intended context, implements the requested fault, and allows it to manifest during execution.

## IV-D Offline Iterative Refinement and Supervised Fine-Tuning

Candidates that fail either semantic or fault-relevance checks, or fail to compile or execute successfully, are refined offline.
The mismatch is converted into structured feedback covering Scenic syntax and compilation, physical or semantic validity, fault-specification consistency, and execution-level fault manifestation. Depending on the failure, the feedback may request corrected actor placement, adjusted activation timing, stronger fault severity, or removal of unintended deadlocks and early termination.

Let $\Delta(S_{F})$ denote the aggregated semantic and execution mismatch relative to the manually engineered reference. Starting from $S_{F}^{(0)}$ , the generator produces the next candidate as

 $S_{F}^{(k+1)}=\mathrm{Refine}\!\left(S_{0},F,S_{F}^{(k)},\Delta(S_{F}^{(k)})\right),$ 

(7)

until

 $|\mathbf{d}_{C}(V_{\mathrm{ref}},V_{F}^{(k)})_{i}|\leq\tau_{i},\quad\forall i,$ 

(8)

and

 $M(S_{F}^{(k)})\in\Omega.$ 

(9)

Here, $\mathrm{Refine}(\cdot)$ denotes rule-guided LLM regeneration using the original baseline scenario, fault specification, current candidate, and structured feedback prompts. It is not a reinforcement-learning policy or an external optimizer that directly edits the Scenic program.

The resulting scenario $S_{F}^{\star}$ is retained as the corrected target for $(S_{0},F)$ . Repeating this process over $N$ framework-construction examples yields

 $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ref}}=\left\{\left(S_{0}^{(j)},F^{(j)},S_{F}^{\star(j)}\right)\right\}_{j=1}^{N}.$ 

(10)

We then fine-tune the original generator $\pi_{\theta}$ on $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ref}}$ using supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Each training example uses the baseline scenario and fault specification $(S_{0},F)$ as input and the corresponding refined Scenic program $S_{F}^{\star}$ as the target. The trainable LoRA parameters are optimized with teacher-forced causal language modeling:

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=-\sum_{t=1}^{|S_{F}^{\star}|}\log P_{\theta}\!\left(s_{t}^{\star}\mid S_{0},F,s_{<t}^{\star}\right),$ 

(11)

where $s_{t}^{\star}$ is the $t$ -th token of $S_{F}^{\star}$ and $s_{<t}^{\star}$ denotes its preceding tokens. The baseline scenario and fault specification provide the conditioning context, while the loss is computed over the target Scenic program.

Although the loss is evaluated token by token, the model is conditioned on the complete $(S_{0},F)$ pair and the preceding program context. Across diverse training exampl
conclusion:
This paper presented FaultGene, an LLM-based framework for generating fault-augmented tests for HIL resilience validation. Given a baseline Scenic/CARLA scenario and structured fault specification, FaultGene generates executable tests for closed-loop evaluation across modular and end-to-end AD architectures. Manual ADDT references and execution feedback are used only for offline supervision construction and fine-tuning, while deployment requires neither reference executions nor iterative refinement. On held-out scenario–fault combinations, FaultGene improves semantic alignment, compilation, and execution success over one-shot generation while preserving the main HIL sensor- and compute-fault sensitivity trends.

FaultGene reduces manual Scenic editing and fault-augmented tests construction to providing a baseline scenario and fault specification. Although evaluated on ADS, the framework can be adapted to other CPS by replacing the scenario representation, execution metrics, and fault-injection interfaces with domain-specific counterparts. Similarly, although the current evaluation uses LLFI and NVBitFI, FaultGene is not tied to these tools and can incorporate other fault-injection backends. A current limitation is that timing effects are evaluated after generation rather than incorporated into the generation objective. Future work will integrate HIL timing measurements and broader fault-injection backends into the feedback process to expose both safety- and timing-critical failures.

title: CulturalRiddles: A Multicultural Benchmark of Riddles
abstract: As LLMs expand their language coverage, evaluating how well they understand and represent diverse cultures becomes increasingly important. However, many benchmarks remain English-centric, with limited cultural coverage and a focus on factual knowledge over its application in real-world cultural contexts. We propose CulturalRiddles, a benchmark of original, culturally grounded riddles created entirely by humans through a participatory community effort, spanning 62 cultures (45 countries, 51 languages). These riddles are deeply rooted in their respective cultures and require abductive and compositional reasoning, alongside detailed factual and social knowledge, language skills, and an understanding of culturally specific associations. We benchmark 28 LLM configurations using both automatic and large-scale human evaluation. Even frontier models achieve at most 22% accuracy in some communities. We publicly release all artifacts alongside an open contribution process to expand the benchmark's linguistic and cultural coverage.

title: Graph Topology Meets Energy-Driven Pathfinding: Preserving Contextual Consistency in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) frequently integrates knowledge graphs (KGs) for complex multi-hop question answering. However, their performance is increasingly bottlenecked by the knowledge structuring and reasoning processes. (i) Severe semantic loss: Distilling continuous texts into discrete symbols strips away contextual nuances and narrative coherence. (ii) Pronounced modality mismatch: Fragmented graph structures clash with the continuous texts LLMs are pre-trained on, while rewriting them into natural language introduces generative noise and omits information. To address these limitations, we propose ThreadRAG, a semantic-topology-based RAG framework for context-preserving knowledge structuring and modality-native evidence reasoning. ThreadRAG introduces a Semantic Topology Mapper (STM), which organizes retrieved documents into context-intact Semantic Nodes and constructs a Semantic Topology Graph (STG) through narrative, semantic, and lexical edges. It further incorporates Energy-Driven Pathfinding (EDP), which identifies query-relevant subgraphs via energy diffusion and deterministically linearizes them into coherent textual evidence paths. Experiments on three multi-hop QA benchmarks demonstrate that ThreadRAG consistently outperforms strong baselines. Notably, it achieves a 14.4% EM improvement over text-centric methods on HotpotQA and surpasses the best baseline by 5.8% EM on 2WikiMultihop, while reducing token cost to 23.3% of the strongest baseline.

body_start:
Abstract

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) frequently integrates knowledge graphs (KGs) for complex multi-hop question answering. However, their performance is increasingly bottlenecked by the knowledge structuring and reasoning processes. (i) Severe semantic loss: Distilling continuous texts into discrete symbols strips away contextual nuances and narrative coherence. (ii) Pronounced modality mismatch: Fragmented graph structures clash with the continuous texts LLMs are pre-trained on, while rewriting them into natural language introduces generative noise and omits information. To address these limitations, we propose ThreadRAG, a semantic-topology-based RAG framework for context-preserving knowledge structuring and modality-native evidence reasoning. ThreadRAG introduces a Semantic Topology Mapper (STM), which organizes retrieved documents into context-intact Semantic Nodes and constructs a Semantic Topology Graph (STG) through narrative, semantic, and lexical edges. It further incorporates Energy-Driven Pathfinding (EDP), which identifies query-relevant subgraphs via energy diffusion and deterministically linearizes them into coherent textual evidence paths. Experiments on three multi-hop QA benchmarks demonstrate that ThreadRAG consistently outperforms strong baselines. Notably, it achieves a 14.4% EM improvement over text-centric methods on HotpotQA and surpasses the best baseline by 5.8% EM on 2WikiMultihop, while reducing token cost to 23.3% of the strongest baseline.

11footnotetext: Corresponding author.

## 1 Introduction

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has become a powerful paradigm for enhancing large language models (LLMs) on knowledge-intensive tasks by grounding generation in external evidence Gao et al. (2023). However, complex multi-hop question answering (QA) remains challenging for existing RAG systems Lewis et al. (2020); Izacard et al. (2022); Trivedi et al. (2023). Unlike single-hop QA, multi-hop QA requires models to identify scattered evidence across multiple documents, connect them through latent relations, and perform multi-step reasoning Shao et al. (2023).

Graph-enhanced RAG methods address this challenge by introducing structural priors over retrieved knowledge. Despite their promise, existing graph-RAG paradigms often suffer from a mismatch between how knowledge is structured and how LLMs perform reasoning. As illustrated in Figure 1, this mismatch manifests in two key limitations. First, existing graph construction pipelines can incur substantial semantic loss. Triplet-based knowledge graphs compress continuous text into rigid symbolic tuples, often discarding contextual nuances, while chunk-based graphs split documents into isolated segments, leading to semantic truncation and noisy boundaries. Such fragmentation weakens the continuous contextual pathways required for multi-hop reasoning. Second, existing graph representations introduce a modality mismatch at inference time. LLMs are primarily optimized to consume coherent natural language sequences, whereas graph-RAG methods typically provide fragmented graph paths or rely on generative verbalization to convert subgraphs into text. These conversions can introduce redundancy, hallucinated transitions, or omission of critical evidence, thereby limiting the effectiveness of structural priors.

Figure 1: Comparison of graph-RAG paradigms. Left: Our proposed ThreadRAG (a) structures raw texts into a Semantic Topology Graph (STG) and extracts Semantic Topology Paths (ST-Paths), preserving semantic context and aligning modality for LLM deduction. Right: Existing paradigms, Triplet KG (b) and Chunk KG (c), fragment texts into discrete components, introducing severe semantic loss and modality mismatch.

To address these limitations, we propose ThreadRAG, a semantic-topology-based RAG framework that preserves textual context during knowledge structuring and converts graph evidence into LLM-native reasoning sequences. ThreadRAG consists of two key components: a Semantic Topology Mapper (STM) for high-fidelity knowledge structuring, and an Energy-Driven Pathfinding module (EDP) for query-aware evidence selection and topological linearization.

A Semantic Topology Mapper for high-fidelity knowledge structuring.
To mitigate semantic loss introduced by conventional graph construction, STM structures retrieved documents into an LLM-oriented Semantic Topology Graph (STG). Instead of extracting symbolic triplets or relying on isolated chunks, STM organizes retrieved documents into self-contained Semantic Nodes that preserve local textual context. It then connects these nodes through complementary topological relations, including narrative, semantic, and lexical edges. Narrative edges preserve the original textual order, while semantic and lexical edges capture cross-node associations beyond surface adjacency. This design allows STG to retain the semantic continuity of raw text while exposing the relational structure needed for evidence navigation. These relations transform fragmented retrieved evidence into a navigable topology without discarding the natural context required for multi-hop reasoning.

An Energy-Driven Pathfinding module for modality-native knowledge representation.
To bridge the modality mismatch between discrete graph structures and sequence-based LLM reasoning, EDP converts query-relevant topology into continuous textual evidence paths. Given a query, EDP first identifies relevant Semantic Nodes as reasoning anchors, and then performs energy-driven propagation and dynamic pruning over the STG to obtain a compact, query-specific evidence subgraph. Instead of directly prompting the LLM with discrete graph paths or using free-form generation to verbalize the subgraph, EDP deterministically linearizes the selected nodes according to their topological and narrative structure. This process preserves the structural priors of the graph while presenting evidence in a form naturally compatible with LLM pretraining. The resulting Semantic Topology Paths provide continuous, context-preserving, and sequence-native evidence, enabling more coherent and reliable multi-hop reasoning.

We conduct comprehensive evaluations across three multi-hop QA benchmarks. ThreadRAG consistently surpasses the best mainstream graph-enhanced paradigms across all three datasets (e.g., achieving a 3.4% EM improvement over KnowTrace on HotpotQA). In graph representation evaluations, replacing traditional global graphs with our STG yields a 12.6% EM improvement. Furthermore, our sequence-native STG-Paths strictly dominate all prevailing knowledge representation modalities, peaking at 0.588 EM on 2WikiMultihop. These results indicate that high-fidelity knowledge structuring and topological linearization significantly boost LLM deduction accuracy. Our contributions are as follows:

• 

We propose a Semantic Topology Mapper that reduces semantic loss by organizing retrieved text into a context-preserving Semantic Topology Graph.

• 

We introduce an Energy-Driven Pathfinding module that selects query-relevant evidence and linearizes discrete graph structures into sequence-native prompts for LLM reasoning.

• 

We present ThreadRAG, a unified graph-enhanced RAG framework that consistently improves multi-hop QA performance over strong baselines across three benchmarks.

Figure 2: Overview of ThreadRAG. Given a query and top- $k$ retrieved contexts, the STM structures raw text into STG. The EDP then isolates a query-relevant subgraph via energy diffusion and linearizes it into modality-native prompts. Finally, an adaptive agent uses these prompts to iteratively refine retrieval or synthesize answers.

## 2 Related Work

Semantic Loss in Graph RAG. Integrating KGs into RAG provides explicit structural priors for complex reasoning. Mainstream paradigms like GraphRAG Edge et al. (2024) extract rigid entity-relation triplets, which inadvertently strip away contextual nuances and cause severe semantic loss. To preserve semantics, early NLP QA approaches Fang et al. (2020); Qiu et al. (2019); Ding et al. (2019) retain original text spans. However, their heterogeneous node designs target GNN aggregation rather than LLM prompt reconstruction, irreversibly fragmenting the logical sequence. To better align with LLMs, recent methods such as HippoRAG Gutiérrez et al. (2024) utilize broader text-chunk nodes. While mitigating symbolic extraction loss, their unconstrained chunk assembly introduces semantic truncation and structural noise. Consequently, these paradigms suffer from semantic loss, depriving LLMs of the continuous contextual pathways essential for multi-hop reasoning. We address this bottleneck by proposing a topological framework that seamlessly embeds structural priors without compromising narrative integrity.

Modality Alignment in Graph RAG. A critical bottleneck in graph-augmented reasoning is the inherent modality gap between discrete graphs and continuous natural language. Several structural reasoning methods Luo et al. (2024); Sun et al. (2024); Tan et al. (2025) compel LLMs to process fragmented symbolic data over discrete entity-relation paths. This modality mismatch permanently strips away crucial contextual nuances like temporal constraints. To bridge this, generative rewriting approaches Wu et al. (2024); Sarthi et al. (2024) employ LLMs to rewrite subgraphs into natural language, introducing substantial token overhead and hallucination risks. Conversely, chunk-as-node approaches Pham et al. (2026); Yue et al. (2026) preserve text spans but merely concatenate nodes as isolated chunks, failing to reconstruct cross-document narrative coherence. ThreadRAG addresses these limitations via a Topological Pathfinding mechanism. Using topological linearization, it restructures fragments into a coherent sequence. This aligns graph topologies with the LLM’s native modality, enabling multi-hop comprehension without generative rewriting overhead.

## 3 ThreadRAG

In this section, we present the overall architecture of ThreadRAG (Figure 2). The framework primarily consists of an STM module that structures retrieved contexts into an STG (Sec. 3.1), a EDP module that extracts and linearizes query-relevant subgraphs into continuous text sequences (Sec. 3.2), and an adaptive reasoning agent that iteratively refines the evidence base to synthesize the final answer (Sec. 3.3).

## 3.1 Semantic Topology Mapper

Existing graph-RAG methods fragment continuous texts into discrete components, destroying narrative continuity and inducing severe semantic loss. Motivated by this, our Semantic Topology Mapper (STM) extracts context-intact semantic nodes and interconnects them via narrative, semantic, and lexical edges into an STG. This fundamentally anchors structural reasoning priors directly into native text sequences, thereby transforming fragmented documents into a high-fidelity network.

Semantic Node extraction
Given a query $q$ , an LLM extracts key entities $\mathcal{E}_{k}$ to construct a retrieval query set $\mathcal{Q}_{\text{ret}}=\{q\}\cup\mathcal{E}_{k}$ . These queries are independently issued to a hybrid retrieval index over a local Wikipedia corpus, combining BM25 lexical matching with dense semantic retrieval using equal weights. The retrieved passages are pooled, deduplicated, and ranked according to the fused retrieval score to yield the top- $k$ context set:

 $\mathcal{D}=\operatorname{top\text{-}k}\bigg(\bigcup_{q_{j}\in\mathcal{Q}_{\text{ret}}}\operatorname{HybridRetrieve}(q_{j})\bigg)$ 

(1)

For each document $d_{i}\in\mathcal{D}$ , the raw text is tokenized into a sequence $X=\{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}\}$ . This sequence is processed through a lightweight encoder to obtain contextualized hidden representations $\mathbf{h}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ for each token $x_{j}$ . To identify semantic breakpoints, each representation $\mathbf{h}_{j}$ is mapped to a boundary probability $p_{j}\in[0,1]$ via a MLP(see Appendix D for detailed configurations):

 $p_{j}=\sigma(\mathbf{W}_{2}(\operatorname{ReLU}(\mathbf{W}_{1}\mathbf{h}_{j}+\mathbf{b}_{1}))+b_{2})$ 

(2)

where $\sigma$ denotes the sigmoid activation function, and $\mathbf{W}_{1},\mathbf{W}_{2},\mathbf{b}_{1},b_{2}$ are learnable parameters. Tokens satisfying $p_{j}>\theta$ , given a predefined threshold $\theta$ , act as cut-off points. The continuous document is deterministically partitioned at these boundaries to yield a set of Semantic Nodes $\mathcal{V}=\{v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{m}\}$ . Each node $v_{k}\in\mathcal{V}$ is formally represented as a tuple:

 $v_{k}=(t_{k},d_{k},s_{k},\tau_{k})$ 

(3)

where $t_{k}$ is the raw natural language text span, $d_{k}$ is the document identifier, and $[s_{k},\tau_{k})$ denotes the exact character-level position interval of $t_{k}$ within $d_{k}$ . Compared to existing LLM-based extraction paradigms, this feed-forward mechanism achieves context-intact segmentation with millisecond-level latency and strictly avoids generative noise.

Semantic Topology Graph construction
Given the node set $\mathcal{V}$ , the STG is completed by constructing three complementary types of edges that capture distinct relational signals between SNs. Each edge type encodes a different dimension of inter-node relatedness, and their weights are fused under a unified formulation.

Narrative edges $\mathcal{E}_{\text{nar}}$ connect positionally adjacent nodes within the same document to preserve the original reading order. Nodes sharing $d_{i}$ are sorted by start position $s_{j}$ , with a directed edge $(v_{j},v_{j+1})\in\mathcal{E}_{\text{nar}}$ added between consecutive pairs.

Semantic edges $\mathcal{E}_{\text{sem}}$ capture cross-document topical relatedness. Each node $v_{i}$ is represented by a dense embedding $\mathbf{h}_{i}$ , connecting top- $k$ cross-document pairs $(d_{i}\neq d_{j})$ with weight:

 $\text{Sim}_{\text{sem}}(v_{i},v_{j})=\frac{\mathbf{h}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{h}_{j}}{\|\mathbf{h}_{i}\|\,\|\mathbf{h}_{j}\|}$ 

(4)

Lexical edges $\mathcal{E}_{\text{lex}}$ capture explicit entity co-reference. For named entities $\mathcal{N}_{i}$ extracted from $v_{i}$ , cross-document pairs sharing entities are connected via Jaccard similarity:

 $\text{Sim}_{\text{lex}}(v_{i},v_{j})=\frac{|\mathcal{N}_{i}\cap\mathcal{N}_{j}|}{|\mathcal{N}_{i}\cup\mathcal{N}_{j}|}$ 

(5)

The final edge weight $W(v_{i},v_{j})$ balances local narrative continuity against global cross-document association:

 $\begin{split}&W(v_{i},v_{j})=(1-\gamma)\bigl(\alpha\cdot\text{Sim}_{\text{sem}}(v_{i},v_{j})\\
&\quad+\beta\cdot\text{Sim}_{\text{lex}}(v_{i},v_{j})\bigr)+\gamma\cdot\mathbf{1}_{\text{nar}}(v_{i},v_{j})\end{split}$ 

(6)

where $\mathbf{1}_{\text{nar}}(v_{i},v_{j})=1$ iff $(v_{i},v_{j})\in\mathcal{E}_{\text{nar}}$ , $\gamma\in(0,1)$ scales the narrative prior, and $\alpha+\beta=1$ . The complete edge set $\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{E}_{\text{nar}}\cup\mathcal{E}_{\text{sem}}\cup\mathcal{E}_{\text{lex}}$ alongside $\mathcal{V}$ defines the STG $\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E})$ .

## 3.2 Energy-Driven Pathfinding

Current methods relying on fragmented graph components or generative rewriting struggle with a modality mismatch and suffer from generative noise or critical information omission. Our Energy-Driven Pathfinding (EDP) module addresses this by executing a context-preserving pathfinding mechanism over the STG. By isolating a query-specific subgraph and deterministically reconstructing it into continuous textual sequences, EDP overcomes structural fragmentation via anchor-driven energy diffusion and topological linearization.

Anchor Identification. Given the STG $\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E})$ and a query $q$ , the pathfinding stage begins by identifying a set of anchor nodes as entry points. Each node $v_{i}$ is scored by combining its semantic relevance to $q$ with an entity-level matching signal:

 $s_{i}=\text{Sim}_{\text{sem}}(\mathbf{h}_{i},\mathbf{h}_{q})+\lambda\cdot\max_{e_{j}\in\mathcal{E}_{k}}\text{Sim}_{\text{sem}}(\mathbf{h}_{i},\mathbf{h}_{e_{j}})$ 

(7)

First, ThreadRAG relies on capturing structural priors through narrative, semantic, and lexical edges, so its performance improvement may not be significant in tasks with extremely sparse document links or where cross-document evidence chains are virtually non-existent, such as single-document standard QA tasks. Additionally, due to the dynamic nature of text segmentation and the complexity of multi-hop paths, even after energy diffusion and graph pruning, there may still be a few long-range contextual dependencies that the pathfinding mechanism fails to perfectly linearize in the exact chronological or logical order. This could result in minor narrative fragmentation during prompt reconstruction, affecting the reasoning accuracy of downstream LLMs. In future work, we aim to address these two issues. conclusion: In this paper, we propose ThreadRAG to tackle complex multi-hop reasoning challenges. ThreadRAG integrates a Semantic Topology Graph (STG) for knowledge structuring and a Modality-Aligned Reasoning Mechanism via Energy-Driven pathfinding. As a core contribution, ThreadRAG linearizes discrete graph structures into continuous natural language sequences, effectively bridging the modality gap and preserving crucial narrative context. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that ThreadRAG achieves superior performance across multiple benchmarks, surpassing existing state-of-the-art baselines with low computational overhead.

title: Your Benchmark Is an Empirical Measure Over Difficulty
abstract: A benchmark is not merely a collection of test questions; it naturally induces an empirical measure over difficulty. In this work, we develop this measure-based view of benchmark evaluation. This perspective allows us to identify and formalize two central failure modes: measure mismatch, where the benchmark difficulty distribution differs from the intended difficulty distribution, and coverage gaps, where uncovered regions along the difficulty axis prevent benchmarks from detecting meaningful localized training progress. We propose two diagnostic metrics that capture these two failure modes and provide rigorous theoretical guarantees. Empirically, we analyze 25 popular benchmarks spanning 7 domains using carefully estimated item difficulties. Our results show that many benchmarks implicitly overweight certain difficulty regions, so their leaderboard conclusions should be interpreted with caution; others leave substantial portions of the difficulty axis uncovered, limiting their ability to monitor the model improvement process. Finally, we turn diagnosis into action by introducing BenchFill, a simple difficulty-targeted item rewriting algorithm that effectively reduces local coverage gaps.

body_start:
Abstract

A benchmark is not merely a collection of test questions; it naturally induces an empirical measure over difficulty. In this work, we develop this measure-based view of benchmark evaluation. This perspective allows us to identify and formalize two central failure modes: measure mismatch, where the benchmark difficulty distribution differs from the intended difficulty distribution, and coverage gaps, where uncovered regions along the difficulty axis prevent benchmarks from detecting meaningful localized training progress. We propose two diagnostic metrics that capture these two failure modes and provide rigorous theoretical guarantees. Empirically, we analyze 25 popular benchmarks spanning 7 domains using carefully estimated item difficulties. Our results show that many benchmarks implicitly overweight certain difficulty regions, so their leaderboard conclusions should be interpreted with caution; others leave substantial portions of the difficulty axis uncovered, limiting their ability to monitor the model improvement process. Finally, we turn diagnosis into action by introducing BenchFill, a simple difficulty-targeted item rewriting algorithm that effectively reduces local coverage gaps.

 Project Website: benchmark-difficulty-measure.github.io

 GitHub Code: https://github.com/ASTRAL-Group/benchmark-difficulty-measure

 BenchFill Datasets: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Yifan99/BenchFill

11footnotetext: 

Equal contribution.

Correspondence to Yifan Sun
<yifan50@illinois.edu> and Huan Zhang
<huan@huan-zhang.com>.

## 1 Introduction

Benchmark evaluation looks simple: we run models on a set of questions and average the results. The resulting score is then used in two main ways: to compare models on leaderboards (Alzahrani et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2018; Liang et al., 2022; Myrzakhan et al., 2024), and to monitor progress during training (Liu et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025; He et al., 2025; Bercovich et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025). But this simplicity hides a basic issue: the conclusion depends not only on how well models perform, but also on how benchmark questions are distributed Siska et al. (2024); Zhang et al. (2026).

Consider first the leaderboard setting in Fig. 1(a), where we want to compare two models. Suppose they perform similarly on easy questions but differ substantially on hard ones. If the benchmark places most of its weight on easy questions, while the difficulty distribution of interest places more weight on harder questions, the two evaluations can lead to different conclusions for the same pair of models: the benchmark may suggest that the two models are nearly tied, even though under the desired difficulty distribution they are clearly separated. Now consider the training setting in Fig. 1(b), where we want to track whether a model is improving. Suppose the model improves substantially over a local difficulty range. If the benchmark has few or no questions in that region, the benchmark score may barely change, even though the model has made real progress.

These two failure cases suggest that benchmark conclusions depend critically on how questions are distributed. To study this structure systematically, we organize benchmark questions along a difficulty axis, which provides a natural progression from easier to harder problems. The key conceptual step is to use difficulty as a way to define the distributional structure of the benchmark itself. This view recasts a benchmark from a collection of test questions into an empirical measure over difficulty, with each question contributing equal evaluation mass at its difficulty level.

This measure-theoretic formalization is useful because it turns the two failure cases above into precise and analyzable problems about the benchmark-induced difficulty measure. The first is a measure mismatch problem: the benchmark may distribute its mass differently from the target difficulty distribution that represents the intended evaluation objective, so benchmark conclusions can differ from the conclusions under the target difficulty distribution. The second is a coverage gap problem. Because the benchmark is an empirical measure supported only on finitely many difficulty points, there may be intervals of difficulty with little or no benchmark mass. A substantial performance gain concentrated in such an interval may therefore produce little or no change in the benchmark score. To our knowledge, this is the first work to identify and formalize measure mismatch and coverage gaps as two fundamental failure modes of benchmark evaluation.

These two problems naturally lead to two simple diagnostic metrics: the Wasserstein distance Villani and others (2009) between the benchmark measure and a target difficulty distribution, and the maximum gap between adjacent benchmark difficulty points. We provide theoretical results showing that these quantities directly characterize distributional mismatch and the detectability of localized improvements. Empirically, we analyze 25 popular benchmarks spanning 7 domains. We estimate question difficulty using Item Response Theory and compute the proposed metrics. Our results show that both issues are prevalent across benchmarks.

Our key contributions are summarized as follows:

• 

We introduce a new measure-based perspective on benchmark evaluation, representing a benchmark as an empirical measure over difficulty. This perspective formalizes measure mismatch and coverage gaps, motivates two diagnostic metrics, and yields rigorous theoretical guarantees.

• 

We conduct an empirical study across 25 benchmarks spanning 7 domains, showing that both difficulty-distribution mismatch and large coverage gaps are widespread in current benchmarks.

• 

We propose BenchFill, a difficulty-targeted gap-filling algorithm. With only three inserted items per benchmark, BenchFill reduces the sum of the top three difficulty gaps by $21.09\%$ – $38.88\%$ .

Figure 1: Two benchmark failure cases. In both panels, the curves show true model conditional performance as a function of question difficulty.
(a) Measure Mismatch.
The benchmark emphasizes easy questions, where the models perform similarly, while the difficulty distribution we care about places more weight on harder questions, where they differ substantially.
Because the benchmark and the target distribution weight the difficulty axis differently, they lead to different conclusions for the same two models.
(b) Coverage Gaps. A model actually improves substantially over a localized difficulty region. Because the benchmark has no questions in that region, this improvement is not reflected in the observed benchmark score, causing meaningful training progress to be missed.

## 2 Formalization and Theory

## Difficulty space and model performance function.

We represent the difficulty of a benchmark item, e.g., a question, by a continuous variable $z\in[0,1]$ , where larger values correspond to harder items. For a model $\theta$ , let $s_{\theta}(z)\in[0,1]$ denote its conditional expected performance on items with difficulty $z$ , e.g., pass@1.

## Benchmark distribution and score.

Let a benchmark $B=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ consist of $n$ items, and let
 $z_{i}\in[0,1]$ denote the difficulty of item $x_{i}$ . The benchmark score is $S_{B}(\theta):=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}s_{\theta}(z_{i})$ . This average implicitly induces an empirical measure over the difficulty axis,

 $\nu_{B}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta_{z_{i}},$ 

where $\delta_{z}$ denotes a point mass at difficulty $z$ . Under this representation, the benchmark score is exactly an integral with respect to the benchmark-induced difficulty measure, $S_{B}(\theta)=\int s_{\theta}(z)\,d\nu_{B}(z)$ .

## Performance difference between two models.

For two models $\theta$ and $\theta^{\prime}$ , define the difficulty-conditioned performance difference as $\Delta(z):=s_{\theta^{\prime}}(z)-s_{\theta}(z)$ , where the dependence of $\Delta$ on $(\theta^{\prime},\theta)$ is omitted for notational simplicity. The performance difference observed on benchmark $B$ is

 $D_{B}(\theta^{\prime},\theta):=S_{B}(\theta^{\prime})-S_{B}(\theta)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Delta(z_{i})=\int\Delta(z)\,d\nu_{B}(z).$ 

## 2.1 Measure Mismatch

## Benchmark-induced coupling.

The quantity $D_{B}(\theta^{\prime},\theta)$ implicitly couples two distinct objects: the model-dependent function $\Delta(z)$ and the benchmark-dependent measure $\nu_{B}$ . Thus, a leaderboard comparison is not merely determined by the difficulty-conditioned performance difference between the models; it also depends on how the benchmark allocates mass over the difficulty axis. If this allocation differs from the difficulty distribution of interest, the benchmark aggregates the same model difference under a mismatched measure. This mismatch can distort the observed model gap and, in severe cases, change the induced ordering.

## Target distribution.

Formally, we introduce a target distribution
 $\mu\in\mathcal{P}([0,1]),$ 
which represents the intended evaluation distribution over the difficulty space. This target distribution may encode the desired application mix. Under $\mu$ , the target score of model $\theta$ and the target performance difference between $\theta^{\prime}$ and $\theta$ are defined as

 $S_{\mu}(\theta):=\int s_{\theta}(z)\,d\mu(z),\hskip 20.00003ptD_{\mu}(\theta^{\prime},\theta):=S_{\mu}(\theta^{\prime})-S_{\mu}(\theta)=\int\Delta(z)\,d\mu(z).$ 

The discrepancy between $D_{B}(\theta^{\prime},\theta)$ and $D_{\mu}(\theta^{\prime},\theta)$ arises from the mismatch between the benchmark measure $\nu_{B}$ and the target distribution $\mu$ . This viewpoint allows us to study distortions in leaderboard comparisons as a distribution mismatch problem.

## A metric for distribution mismatch.

We measure how well the difficulty distribution of a benchmark matches a target difficulty distribution using the 1-Wasserstein distance. Specifically, for a benchmark $B$ with empirical difficulty measure $\nu_{B}$ and a target distribution $\mu$ on $[0,1]$ , we define its Difficulty Distribution Mismatch (DDM) as

 $\mathrm{DDM}(B;\mu):=W_{1}(\nu_{B},\mu)=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\nu_{B},\mu)}\int_{[0,1]^{2}}|u-v|\,d\pi(u,v),$ 

where $\Pi(\nu_{B},\mu)$ denotes the set of all couplings of $\nu_{B}$ and $\mu$ . Intuitively, $W_{1}(\nu_{B},\mu)$ measures how much probability mass must be transported, and how far, to transform the benchmark difficulty distribution into the target one. The following theorem shows that this mismatch directly controls the distortion between benchmark-based and target-based performance differences.

Theorem 2.1 (Distribution mismatch controls score distortion and rank stability).

Suppose the performance difference function $\Delta$ is $L$ -Lipschitz. Then

 $\bigl|D_{B}(\theta^{\prime},\theta)-D_{\mu}(\theta^{\prime},\theta)\bigr|\leq L\,W_{1}(\nu_{B},\mu).$ 

Consequently, if $|D_{\mu}(\theta^{\prime},\theta)|>L\,W_{1}(\nu_{B},\mu)$ , then

 $\operatorname{sign}\bigl(D_{B}(\theta^{\prime},\theta)\bigr)=\operatorname{sign}\bigl(D_{\mu}(\theta^{\prime},\theta)\bigr),$ 

so the benchmark-induced ordering agrees with the target ordering, i.e., no rank flip can occur.

Theorem 2.1 shows that $W_{1}(\nu_{B},\mu)$ bounds how much the benchmark-induced score difference can differ from the target score difference. A small $W_{1}(\nu_{B},\mu)$ means that the benchmark provides a faithful approximation to the target evaluation, while a large $W_{1}(\nu_{B},\mu)$ indicates that the benchmark may overemphasize some difficulty regions and underrepresent others, potentially distorting model comparisons and even changing their induced ranking. App. B.1 provides the full proof and extends this result to the finite-sample setting.

## A principled target distribution without prior information.

When prior information is available, it is natural to choose $\mu$ to reflect the intended evaluation objective over the difficulty space. In many settings, however, such prior knowledge is unavailable. In that case, choosing a non-uniform target would implicitly privilege some difficulty regions over others without evidence. To characterize a principled default choice, we consider an agnostic setting in which the location of the performance difference along the difficulty axis is completely unknown. We consider the class

 $\mathcal{F}_{\rho}:=\left\{\Delta:[0,1]\to[-1,1]\ \text{measurable}:\int_{0}^{1}\Delta(z)\,dz=\rho\right\},\hskip 20.00003pt\rho\in(-1,1).$ 

This class encodes an uncertainty set: the signed performance difference has a fixed average level $\rho$ over the difficulty axis, but its location is otherwise unrestricted.

For any candidate target distribution $\mu\in\mathcal{P}([0,1])$ , define its worst-case retained difference by

 $V_{\rho}(\mu):=\inf_{\Delta\in\mathcal{F}_{\rho}}\int\Delta(z)\,d\mu(z).$ 

The following theorem shows that, under complete uncertainty about where along the difficulty axis the performance difference occurs, the uniform distribution is the unique maximin target, and is the only choice whose worst-case retained difference remains equal to the average difference $\rho$ .

Theorem 2.2 (Uniform target as the unique maximin choice).

For $\rho\in(-1,1)$ , we have

 $\sup_{\mu\in\mathcal{P}([0,1])}V_{\rho}(\mu)=\rho,$ 

and the unique maximizer is the uniform distribution $\lambda=\mathrm{Unif}[0,1]$ .

Theorem 2.2 does not claim that the uniform distribution is universally optimal. Rather, it justifies the uniform target as a principled default when no prior information over the difficulty space is available. In that case, adopting the uniform target avoids introducing an additional preference over difficulty regions and provides a neutrality criterion for benchmark evaluation: the evaluation does not privilege any difficulty region a priori. Full proof is provided in App. B.1.

## 2.2 Coverage Gaps

## Discrete benchmark measures may fail to monitor local training improvements.

Benchmarks are often used not only for final model comparison, but also to monitor training progress (He et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025). However, training improvements are often local rather than uniform: a model may improve substantially over a particular difficulty range while improving only modestly elsewhere.

Recall that a benchmark score is an integral with respect to the benchmark empirical measure $\nu_{B}$ . Since $\nu_{B}$ is a discrete measure supported only on the finitely many benchmark difficulty points, it assigns zero mass to every interval that contains no benchmark item. Consequently, even if the model improves substantially on a nontrivial contiguous difficulty region, the benchmark score may not reflect this improvement when the region contains no benchmark item. In this sense, a benchmark can fail as a progress monitor when its local resolution is insufficient.

## Maximum gap.

We first characterize the local resolution of a benchmark through its maximum gap. Let $0\leq z_{(1)}\leq\cdots\leq z_{(n)}\leq 1$ be the ordered benchmark difficulty points, and define $z_{(0)}:=0$ and $z_{(n+1)}:=1$ . The maximum gap of benchmark $B$ is

 $G(B):=\max_{0\leq j\leq n}\bigl(z_{(j+1)}-z_{(j)}\bigr)$ 

(1)

i.e., the length of the largest interval on the difficulty axis that contains no benchmark point.

## A hypothesis testing formulation.

To formalize whether a benchmark can reliably detect localized training improvements, we cast the problem as a hypothesis test. Under the null hypothesis, there is no improvement. Under the alternative, the post-improvement performance exceeds the pre-improvement performance by at least $a$ over some contiguous difficulty interval of width $w$ . The following theorem shows that the benchmark maximum gap $G(B)$ is the exact asymptotic minimax detection boundary.

Theorem 2.3 (Maximum gap as an exact asymptotic minimax detection boundary).

Fix a test level $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and $a\in(0,1]$ . Let $s^{-},s^{+}:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ denote the pre- and post-improvement performance curves, respectively. For a benchmark $B$ , let $\Pi_{\alpha}^{*}(B;w,a,k)$ denote the minimax worst-case power of level- $\alpha$ tests based on $k$ repeated samples per benchmark item for testing

 $H_{0}:\ s^{-}=s^{+}\hskip 20.00003pt\text{versus}\hskip 20.00003ptH_{1}:\ \exists\ \text{interval }I\subset[0,1],\ |I|=w,\ s^{+}(z)-s^{-}(z)\geq a\ \ \forall z\in I.$ 

1. 

If $w\leq G(B)$ , then $\Pi_{\alpha}^{*}(B;w,a,k)=\alpha$ for every $k\in\mathbb{N}$ .

2. 

If $w>G(B)$ , then $\lim_{k\to\infty}\Pi_{\alpha}^{*}(B;w,a,k)=1$ .

Therefore, $G(B)$ exactly characterizes the asymptotic minimax detection boundary for benchmark $B$ .

Theorem 2.3 shows that the discrete geometry of the benchmark induces a sharp detectability phase transition. If the width of a local improvement does not exceed the maximum adjacent difficulty gap, then no level- $\alpha$ test can achieve nontrivial worst-case power, regardless of how many repeated evaluations are performed. In other words, such an improvement can be completely invisible to the benchmark in the worst case. Once the improvement width exceeds the maximum gap, repeated evaluation can eventually make the signal detectable. In this sense, $G(B)$ characterizes the intrinsic local resolution limit of benchmark $B$ .
The full proof is given in App. B.2.

## 3 Empirical Diagnosis of Current Benchmarks

We believe this empirical-measure view has the potential to open new ways to rigorously study and rethink benchmark evaluation.
